items.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
paragraphs: Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.
Community drop-in sessions about the vision, external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.
Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

items.title: Firms help migrants pose as artists and tech experts for 'Global Talent' visas, BBC finds
paragraphs: Things would be made to look like our undercover reporter had been an artist for some time, said Peter (pictured)
ByBilly Kenberpolitics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemppolitics reporter
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.
The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.
Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.
We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.
No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.
In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.
A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.
"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.
Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.
The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.
A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".
They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.
Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.
Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media
During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:
At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying
The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application
For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.
The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.
A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."
An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".
Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".
The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.
About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.
The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.
Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".
We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent
Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.
"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.
Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.
Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.
During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.
Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.
The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.
It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.
Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.
This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.
Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.
The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.
The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.
The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal
During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.
The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.
"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."
He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".
When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.
"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".
"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."
The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".
Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.
The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.
The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".
It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.
Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.
"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."
Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write
Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.
Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.
The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.
Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

items.title: Children’s exposure to home wood-burning could be as significant as traffic exhaust, study suggests
paragraphs: Children’s exposure to home wood-burning could be as significant as exposure to traffic exhaust, suggests new research across six European towns and cities.

Scientists measured the air in buildings where children spend much of their time; in schools, sports centres and homes. Specifically, they looked at polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH), a family of pollutants that are given off when fuels are burned.

Dr Barend van Drooge, from Barcelona’s Institute for Environmental Assessment and Water Research (IEAWR) and senior author of the study, said: “Some of these compounds are related to cancers after prolonged exposures, as recognised by the International Agency for Cancer Research, and evidence exists that they delay cognitive development.”
Measurements were made in and around Athens, Barcelona, Colchester, Copenhagen, Helsinki and Lisbon.
Van Drooge continued: “Urban areas with wood-burning, such as Colchester and Athens, had the highest PAHs levels. Barcelona and Lisbon, where wood-burning is not practised, had the lowest levels.”
In Colchester and Athens, PAH exposure was greater than the World Health Organization guidelines.

Maria Antonia Aretaki, of the IEAWR in Barcelona and first author of the study, said: “Understanding the pollutants in children’s everyday surroundings is an important step towards protecting their health. Children are particularly important given their vulnerability to environmental pollutants and the potential health implications from exposure during childhood.”

Sports centres had the lowest concentrations. This was followed by schools, through some, especially those in Lisbon, were affected by nearby busy roads. Ventilation and indoor sources were important, but the homes with some of the greatest PAH were in areas with wood-burning, and many had open fireplaces and stoves.
Winter PAH concentrations were greater than summer.

The researchers divided the PAH into two types, according to molecular weight. In the Colchester homes, the high-molecular-weight PAH in winter were more than 10 times those in summer. The low-molecular-weight PAH were around three times greater.

Van Drooge continued: “Wood-burning is known to be an important emitter of PAH, but it was surprising that it has become such an important contributor to the overall presence of PAHs in urban areas. However, none of the cities exceeded unacceptable limits for lifetime cancer risk.”

Within the UK, the impacts of wood-burning are unlikely to unique to Colchester. Separate analysis of energy performance certificates by researchers at University College London showed that Colchester ranked 120th out of 333 local councils for density of wood burners per square kilometre. Worthing, Norwich and Reading all had around four times more.

A wintertime study of 53 children from two primary schools in Anglesey (Ynys Môn) found that children living in homes with wood burners could be exposed to over three times more particle pollution than those in non-wood-burning homes. The Anglesey study also found that homes had more air pollution than schools.

In Greece, wood-burning increased during the financial crisis that began in 2008. The cost of heating oil soared and many people turned to wood heating. This contributed to increased deaths associated with particle pollution in Athens, especially for those aged over 70. In some Greek towns, wood-burning leads to PAH that are 100 times greater in winter compared with summer.

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 1
paragraphs: One million people come to see Pope Leo at night in Argentina. The Pope talks to many young people. He asks them to be kind. He tells them not to worry only about money, online popularity, or good looks.

Many happy people wave their phones and bring their babies for a blessing. The pope is visiting three countries in South America to talk about God and help poor people. He also asks the country’s leader to help people who do not have much money.
Many young people are very happy to see the pope and listen to his words.
Difficult words: popularity (when many people like someone), wave (to move your hand when you are saying hello to someone), blessing (a time when people ask for God’s help).

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 2
paragraphs: Pope Leo spoke to a crowd of one million people during a night event in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He told young people not to focus only on money, physical appearance, or getting likes on social media.

This gathering was part of his 12-day trip through South America, which also includes visits to Uruguay and Peru. Large crowds came to see the pope, including 2.5 million people at a historic Mass earlier in the week.

Pope Leo is visiting Argentina to support Catholic followers and help poor communities. During his trip, he also asked Argentina’s president not to hurt poor people with government spending cuts. Many residents and students thanked the pope for caring about people in need.

Difficult words: physical appearance (the external, visible features of a person), gathering (when many people meet together for a specific event), cut (reduction made to financial spending, resources, or services).

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 3
paragraphs: Pope Leo drew a crowd of one million people at a nighttime vigil in Buenos Aires on Tuesday during his 12-day South American tour.

The pontiff addressed the gathered youth, urged them not to be consumed by the pursuit of wealth, physical appearance, or social media popularity, and warned against humiliating others online. This event followed an outdoor Mass in Cordoba earlier that day, which attracted 650,000 attendees, and a record-breaking gathering of 2.5 million people in Buenos Aires on Monday.

As the first pope to visit Catholic-majority Argentina since 1987, Leo seeks to revitalize the Church’s presence in the region against growing evangelical competition. Throughout his visit, the US-born pope has also voiced strong criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei’s strict austerity policies. He argued that government spending cuts disproportionately harm the country’s poorest citizens.

Difficult words: pontiff (the Pope, who acts as the chief bishop and leader of the Roman Catholic Church), pursuit (chasing or striving to achieve something), austerity (severity in government spending cutbacks and financial discipline).

items.title: ‘If I wanted to plan a murder’: Beau Lamarre-Condon tells court what he would have done
paragraphs: Beau Lamarre-Condon has told a Sydney court he never planned to murder anybody and if he did, he reiterated he would use stolen vehicles and a gun not linked to him.
But the prosecutor responded: “No one’s saying it was a good plan, that’s why you’re sitting here.”
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sat in the witness box for the seventh day, Lamarre-Condon was asked about driving his mother to pick up a hire car under her name on the evening before the alleged murders.
As part of his cross-examination, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC repeatedly suggested to Lamarre-Condon that he was planning to murder Baird.
But the accused told the New South Wales supreme court on Friday: “It was never a plan to murder anybody.”
“You wouldn’t bring a vehicle linked to your mum for a murder,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.
“If I wanted to a plan a murder, I would have two stolen vehicles ready to go; I would have a gun that’s not linked to me. I know exactly how to do it. I work with youth gangs.”
Hatfield told Lamarre-Condon: “No one’s saying it was a good plan, that’s why you’re sitting here, isn’t it?”

The former officer maintained he and his mother spoke in the car about his suicidal ideation, and he had turned off his phone because he did not want to talk about work or personal things in the vicinity of the device.
On Friday afternoon, Hatfield began questioning Lamarre-Condon about the disposal of the bodies and the clean up of the alleged scene of the crime.
He suggested to the accused that he began going through Baird’s phone on the afternoon of the shootings and using it to send messages.
“This is where there’s lots of times where there were blackouts,” Lamarre-Condon told the court.
He agreed the messages were sent by him but could not give an accurate recollection of what he did.
A day later, he met up with a friend at a Sushi Train restaurant, where they spoke about disposing the bodies, Lamarre-Condon told the court.
The other man was young and was hoping to become a police officer, the jury heard.
Lamarre-Condon claims the friend suggested sinking the bodies with concrete, which was questioned by Hatfield.
“You’re taking advice from this young, immature guy about what do to with the bodies … is that seriously your evidence?” the prosecutor asked.
“You won’t take responsibility for the decision of how you treated the bodies, you want to blame [your friends].”
Lamarre-Condon responded: “He gave me the suggestion, I’m not saying he put all the ideas in my head.”
The prosecutor said it was “quite an extreme thing to be taking two men’s bodies and treat them the way you did” and the former police officer agreed his conduct was “not OK”.
But Hatfield replied: “I didn’t ask whether it’s OK. It’s beyond argument it’s not right.”
“It’s extraordinary conduct that was inconsistent with manslaughter and inconsistent with any accidental killing,” he told the court.
Lamarre-Condon admitted that on the night of 20 February 2024, he activated Baird’s phone near the Paddington home and began responding to the dead man’s notifications and sending messages.
The crown prosecutor suggested he was thinking about how the evidence from his phone would look and was “thinking strategically”.
Lamarre-Condon said it was “common sense”.
Hatfield asked: “Common sense when you’re carrying out a murder, is that right?”
The accused responded: “I didn’t carry out murder; I’m guilty of manslaughter.”
Earlier on Friday, Lamarre-Condon was asked about buying a sim card under the name “Bob Ballard” on 15 January 2024, about a month before the shootings.
He told the jury in his double murder trial it had “nothing to do with Jesse Baird”.
He was attempting to compile statements about “bullying from a certain sergeant” but was worried about speaking publicly on the issue, Lamarre-Condon said.
“I was wanting to go and compile all these statements and go to the media,” he said.
“I didn’t want to communicate at all from my phone because you can become a target … there would be repercussions.”
Under cross-examination by Hatfield, Lamarre-Condon agreed he was using the new sim card to contact former and current officers.

But asked why his phone records showed he only contacted one police officer on this sim, Lamarre-Condon said it only revealed his normal phone calls, telling the court: “You can’t see what I did on Signal.”

The prosecutor said he could have used the encrypted messaging app Signal on his normal phone, but Lamarre-Condon claimed police could make him unlock his own device and view his Signal records if he was investigated for talking to the media.
Hatfield also questioned why Lamarre-Condon had Davies’s contact details on his phone.
The former officer claimed Davies’s details were on his Instagram.
“I went and blocked numerous Instagram [accounts] from my own Instagram because of this incident,” he said, referring to the shootings.
“I even blocked Jesse’s family members from my account. I didn’t want any of that.”
He deactivated his social media accounts soon after.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

items.title: More than 60% of Germany’s female soldiers report harassment or abuse
paragraphs: Germany’s defence minister has promised a “zero tolerance” approach to sexual abuse in the armed forces after a study found soldiers, particularly women, faced extensive harassment within the ranks.

The first comprehensive study of its kind into the Bundeswehr, conducted by the Centre for Military History and Social Sciences in Potsdam and released this week, comes as the military is trying to attract new recruits in response to global threats.

It found that more than 60% of female soldiers had reported experiencing some form of sexual harassment or abuse while on duty, ranging from sexually explicit remarks and degrading rituals to sexual violence.

Nearly 40% of the 4,000 women who responded to the survey said they had been addressed with suggestive comments and sexualised remarks, while 15% reported being harassed with mobile phone pictures taken against their will and in some cases altered using AI.
Just over 8% reported having been physically attacked, and 2% said they had been the victims of sexual violence.
Around 19% of male ‌soldiers had experienced a similar form of sexual misconduct, with non-binary or gay soldiers disproportionately affected, the study found.

Boris Pistorius, the defence minister, said the figures were “unacceptable”, in particular for a military that is trying to considerably increase its numbers. The Bundeswehr has pumped billions into boosting both personnel and equipment. Military bosses have set a target of 260,000 active-duty troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035, in the hope of avoiding the introduction of conscription.

Pistorius said he was struck by the finding that women in units with a higher proportion of other women were less frequently affected, which he said “argues in favour of recruiting more women into the Bundeswehr”.

He said he had been advised by some colleagues to ditch the study, over fears it would sully the reputation of the military. To do so, he said, would be akin to “turning a blind eye”, which in the long term would do more damage to the Bundeswehr. The study would be repeated every year, he added.
“Zero tolerance applies to sexual harassment within the Bundeswehr,” the minister said.

Pistorius expressed concern over a high level of reluctance to report incidents. About a third of those surveyed said they did not or would not report incidents because of a lack of trust in what their superiors would do.
Before the study results were made public, Pistorius set up a hotline this month, meant to serve military personnel, which is to be staffed around the clock, and is called HELP.

In future, Pistorius said, those who made complaints should receive more information about the status of their proceedings, after victims said they were often left in the dark, but expected to continue serving.

The ministry said that, of 45,000 active or former members of the armed forces contacted to participate in the survey, 18% responded. It said its analysis showed that the figures were nevertheless representative.

items.title: Minister’s office said contractor should handle CFMEU or lose work in Victoria, Big Build inquiry hears
paragraphs: A major contractor on a troubled Victorian rail project shut down by union officials was warned that the minister’s office felt it would not “have any more work” in the state if it did not resolve the industrial dispute, a royal commission has heard.

The royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria heard from a Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (Vida) official for the first time on Friday.
Vida was strongly criticised by counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, on Thursday for its failure to disclose relevant evidence in a timely manner to the investigation.
The commission’s November public hearings, which are set to run until 20 November, are focusing on a 2022 level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury.

The commission previously heard that Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) officials shut down the site because of purported safety concerns, only for them to allow it to continue after two of their own health and safety representatives were appointed, and the project changed its traffic and labour hire companies to CFMEU-aligned firms.

Peter Wilkinson, a former Vida official who is now the executive general manager of the Suburban Rail Loop authority and a civil engineer, said that at the height of an industrial dispute at Gap Road he spoke about the need for work to resume on the project with Evan Tattersall, his manager at Vida.

He said Tattersall told him on either 6 or 7 June 2022 that he had discussed the issue with the minister’s office, and Wilkinson assumed that meant the office of the then-minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan.
Tattersall told him, Wilkinson said, “that if they can’t handle the industrial [relations] in Victoria, they can’t have any more work”.
Tattersall was referring to the contractors on the site, John Holland and CPB Constructions, Wilkinson said.

Wilkinson said he was aware at the time that the contractors were tendering for the airport rail, another major state government funded infrastructure project, but that he did not know if the minister’s office also knew this.

Wilkinson said Tattersall did not tell him what he should do with the information from the minister’s office, but he passed it on to Joe Aygur, the general manager of the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project’s delivery.
Aygur told the commission about the warning on Tuesday.

When asked by Young why no record of his conversation with Tattersall existed, Wilkinson said “probably one reason is that it was moving very quickly, so it was conversation that we had to keep it moving, rather than there being a need to formally record it.”
Wilkinson was also asked about a meeting scheduled in Allan’s parliament house office for 5pm on 7 June 2022 – the day work recommenced at Gap Road.
He was listed as an optional attendee on an online invite for the meeting, but said he could not recall if he attended.

The commission also heard on Friday from Stephen Villella, who worked for CPD Constructions and was the delivery director at the site, about the meeting at the union headquarters that ultimately ended the dispute.
He said it had been “extremely galling” for construction company officials to have to “bend the knee” by meeting with the CFMEU to resolve the matter.
Villella said none of the safety concerns raised by the union were serious enough to force work to stop at the site.
Workers on the project were fearful of the CFMEU and would stay in the lunchroom for long periods once they started to attend.
“They didn’t want to come [to work] at all,” Villella said.
“They were fearful of what would happen to them organisationally and individually if they did.”

Villella said he disagreed with evidence given early in the week by a former CFMEU organiser Paul Tzimas about those on site choosing not to work, saying they were heavily pressured by union officials.
Villella said that in the meeting with the CFMEU, a union organiser Joe Myles suggested collaborating would assist in winning future tenders such as the Melbourne airport rail project.
He said Myles also suggested he had direct lines to Allan’s office.
Villella said he was not surprised by Myles’ claim about having communication to the ministers office, as he had seen what had happened to the industry over the past 10 years.
Villella said Myles left abruptly in the first half of the about 30 minute meeting, which he said felt like a snub.
But he rejected a suggestion by counsel for Myles that it was not the union official, but rather Tzimas, who raised the list of union demands for the Gap Road project.
After construction managers agreed to the demands, work on the site resumed as normal.
“Amazingly, all our safety issues ceased,” Villella said.

Chris Carr SC, senior counsel assisting the commission, said that after the rebuke issued by Young on Thursday to Vida, he was “happy to report there has been substantial production of highly relevant material overnight”.
He said that production had led to several lines of inquiry, which meant the commission was unlikely to hear from witnesses again until Tuesday.

items.title: ‘Looks like we’ll have to talk to people’: Australia sent back to time before email with major Microsoft outage
paragraphs: Australian schools, courts and government services have been hurled back in time to how business used to be done after a global Microsoft outage caused emails and online meetings to go dark.

Australians began reporting issues with Microsoft 365 – which includes Outlook and Teams – just before 5am AEST on Friday, according to Down Detector. The problem appeared to peak at 9.22am with more than 5,500 reports of problems, including trouble opening and sending emails, before reports began to dip.

A Microsoft spokesperson said the company “had no indication of a cyber-attack” and suggested the issue could be related to a configuration change to its servers that was causing some to become overloaded and taken offline.
In an update to its website on Friday afternoon, the company said efforts to fix the issue were not “taking as expected”.

Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres. The agency put in place a priority callback system for those unable to complete urgent transactions during the outage.

“Some transactions in Service Centres and Call Centres are unavailable at this time,” it said. “Customers are encouraged to delay their visit to a Service Centre and to complete transactions online, where possible.”

Earlier in the morning, the federal home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appeared at a press conference with the Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, and the Asio director general, Mike Burgess. Both said their systems had been affected by the outage, but they provided no further details.
Burgess said the spy agency’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The Australian Medical Association (AMA) said it had received reports that some hospitals and health clinics were experiencing clerical issues, but there had been no impacts to patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” the AMA president, Dr Michael Bonning, said.
“We don’t use any of these things for direct patient care. It’s always the authorisation in systems, so we’ve always got workarounds for that.”
Schoolbytes, a cloud-based administration platform used by schools in NSW, was “temporarily” unable to access emails due to the outage.

A text sent to a parent regarding the platforms outage said: “If you emailed the school after 3.15pm yesterday, or need to communicate with us regarding absences or changes to routines please call the office …”
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage was affecting its email system. Victoria’s county court said its scheduled hearings were expected to go ahead as planned.
On social media, people shared how the outage was affecting their workday.
One Brisbane-based person posted on LinkedIn: “It’s all SMS and phone calls today … looks like we will have to talk to people while Microsoft sort out their email issues!”
On Reddit, some users reported that while Outlook emails were down they could still access Microsoft’s workplace messaging platform, Teams.
“They could have taken Teams out with them so I’d be able to … just sit here and do absolutely nothing,” one Reddit user wrote.

Some services remained unaffected by the outage. The two major supermarkets – Coles and Woolworths – were operating as normal inside their stores. However, Coles said its internal email system has been affected.
The National Broadband Network said it was monitoring the outage, but remained unaffected.

The National Cyber Security Coordinator warned cybercriminals often seek to take advantage of the “uncertainty around these types of disruptions” with scam emails, texts, calls or social media messages.

“I encourage every Australian to remain vigilant and be cautious of unsolicited contact. Do not click on unexpected links, open attachments, or provide personal information. If you’re unsure, hang up and call back,” the coordinator wrote on social media.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University, said the outage appeared to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue which brought down Optus’s network in 2023.
He said when some of the servers have configuration issues, it means customers are forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.
“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down.
“And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem: in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”

items.title: The Papers: 'Nvidia chief quits' and 'Six women say they too were preyed on by Brand'
paragraphs: Nvidia features prominently on many of Friday's front pages. The Financial Times describes what it calls the "spectacular fall" of Jensen Huang, who it says was allowed to mould much of the White House's policy on artificial intelligence. One major shareholder in the firm tells the paper the fallout will be "painful".
The i Paper says there is now a succession battle under way at Nvidia, and that Huang's departure "could disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped to shape".

The Guardian describes Huang as someone who rose from "washing dishes at a restaurant to a billionaire rockstar of the artificial intelligence boom". It says the current crisis enveloping him, and the company he ran, is "a lesson in humility that investors were not expecting Huang to receive decades on" from his job in the kitchen.

The Times sets out the stories of six more women who have accused Russell Brand of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour. The comedian was jailed for more than 10 years on Monday for rape and sexual assault. The paper says his lawyers did not respond to the latest allegations.
The Sun claims that Brand is being assessed for a transfer from Wandsworth Prison to the high security jail at Wakefield, which houses many sex offenders.

The Daily Telegraph says the Labour Party grandee Lord Blunkett wants ministers to slash their own budgets to pay for the welfare reform which is expected to result from Alan Milburn's review of youth unemployment. Writing in the paper, the former home secretary urges his colleagues to provide the government with "sufficient resource to kickstart this important work".

The Daily Mail says "eagle-eyed observers" have spotted similarities between Prince George's drawing of a kingfisher - which features in this month's Country Life - and a YouTube tutorial uploaded in 2019. The paper has spoken to the artist, Matt Fussell, whose sketch is of the same bird, from the same angle, in the same colours. He says: "While I can't say for certain whether he used my lesson, the similarities are exciting... and he should be incredibly proud".

items.title: Cricket sandpaper scandal claims '100% wrong', Australia captain says
paragraphs: Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility.

But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong.
"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January.
Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales.
"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," said Cummins.
"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others - and, I think, Australian cricket.
"I support him to tell his story, 100%, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."
In a media conference he arranged himself, Cummins began by promising to answer all questions because, he said: "I don't want to talk about this again after today."
At times emotional, Cummins addressed a wide range of topics, including:
Advice that some of Khawaja's claims are defamatory, but he will not take legal action
He had been in contact with Khawaja and Smith since the book was published, but not Warner
His belief that the one-year bans handed to Smith and Warner, and a nine-month suspension to Bancroft were "heavy handed"
He had no recollection of Australia tampering with the ball in the 2017-18 Ashes series against England
He had met with Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, who has reviewed the files from the original investigation
Explaining why sandpaper would have been present in the dressing room and that it was sometimes used by bowlers in training in order to practise with a reverse-swinging ball
Khawaja's allegations have reopened the debate about the sandpaper plot, the investigation into the cheating, the culture of Australian cricket and the reputations of those involved.
The story has dominated the media in Australia and caused headlines around the cricketing world.
Khawaja has been supported by Warner and Chadd Sayers, a seam bowler who was part of the Australia squad on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

However, his allegations have been rejected by Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach and former England batter Graeme Hick, one of Lehmann's assistants. Mitchell Starc, another bowler on the tour, has also denied Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has put a spotlight on Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon. The four were Australia's attack in Cape Town and remain their first-choice bowlers eight years later.
The quartet have always denied any knowledge of the plot, including in the release of a joint-statement in 2021.
In his book - Sabr - Khawaja alleged Australia were urged to find ways of getting the ball to swing by a coach, while Bancroft was later encouraged to cheat.
Khawaja also said he asked for the entire team to take responsibility for the controversy in Cape Town, but his request was rejected by two unnamed players.
Cummins said he does not recall any suggestion that the team should have shared the responsibility, or that it was rejected.

On the idea that the whole team were aligned in a plot to tamper with the ball, he said: "There was no masterplan around using illegal methods. People assume you've gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge masterplan.
"That is not the case. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen."
"There's big leaps where Usman is being vague."
In his book, Khawaja detailed how he was not interviewed as part of the investigation despite sitting next to Bancroft in the changing rooms during the Test at Newlands.
Both Khawaja and Warner have criticised the investigation, which Greenberg has said he will not reopen.

Cummins confirmed he has met with Greenberg and, although the captain said he did not want to break a "confidence", that Greenberg has reviewed the sandpaper files since the release of Khawaja's book and found the accounts in the investigation to be "consistent".

Cummins has played 77 Tests for Australia and has been captain sine 2021. He said he has seen only one instance of ball-tampering in his career, during a domestic Sheffield Shield match, when a player took a bottletop on to the field.
However, he did admit that balls can sometimes be altered during training sessions, if bowlers want to practise in a certain way, or batters want to face a ball of a particular condition.
Cummins said it was not unknown for training balls to be scuffed in such circumstances, using sandpaper or even a Stanley knife.

When it was put to Cummins that he, as a bowler, must have suspected that the Cape Town ball had been tampered with, the 33-year-old described that bowlers often touch a ball as little as possible, in order to keep it dry and in a state where it will reverse-swing.

At the time of the sandpaper scandal, Cummins was 24 and playing in his 13th Test. Asked about a potential culture of ball-tampering in that era, Cummins said he noticed things then that he now realises could have been cheating.
On why Khawaja has chosen to speak now, at the end of his career, rather than in the intervening eight years, Cummins said the episode could have "weighed heavy" on the left-hander.

Addressing the culture of the Australia team eight years ago, Cummins said: "I didn't like the way we spoke to umpires, the opposition. I think there was a bit of an arrogance and a bit of an ugliness at times that didn't sit well with me as a young guy.
"Now I'm captain, I have spent a lot of time making sure that that's not the case."

Speaking about Cummins' news conference on Fox Cricket, where he is working as an analyst for Australia's one-day series against England which got under way on Friday, Warner said: "I stick with Uzzie. It's the truth. The captain threw Uzzie under the bus.
"We've got to live with the consequence daily. I feel it was a botched investigation. To get it over and done with. This won't rest.
"I'm not going to accept [things] until the truth is out."
Khawaja's claims - in his book, in interviews and on social media - have re-opened old wounds in Australian cricket, drawing battlelines that have verged on civil war.
Over the past few days, constant questions have been asked of who knew what and if the truth has been covered up in the intervening eight years.
The most pressure has been on the bowlers who played for Australia in Cape Town, - none more so than Cummins, given his rise to the captaincy.
He has been urged to front up, to show leadership. In an indoor cricket centre in Sydney, Cummins did just that.

Others connected to the scandal who have faced the media in the past few days – Lehmann, Starc and Mitchell Marsh – have almost implicated themselves with vague responses to straight questions. Not Cummins.
The captain did not duck or dodge any of the subjects that were thrown at him by a huge throng of assembled journalists. He did so without any intervention from a media manager.
What was most striking was his criticism of Khawaja, once a team-mate and friend. In being so forceful of his rejection of what Khawaja has claimed, Cummins appeared to be a reliable witness.
The question is whether this will be enough to end the speculation. Khawaja is sure to have another say. So too Warner, who is yet to release a book of his own.
Cummins cannot prove a negative, so can use only his words when it comes to convincing the world he was not involved in the sandpaper plot.
On this occasion, Cummins was impressive. Still, when he says he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, that feels like wishful thinking.
Facing more than a dozen TV cameras, and a gaggle of reporters several times as large, Cummins answered questions for over an hour - determined to put so-called "sandpapergate" to rest.

He was patient and cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him, even at one point shooing away a minder from Cricket Australia who tried to wrap things up.

Cummins was careful in his criticism of Khawaja, despite needling questions from the media gathered, but he was also frank - using strong words to reject his claims and admitting he was annoyed Khawaja had put him in this position.
He spoke of a mix of amusement and uneasiness at the camera crews now parked outside his house.

He rejected media speculation that his captaincy could be under threat. He admitted he was struggling to reconcile his years-long friendship with Khawaja with the events of the past week: "That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days... friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations."

But gesturing to the Sheffield Shield match going on outside the batting nets, and referencing the ODI about to begin in Perth, he said he was also incredibly frustrated that the sandpapergate scandal is still a distraction for Australian cricket.
"It's been eight years. We're moving on. So ‌you have got to draw a line at some point."

items.title: Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
paragraphs: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., seen above on Aug. 8, 2026 in St. Paul, Minn., has announced he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate Majority Leader. Stephen Maturen/Getty Images hide caption

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate majority leader, pushing the party into a fresh debate over its future just days after sweeping victories in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen made the announcement on Thursday, saying voters sent a clear message in the midterms — that they want "change from the status quo."

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said in a statement. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

Van Hollen, 67, was elected to the Senate in 2016 after spending more than a decade in the House representing a Maryland suburb outside of Washington, D.C. One of his party's more progressive members, he gained national attention last year lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after he was wrongfully deported to a prison in El Salvador.

His announcement comes at a moment when progressive activists, as well as some Democratic lawmakers, are calling for Schumer, 75, to be replaced as party leader. Schumer has served in the role since 2017, but drew the ire of many inside the Democratic base for not taking a tougher stance against President Trump during a fight over government funding in early 2025.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer wrote on social media following Van Hollen's announcement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters at the Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption

While Schumer has maintained he has the votes to become majority leader, he has faced growing resistance from inside the Democratic caucus. Earlier this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont Independent who aligns with Democrats, said he would oppose Schumer. He made the announcement next to Michigan Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who did not say outright she would oppose Schumer, but told reporters, "I am seeking change."
Several incoming Democratic lawmakers have similarly expressed opposition to Schumer's bid for majority leader, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed.

"I deeply appreciate Senator Schumer," El-Sayed told NPR this week. "But this is about leadership for the American public, and if all we do is kind of go back to what we've been doing in a moment where we've been given a mandate, I worry that we may not earn our mandate."
Multiple Democrats have publicly come out in support of Schumer, including Arizona's Ruben Gallego, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks.

Democrats will vote by secret ballot for majority leader in early December. Whoever wins will preside over a majority of 55 seats, though that could grow to 56 depending on the final tally in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.

items.title: Chips, creek water and Take Me Home, Country Roads: how an Australian teenager survived six nights in the bush
paragraphs: A teenage boy who survived almost a week lost in dense Australian bushland sang John Denver’s Take Me Home, Country Roads as he held out hope of rescue on long nights alone in the wilderness.
William, whose surname has been withheld, was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend in Victoria’s east last Friday.

The 17-year-old was reported missing at about 4pm that day after failing to return from a trip to retrieve further camping equipment. He was wearing only shorts and work boots and had left his phone, food supplies and water behind.

After an extensive operation of more than 100 people, including the police dog and rescue squads, the police air wing found William on Thursday morning lying down in a creek near Walhalla, 130km east of Melbourne.
He lost his way after taking a wrong turn on a track, and later slipped and fell down a cliff.

He told Seven’s Sunrise program John Denver’s country classic, which repeats the line “take me home, to the place I belong”, was a childhood favourite of his that brought him solace as he braved harsh conditions and loneliness.

“It’s a good childhood song of mine. It brings me great comfort,” he said from his hospital bed in Traralgon on Friday morning. “I started doing it one night, made me feel OK, so I just kept doing it.”

William shared an emotional reunion with his mother, Elizabeth Barkley, soon after being rescued. She told reporters on Thursday between tears that she was “over the moon” and he was “never leaving the house again”.
William told Sunrise their warm embrace was the “best moment of my life”.
“I think she’s going to stand true with that comment,” he said with a laugh. “She’s giving me a firm look from across the room at the moment, so not expecting to go out any time soon.”
William said he was “doing great” after enjoying a “great sleep” in a “comfy bed” on Thursday night and “finally getting some food into me”.
“I’m over the moon to be safe,” he said. “The nights were pretty cold. I think a couple of times it was raining. Hot days, so I got a bit sunburnt, pretty treacherous surroundings.
“I honestly didn’t think I’d make it six days.”

After seeing the helicopter flying overhead, William, who was sheltering on a rock under towels and heavily sunburnt, gave a wave and fist-bump before being airlifted to safety. He said he was feeling “pure euphoria”.
“Just happiness and gratefulness that a moment that I thought might never happen, has happened, and I am finally going to see my mum again,” he said.
“There were a few times were I’m thinking ‘geez, it’s getting dark out here, I don’t know if they’re going to see me’.”
William got by on a packet of chicken-flavoured chips, which he rationed over several days. He said he also drank water from the creek that he was sheltering by.

“Last night I had dinner … and I had some Macca’s, which was good, so I got plenty of food in,” he said. “I’m super grateful for all the paramedics and nurses, search and rescue … everyone that was involved.”
Pilot Dave Wylie told reporters it had been an incredibly challenging search for crews and it was lucky William was sheltering in an open area.
“A lot of the areas are so thick that you can’t actually see the forest floor so even if someone was there, potentially you could fly right past them,” he said.
“If he wasn’t in the open area like he was, we absolutely could have flown right past him without seeing him.”

William was being transported to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for further observation and testing by specialists, after suffering from dehydration. He was in a stable condition on Friday afternoon.
Barkley told Nine’s A Current Affair she was in awe as to how well her son had handled days alone in the bush.
“I just couldn’t believe he survived that long,” she said. “But he’s a footballer. He’s tough, he’s very, very fit.
Barkley said William had missed a turn on a track and became lost on Friday and curled up under some bushes when it got dark.
“I had instinct … I knew he was still alive,” she said of the following days. “I knew in my heart … And I was just praying, and praying, and praying.”
