items.title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
paragraphs: Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.

"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

items.title: Is Outlook down? Widespread outage hits Microsoft email and other apps
paragraphs: A Microsoft logo and sign outside the Microsoft Visitor Center are seen at the company's headquarters Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. Lindsey Wasson/AP hide caption
A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.
Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft said it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.

In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas."

Microsoft explained that a portion of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load" — which it said was "likely contributing to the connectivity errors." The company determined a number of servers were "unexpectedly unavailable" due to a problem that caused them to fail during "automated health checks."

It was not immediately clear what exactly caused that failure. But Microsoft later said it was testing a fix and rolling out an alternative method for these checks to bring impacted servers back online.
"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.
Earlier in the day, the company said it had "successfully restored" problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

items.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
paragraphs: Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.
The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".
The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".
While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.
Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.
Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."
Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."
The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.
The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

items.title: Junior doctor burnout putting maternity patients at risk, says regulator
paragraphs: Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.
Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.
The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.
The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties
They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties
One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees
Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.
"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."
He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."
Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.
He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby.

"I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."
He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago.
"The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."
Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing.

"There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry.

"It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."
Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.
While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world.

"Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."
The main challenge, she says, are the sheer number of demands placed on a doctor in her field.

"It could be that there's two or three ladies whose babies need delivering, and then somebody else coming in on maternity triage whose baby isn't moving, and you might also be getting calls from A&E about a lady having a miscarriage who's bleeding really heavily.
"There's just one of you to manage all those jobs."
Broughton says while she has largely had positive experiences, it is important to step back and look at the wider culture.
"You do hear things from other hospitals about people feeling nervous about calling the consultant...which isn't great."
Dr Kat Barton, chair of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) National Trainee Committee, says workplace issues end up affecting patients.
"Many of us feel overstretched and close to burnout. This reflects staff shortages, working beyond our hours, and knowing that despite our best efforts, the care women receive is being affected.
"We know the safest care comes from teams that are well-supported, well-resourced, and listen to each other and to women and families.

"We need the government to invest in safe staffing at every level, protect our time for training, and support our wellbeing and careers, so we can give women the safe, compassionate care they deserve."
Recent high profile maternity reviews, which looked at outcomes for mothers and babies, also highlighted concerns about workplace culture, leadership and the ability of staff to raise concerns.

Obstetrics and gynaecology trainees were more positive than average about some aspects of patient safety reporting, the GMC survey indicated, including how to report patient safety incidents and near misses.

A DHSC spokesperson said: "In all the investigations carried out in recent years into failings in maternity services, one of the key lessons has been that members of staff must feel empowered to speak up if they have concerns about workload, or patient safety, and their concerns must be acted upon.

"All NHS trusts are now required to have a dedicated Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and internal pathways for staff to raise concerns about the working environment, patient safety, or their own wellbeing.

"Alongside this, we are continuing to grow and strengthen the workforce to help relieve the pressures on busy maternity units, and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year.

"Since coming into the role in July, the Secretary of State has made maternity services a personal priority, and the Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing is working to respond to the concerns raised by staff and families alike, and ensure that every maternity unit meets the highest standards of patient safety and care."

items.title: MI5 will need proof to be believed in future, says Leveson after BBC investigation
paragraphs: The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of MI5 has said it will now have to provide proof to be believed by judges, after a BBC News investigation exposed how the security service lied to three courts.
Lord Leveson, the investigatory powers commissioner and a former Court of Appeal justice, said that as a judge "if the security service said something to me, then I would accept it".
But he said courts would now be "far more reluctant to accept, without evidential proof, things that are said in the future".
Lord Leveson praised the impact of the BBC's investigation into an abusive MI5 agent, which he said had led to changes in how informants are managed.
He spoke to the BBC during the first annual conference of the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (Ipco).
The BBC's investigation had "hit the intelligence community hard", including security services around the world, he said.

The BBC investigation exposed how a neo-Nazi informant - known as Agent X - used his state role as a tool of abuse. He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. He had previously abused another woman and threatened to kill her child.
Despite all this, MI5 protected the agent and helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation, even removing his possessions from a police station.
In his first interview about the case, Lord Leveson said he stood ready to assist the police if asked.
He said that "MI5 have a great distance to go" with courts in the future.
He added the BBC investigation's reach "has been far greater than if this had never happened. So you can take some pride in that."
Lord Leveson said there was also a change in the way that agents, also known as covert human intelligence sources (CHIS), were managed.
Because of the Agent X case, there is a new policy relating to agents and domestic violence, and coercive control.
"There is no doubt that concern is now being focused not merely on the activity of the CHIS, but the impact of the CHIS on other aspects of his or her life.
"I think that everybody learns from disasters, and this for MI5 has been a very serious matter."
The Ipco chief executive, Richard Thompson, now attends meetings of an internal board in MI5, created to oversee changes because of the Agent X case, including changes in culture within the service.
In addition, MI5 must change the way it prepares and gives evidence, after the High Court case.
Lord Leveson said intelligence service chiefs from around the world had contacted him about the case.
They had expressed concern about whether something similar could happen in their organisations, he said.
The Agent X case had "done a great service to everybody", Lord Leveson said

The Ipco investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.

The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into Agent X, but won him legal anonymity. His ex-partner Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.
MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.
But what MI5 said was untrue. It had, in fact, disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.
That officer was found to have repeatedly lied by the IPCO investigation. He has resigned from MI5 since the BBC exposed what happened.

items.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
paragraphs: Rylan is confused when an interview with Timothée Chalamet goes awry

This year's BBC Children In Need show is taking place on Friday, with highlights including Timothee Chalamet pranking Rylan Clark, and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Oscar-nominated actor Chalamet and co-stars Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy will be seen making Rylan sweat during an interview for their new film Dune: Part Three, with the help of three children, hidden behind the scenes.
The show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, on a 400-mile cycle challenge through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales.
Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.
Alex Jones, Rylan Clark, Mel Giedroyc, Tyler West and Sara Cox are the hosts for the live show
The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.
Owain Wyn Evans has been on the 4 Nations Cycle Challenge
Wyn Evans is being joined on his final leg in Wales on Friday by 22-year-old Harri, who is living with hidden lasting effects of a brain tumour.
He is part of The One Show's "challenge squad" - four young people who have signed up for a series of personal missions for the charity.
Zoe has prepared for her dancing challenge with the help of Strictly pro Amy Dowden

The others are 16-year old Zoe, who has Down's syndrome, who will be seen dancing with the cast of High School Musical; Ana, also 16, who has a rare physical condition and is doing a three-day kayaking challenge; and 22-year-old Serena, who will perform live in memory of her late brother and a childhood friend.

The theme of this year's Children In Need is Challenge Yourself 2026, which has also seen Morning Live presenters Michelle Ackerley and Gethin Jones learn instruments to perform with a band live on the night.
Joe Wicks and Emma Bunton are among the other stars who have been involved, while landmarks including the Blackpool Tower, London Eye and Titanic Belfast will be lit in yellow for the occasion.
Children in Need supports more than 1,600 local charities and projects across the UK.
Children In Need is on BBC One and iPlayer from 19:00-22:00 GMT on Friday.

items.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
paragraphs: Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.
Hetton's principal, Vicky Pinkney, says low incomes shouldn't mean poor results

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.
What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?
From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.
Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.
Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.
Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.
"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry, external found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.
So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.
It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.
The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.
For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.
While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.
There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.
Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.
Pupils who feel they "belong" at school tend to perform better in their GCSEs, a government-commissioned study has found
And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.
It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".
But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.
Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.
The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.
The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)
That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.
The likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing GCSEs has barely changed in many years, says John Jerrim, an education professor at University College London

But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks.
"Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says.
She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive.
Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term.
Does the principal think other places could replicate its success?
Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically.
"I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve."

items.title: Donald Trump really wants Tim Cook to run Nvidia
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Jensen Huang resigned this morning as Nvidia’s CEO following reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Right now, the company is being led by its CFO on an interim basis. But President Donald Trump is already throwing around one person he thinks should take over the chipmaking giant: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who stepped down from leading the company on September 1st and moved into an executive chairman role.

Shortly after Huang’s resignation was announced today, Trump posted his idea about Cook on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

In a new episode of Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter podcast published today, Trump made his pitch for Cook again, saying that Apple “would never be what it is today” if Steve Jobs was still “around”:

Well, you know, the expression, Anybody can be replaced? So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released: Tim Cook. He just sort of semi-retired from Apple. He’s done one of the greatest jobs in the history of business.

I think if Tim Cook, who built Apple… If Steve Jobs were around, Apple would never be what it is today. Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world in a fairly short period. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia.

Apple and Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Cook is well-known for his ongoing relationship with President Trump, including gifting the president a 24k gold and glass statue last year. (Trump, after Cook announced his transition plan earlier this year, posted a story about having “the head of Apple calling to ‘kiss my ass.’”)
During the podcast, Trump said he spoke to Huang yesterday and that Huang is “going through hell”:
Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.
But I can tell you this. Somehow, he’ll end up on his feet. I mean, I know him, I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.

I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he is, really… that’s what he told me. I’m president, and he called me. And he said, What I’ve done to my wife and family is... That’s what he talked about.
Trump, on the podcast, called Huang a “tremendous talent.” Other tech leaders have also publicly supported Huang following his resignation.

items.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
paragraphs: Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist
The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.
It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.
The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.
The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.
Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.
Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026
Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.
But after three more gigs this weekend and one added one next, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.
She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.
"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.
"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."
She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.
"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.
"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

Next month she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".
"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.
"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zane were my favourites.
"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

items.title: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been in HMP Wandsworth for a week
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.
Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.
He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.
Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.
"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."
A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.
A member of staff at Wandsworth said there was "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.
"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.
Brand will have had his possessions confiscated when he arrived at HMP Wandsworth
Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing, and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who've been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. According to the charity, Prison Reform Trust, this is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop.
Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, inmates said.
"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain, if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC there are a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.
They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault from mixing with other inmates.
Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences he has been convicted of could make him a target among other inmates.
Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.
"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."
The South London jail is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.
"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." He said it took five weeks to see his young son.
It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.
At this stage nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.
The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

items.title: Ankle injuries are more common than you think - here's how to protect yours
paragraphs: Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles.
"A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front.
"It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over?
"Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them."
She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task.
She says different activities require different shoes.
"If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place.
"Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate."

For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree."

items.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
paragraphs: The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r)
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?
Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.
From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.
But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".
Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.
But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.
"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.
AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious
It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.
But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.
"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."
All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.
Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.
Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.
He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.
But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.
"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."
He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.
Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left
Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.
In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.
In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.
Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.
"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.
In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug

A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".
"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.
But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.
Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.
He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.
"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

items.title: Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
paragraphs: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed a new entry in the Wolfenstein series with a brief tease.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed a new entry in the Wolfenstein series with a brief tease.
is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.

In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.

The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

items.title: Whoop launched a social network where every user has a ‘verified heartbeat’
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app’s new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like “Moments” with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members’ posts.
Whoop claims its platform is “entirely human,” unlike other social media platforms that are “saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content.”

Whoop CEO Will Ahmed says Humans is “the most verifiably human network ever launched. Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat.” Whoop says its existing Teams social feature “will remain available,” allowing people to share strain, recovery, and sleep data along with group leaderboards.

In the Community tab in Whoop’s app, users can scroll through Moments from people they’re following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends’ fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop’s examples, swiping up on a user’s Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your “community” with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.

Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren’t shared by default. There’s also an option to keep Moments posts private and a “Stealth Mode” for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

items.title: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
paragraphs: Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, sending shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill.
Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future.
His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected those allegations as a smear.
And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on his alleged affair.
If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC.
Representatives of Nvidia have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
"Obviously, his behaviour has compounded over time," one long-time tech industry executive said, noting that other executives had been embroiled in revelations of infidelity.
Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.
Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans.
Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts.
Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market.

items.title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.
For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.
Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

items.title: Microsoft Outlook is still down
paragraphs: Microsoft 365 issues have been cutting people off from their email since early Thursday afternoon, and they still aren’t fixed.
Microsoft 365 issues have been cutting people off from their email since early Thursday afternoon, and they still aren’t fixed.
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft quickly acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”

There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but not to the same extent, while Microsoft’s official updates said customers may experience issues across its suite of 365 business services. Microsoft comms director Ben Hope said in a statement that “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online. We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.”

Several hours later, Microsoft has gone through several variations of update notes regarding the issues and its attempts to fix them, saying it’s had problems rebooting servers and being able to monitor their health. As of about 6PM ET, Microsoft has a note saying it’s managed to get some of the affected servers running:

We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.

We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results. As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service.
There’s still no ETA for full restoration, but we will continue to monitor this ongoing outage.
Update, 6:23PM ET: Added latest status update from Microsoft.

items.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
paragraphs: My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
The Casey Nelson tent show, featuring Happy Harry the double-jointed horse, circa the late 1940s

I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.

Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted in his kitchen with his cockatiel, Sweetie Pie

Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.

Clockwise from top left: Ted Trevor aged five; Cora Trevor Williams, Ted’s grandmother, performing an ‘iron-jaw’ act; Billy and Vera (left), who performed trapeze and iron-jaw acts, and Ted’s grandmother, Cora (right); Ted’s mother, Frances ‘Girly’ Foster, on stilts on Pitt Street, Sydney

Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.

“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
‘The reason they call it the old-time showman is because that’s exactly what it was. You had to be a showman to work with whatever you got’

Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”

Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Frances Foster with Slim Dusty at the Brisbane Exhibition in the early 1960s
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.

Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”

The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
Ted in his pool room, where all his favourite photographs are on display
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.

Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”

From left: Shayne Brophy, who was born and bred on the showgrounds, performing a trapeze act. She also did contortions, whip-cracking, wire-walking, and worked in the snake pit; Jan Foster in a knife act in the Foster’s big tent show in the late 1960s. Johnny Foster’s son Pikey was the one throwing the knives, and no one dared to be the target except Jan, his wife. Over many years and thousands of knives thrown, the worst she suffered was one small nick to the ear; Ted’s twin daughters, Sonia and Tracy Trevor, working on their Knock ’Em Can joint in the early 1980s
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.

“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”

These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”

I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

items.title: Xbox owners are getting more customizations for backgrounds and the Guide menu
paragraphs: is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Microsoft is starting to test new customization options for Xbox consoles today. Xbox Insiders will be able to start testing new rotating backgrounds, new library options for digital games, and the ability to move the Xbox Guide menu to the right-hand side.

“Xbox Insiders can now save favorite dynamic backgrounds and shuffle through them automatically,” says Eden Marie, principal software engineering lead at Xbox. “You can also choose Shuffle at the start of any background category. Have your background change each time you sign in, or set it to change hourly, daily, or weekly.”

Microsoft is also improving how you organize disc-to-digital games on an Xbox console. Xbox Insiders who have claimed a digital license from a disc-based game will be able to see these titles in a separate category in the library section. You’ll also be able to hide the digital license icon on game tiles.

Finally, Xbox Insiders will be able to choose whether the Guide menu appears on the left or right side of a screen. “Alpha Skip-Ahead members can try them first,” says Marie. “We’ll bring them to more Xbox Insiders and players over time.”
