items.title: Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn
paragraphs: New York City-based artist Finnegan Shannon has installed a conveyor belt to display art at cultural centre Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, USA, as a commentary on accessibility in art.
According to Pioneer Works, the There’s No Me Without You installation fulfils Shannon’s “longtime fantasy of an exhibition space that would meet their access needs”.

Chairs were placed around the closed-loop 12-foot-long mechanism, letting visitors sit when viewing and engaging with exhibited objects, archival materials and portable DVD players placed on a series of moving trays.

It was created from a restaurant-style system similar to those used in sushi restaurants where the food is delivered via a conveyor belt. The rest of the room on the upper floor of the arts centre was covered in rich fabrics and built-in benches along the perimeter.

“My conveyor belt, technically a retail and restaurant-style display system, is a tool for me to be in less pain when I’m experiencing art,” said Shannon, who was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at birth. “I notice I am a much more patient and curious visitor when I’m sitting down.”
The title of the installation reflects the artist’s relationship to the concept of interdependence.
“If disabled people were in charge, we would have a bunch of varied and deluxe options for sitting and lying down in exhibition spaces,” they said.
“Instead we live in a world where this type of infrastructure is quite basic and sparse.”

The installation is being used to present new commissions by artists with disabilities Joselia Rebekah Hughes, Ariana Martinez and Alex Dolores Salerno. For the three consecutive exhibitions, visitors are invited to interact with the work through touch, sight, and sound.
Air filters with bright colours were included in the middle of the conveyor belt to assist with air quality and masks were encouraged for visitors.
Shannon emphasised the collaborative nature of artistic endeavour through the exhibition.
“We know that on some fundamental level, no solo exhibition is truly a solo endeavor,” Shannon said.
“Putting together an exhibition takes immense collaboration and support – art handlers, facilities staff, curators, registrars, accountants, assistants – and that is all within the institution.”
“You can trace that entanglement further: I’m dependent on workers, paid and unpaid care labor, and friendships, family, and more, both locally and across the globe.”

“I never want someone to come away from an exhibition with my work feeling like they’ve experienced something that is mine,” they said. “Instead I hope they have threads to follow to learn more about the vast world of knowledge that is disability culture.”

Shannon’s other projects have focused on access. Alt Text as Poetry, a collaboration with Bojana Coklyat exploring image description and Do You Want Us Here or Not is a series of museum benches and cushions designed to encourage rest.
Other designs that prioritise accessibility were showcased at The Fashion Institute of Technology’s Adapt/Evolve exhibition in New York last year.
There’s No Me Without You is on show at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn from 12 September to 20 December. For more exhibitions, installations and talks worldwide, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

items.title: Explainer: From undercover employment to corporate data breaches: the "Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

A bipartisan bill that could help U.S. small businesses recognize threats from foreign adversaries, including the risk posed by North Korean workers posing as job candidates, was debated and passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday. It now moves on to the Senate.

The core provision requires the Small Business Administration to develop and distribute educational materials so that businesses can recognize the risks identified by the U.S. government and learn how to respond.

Its official title is the “Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act of 2026." It requires the Small Business Administration to guide businesses on how to identify, prevent, and respond to threats. The bill requires the SBA to develop materials in collaboration with relevant agencies and distribute them through regional offices and existing support programs. The SBA would be expected to use its existing budget to produce new materials.

Rep. Roger Williams, a Republican from Texas’s 25th Congressional District and chairman of the House Small Business Committee, is leading the effort. Williams has specifically identified China, Russia and North Korea as foreign threats the legislation seeks to address. Explaining the need for the bill, he said that “while many small businesses are exposed to foreign threats, they lack the resources and expertise to respond.”
Rep. Derek Tran, a Democrat representing California’s 45th Congressional District, is also involved in the effort. He serves on the House Small Business and Armed Services committees.
Why Is This Important for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises?
“Even small companies have technology and information that needs to be protected”, according to the proposed bill.

For example, even a small software company may have programs it developed in-house. “If a manufacturer’s blueprints or customer and business partner information are leaked, it could harm the business”.
Chairman Williams’ office explained that “many small businesses lack the resources or expertise to identify and respond to increasingly sophisticated threats”.
The bill goes beyond simply alerting businesses to risk; it also provides guidance on prevention methods and where to seek assistance.
It includes guidelines to ensure that while risks are assessed when conducting business or receiving investments overseas, legitimate commercial activities are not unnecessarily restricted.

The bill relies on the Commerce Department’s definition of “foreign adversary,” which includes North Korea. While it does not specifically address North Korea’s use of covert IT workers in U.S. companies, its coverage of cyber intrusions and its catch-all provision for emerging threats could allow the SBA to include such schemes.
During hiring: North Korean IT workers misrepresent their identities and actual work locations to secure remote work positions.
Once hired: They gain access to the company’s computer networks and the data necessary to perform their duties.
If that access is abused: It can lead to the theft of corporate information or extortion.

Last January, the FBI warned of a case in which North Korean IT personnel stole sensitive corporate data and program source code from a company and, after being discovered, used this as leverage to demand money.
In July of the same year, the FBI stated that companies that outsource IT work to third-party vendors may face additional vulnerabilities because they cannot directly manage the hiring process.
This alert is directed at U.S. companies in general. It does not mean that all affected companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
What kind of assistance will companies receive?
The bill requires the SBA to guide companies on how to protect intellectual property, trade secrets, sensitive corporate information, and supply chains.
The proposed bill covers not only cybersecurity but also the import of goods produced through forced labor, counterfeit goods and illicit trade, and predatory investment practices.
The bill now moves to the Senate. There is currently no Senate version of the bill, and this session of Congress ends in early January.
- September 10: The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams (R-Texas), with Rep. Derek Tran (D-Calif.) as the Democratic co-sponsor.
- September 16: The House Small Business Committee voted 22–0 to recommend the bill to the full House.
- October 9: The committee’s official report was submitted.
- November 11: Passed by a voice vote. The Senate must approve it with the same wording, and the President must sign it.

items.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
paragraphs: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

items.title: Duran Duran drummer quits band due to tinnitus
paragraphs: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".
The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.
"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.
He said deciding on the timing had been difficult but he was pleased to be "going out on a real high".

"We've just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers.
"I couldn't have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I'll treasure forever.
"I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John," he said.

Taylor's band members added that he had helped define the sound of the group, performing on 10 hit albums, their two number one singles - Is There Something I Should Know? and The Reflex - and the band's 1985 James Bond theme A View To A Kill.
"His drumming helped define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning and having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all.
"We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness.
"He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band."

items.title: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
paragraphs: US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.
In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".
Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.

He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads.

In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Hegseth (right) awarded the medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias after being reprimanded by him
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell later said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.

During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.
"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.

Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.
Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
paragraphs: Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.

Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.
"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."
The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.

In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.
Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.
Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.

"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

items.title: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
paragraphs: Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.
He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.
Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.
To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.
Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.
Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.
Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).

In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.
Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorous to water.
But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.
Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one.
Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip.
And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind".
There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform.
First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings.

Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade – gradualism, not a short, sharp shock.
Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants.
I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns – at least privately – about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall. This time, they are on board.
One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts.
But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off.

Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs.
Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time.
There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms.
One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging – from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health.
Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place.
York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress".
She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work.
She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on.
Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year.
He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution".

But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail".
So much of politics - like comedy – depends on timing.
For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn.
But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line.
Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts.
Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work".
And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis".
So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations.
But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government.

items.title: Casualties continue to rise after Brooklyn building collapses
paragraphs: A view of the site where a building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York on Wednesday. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption
The New York City Fire Department reported Thursday that more victims had been found after a three-story residential building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn collapsed a day earlier.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said six people had been declared dead at the scene. Two others died in a hospital. 18 other people were injured in the building collapse.
Search efforts are continuing with more than 250 firefighters and emergency workers deployed to the site, according to city officials.
First responders rescue a person after a building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York on Wednesday. Ryan Murphy/AP hide caption
