items.title: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning
paragraphs: In the shadow of Silicon Valley, workers for the city of Oakland, California, worry the region will deploy AI systems that could increase surveillance and inaccurately evaluate their performance. Pushing for protections to ensure workers won’t be laid off or disciplined by AI, their union overwhelmingly voted on 22 October to authorize a strike, with 94.1% in favor.

“We just want the city administration to really be intentional about how it’s engaging with AI products,” said Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and member of International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21. “Sometimes with a fancy new toy, it actually costs more, it’s more difficult to implement and the results are not as good.”

The nearly unanimous vote had an impact. The city government of Oakland and the union reached a tentative, three-year agreement that includes AI-related protections, such as requiring the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI rather than firing them. As a result, the 5 November strike has been put on hold.

The Bay Area union is one of many public-sector labor groups nationwide seeking explicit protections against AI and automation, which union representatives say could worsen working conditions and threaten jobs. Following decades of automation efforts by companies and growing concern about AI since ChatGPT’s debut in 2022, ongoing labor disputes reveal hardening battle lines between public-sector bosses and their increasingly vocal workers.

“The bosses have such zeal for use of this technology,” said John Samuelsen, the Transport Workers Union president and a New York City subway track inspector. “Our members know that automation is the ultimate threat to their jobs … In transport, it’s here, it’s in our faces, we’re fighting it every day.”

Over the past few years, AI and automation technologies have infiltrated multiple sectors and are gradually making their way into public-sector workplaces across the country. Already, nearly 70% of state and local government agencies say they have adopted or are implementing generative AI, according to a survey by Ernst and Young conducted from July to August 2026. At the same time, workers are organizing and starting to win protections.

Policy makers have been moving too slowly to address AI’s potential effects on workers, so workers have to fight for themselves, argues Liz Shuler, AFL-CIO president and founder of its Technology Institute. “We’re using our contract negotiations to institute guardrails that policymakers won’t.”

Some unions have been prepared for this moment, having watched private-sector unions fight similar battles, said Kung Feng, a researcher with the University of California at Berkeley’s Labor Center and former director of San Francisco Jobs With Justice. For example, in 2023, Communications Workers of America recommended AI protections, and won some of them for California workers in October 2026.
“Workers versus billionaires has been the theme of this whole election … and bargain cycle,” Feng said. “This is the contest that we have over the future of technology in the workplace.”

Researchers call it bossware: AI tools that public- and private-sector employers are increasingly rolling out across industries to monitor and supervise employees, according to an October report Feng co-authored. Some tools rank and evaluate workers for hiring, firing and promotions. Others track location and activity, monitor productivity, scan biometrics for timekeeping, use cameras, wearable devices and sensors, or leverage analytics to predict emotions.

Amazon has used algorithms to push workers to operate at dangerous speeds in its warehouses, and now that strategy is being deployed in the public sector, said Lorena Gonzalez, the California Federation of Labor Unions president.
“We think AI doesn’t belong on big-rig trucks, and it doesn’t belong in hospitals and schools,” Gonzalez said.

Some automation technologies could aid public-sector workers, like vehicle safety systems in public transit, but humans should always be in charge, providing oversight, Gonzalez said. Computers have been able to fly a plane for years, but every aircraft carries two pilots who can use human judgment and skill to override the system when necessary, she said.
“If we’re using a computer or AI, it has to be controlled by a human being, not the other way around,” she said.

Employers in the public sector often deploy automation technologies during claimed attempts to improve efficiency and cut costs when budgets are slim, Feng said. But unions have been pushing for AI protections since the late 2010s, and those battles are only intensifying as automation advances and generative AI becomes more common, he said. Workers’ requests include receiving advance notice before a new technology is rolled out, getting information about that technology and ensuring the right to negotiate over its use, he added.

Examples abound of worker pushback. Last year, Pennsylvania became the first state to run a pilot program with OpenAI. The state encouraged employees, like unemployment claim workers and social workers, to use ChatGPT Enterprise to test for time savings.

“But there were no guarantees or agreements for the workers,” said Steve Catanese, president of Service Employees International Union Local 668, which represents more than 10,000 statewide public-sector workers. “With generative AI, workers are building their own gallows sometimes.”

Then the union spoke up, inspired by the California screenwriters’ victory in 2023, one of the longest strikes in Hollywood history that secured protections against AI replacing writers. The Pennsylvania SEIU Local 668 pushed the governor, Josh Shapiro, to agree to a policy guaranteeing that the state’s use of AI will include employee input and supervision, and that the tech won’t be used to discipline workers.

“It’s powerful for elected leaders to say, there will always be human public servants under my watch,” Catanese said, referring to commitments that AI won’t displace workers. He expects these issues to resurface when the union negotiates for a new contract in 2027.

In transportation, public workers in states including Florida and New York are proactively trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles, calling them unsafe and a threat to their jobs. They’re hoping to replicate a 2024 victory in Columbus, Ohio, where the Transport Workers Union secured contracts giving it veto power over any plan by the Central Ohio Transit Authority to deploy autonomous vehicles.
But the TWU doesn’t oppose new technologies, said Samuelsen, the union president. It supports systems that can aid with collision avoidance and improving bus and train timing, he said.

But he worries that many industries are pushing for AI and automation without regard for safety. For example, some airlines have begun experimenting with using drones to inspect aircraft from afar rather than relying on human jet mechanics, who can do a more thorough, up-close inspection.

AI and automation are “in every single element of passenger transport, and even freight transport, that you can imagine. It has completely infiltrated us,” Samuelsen said. “Where there’s no … union that’s willing to fight, workers are doomed.”
This isn’t the first time emerging technologies have negatively affected labor markets and working conditions across industries, union representatives said.
“We’ve seen this movie before,” Schuler said. Unions have faced mass job loss before, such as when automation in assembly-line factories in the midwest reduced manufacturing jobs, she said.

Some legislators, especially at the state level, have been making strides toward new policies. For example, the IFPTE and other unions supported the No Robo Bosses bill in California, which bars employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers. Unions also supported another California bill that prohibited employers from using workplace AI surveillance tools, such as those that could monitor employees’ emotional states. Gavin Newsom signed both into law on 30 September.

Public-sector workers have also backed AI-related legislation in other states. Public-sector unions in New York supported a law, effective December 2025, that protects workers at state agencies from being displaced by AI.

Though tech CEOs have warned of AI’s hypothetical risks to humanity, the more pressing issue is how employees are being negatively affected by the technology today, said Keith Brown, executive secretary-treasurer of the Alameda Labor Council, which serves public and private-sector workers in California’s Alameda county.
“We’ve seen in the news a lot of headlines about the threat of AI destroying civilization,” Brown said. “But for workers, we’ve been facing these harms from AI tech companies for a long time.”

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged spy scandal
paragraphs: Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU Technology Conference on Oct. 21, 2026. Sean Gallup/Getty Images hide caption
Jensen Huang, CEO of the chipmaking juggernaut Nvidia, is stepping down, the company's board announced Thursday.

The decision comes days after the company took the extraordinary step of launching an investigation following news reports alleging that Huang had had an extramarital affair with one of the company's clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency, according to the New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, and said he would cooperate with the investigation.
The company's share price dropped sharply on Wednesday, after the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to an NPR request for comment.

Huang was widely seen as one of the most important business leaders in the United States. Nvidia dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Huang also had President Trump's ear on AI policy, with Trump even calling Huang's phone in September while Huang was onstage during a conference.

The scandal that brought down Huang snowballed quickly over the past two weeks. The New York Times reported in late October that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese woman at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips. Citing unidentified sources, it said U.S. intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on him and possibly try to influence policy. NPR has not independently confirmed this reporting.

A drip-drip of scoops followed — from the Times and other outlets — suggesting that the relationship was romantic, that senior Trump administration officials knew about the allegations some time ago, and that Huang had had a second affair.
China's foreign ministry has said the allegations of spying are baseless and part of a smear campaign against China.
Huang's departure launches Nvidia into uncharted territory.
Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese agent and what the Trump administration knew about it will likely be the subject of an investigation when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"We should all be extremely concerned about this, and the fact that the White House knew about this for weeks, maybe months now, is is is very disturbing as well," said Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, a senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in an interview with NPR.

The company's Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, has been appointed interim CEO. The board said in their statement they would conduct a full search for a new CEO and consider both internal and external candidates.

"There's no obvious replacement," said Stephen Witt, author of a book about Nvidia called The Thinking Machine. "It's not even clear Nvidia can be the same kind of company without Jensen. I have a hard time imagining what Nvidia looks like without Jensen."
Nvidia still plans to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

Huang was one of the longest-serving CEOs in U.S. corporate history, stepping into the role after launching the company with partners over bottomless cups of coffee at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, Calif., 33 years ago. Nvidia got its start making specialized chips to create 3D graphics for computers that would come to be known as graphics processing units, or GPUs.
He was the face of Nvidia and an unlikely celebrity, giving countless keynote speeches and interviews in his trademark leather jacket, or posing for selfies with adoring fans.

Huang was also the company's driving force. Under his leadership, Nvidia made a big and early bet on artificial intelligence, investing heavily to transform its niche graphics chips into general-purpose processing units that were ideal for the volume of computations required to create AI.

That bet would pay off in spades as GPUs became the go-to chip for AI creators. When AI burst into the public consciousness in late 2022 with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT — a chatbot trained and run on Nvidia chips — the firm was worth about $400 billion. Today, it's valued at more than $4 trillion, among the most valuable in the world, and it dominates the market for GPUs.
But analysts say despite Huang's visionary management of the business, he had a blind spot for succession and hadn't articulated a clear plan, at least publicly.

In a Bloomberg interview from mid-October, Huang was vague about succession plans. "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company is already at the company, but 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep."

Huang's adult children, Spencer and Madison Huang, both work at Nvidia. Asked about talk that Madison might be in line to succeed him, he paused, and told Bloomberg: "if that's their aspiration, Spencer or Madison's, they have to go earn it. And it's really, really hard work. It takes a lot of sacrifice."
Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group, a tech research firm, said the company will inevitably be different without Huang, and its future success is unclear.
"They've always had Jensen as this sort of visionary at the front," he said. "I don't think that's replaceable."

items.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
paragraphs: In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

But now, video game creators and artists are pushing back, looking to regain ground the industry has ceded to reactionary ideologies over the last decade by turning the gamification of politics back on Trump. Anonymous art collective The Secret Handshake has been known for its political activism since installing a sculpture of Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at the National Mall in downtown Washington, DC. This spring, the group developed a game entitled Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell and made it available online, as well as installing three free arcade cabinets on the National Mall.

A satire on the Trump administration, the game allows players to control the president in a Pokémon-style challenge that starts with an important choice: order a Diet Coke, or invade Iran. As the game progresses, Trump heads to Iran to collect barrels of oil (called “lube” in the game) and encounters administration members such as vice-president JD Vance, secretary of state Marco Rubio, and “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. It’s unwinnable, which is the point, though you can get a “Game Over” screen by trying to hold Melania Trump’s hand.

The Secret Handshake had never made a video game until Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell. “The ‘form’ was really dictated by the Trump Administration,” a member of Secret Handshake says via email. “It’s not that we wanted to make a video game; it’s that the Pentagon began using video games to promote their war in Iran and make it seem ‘cool’. They actually introduced the idea of a video game, not us. We felt like, well, if they’re going to use video games to promote their war, let’s make a video game satirising that war.”

The collective followed similar logic when creating their second free game, Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All which tasks players with speaking to Trump’s advisers, including a UFC fighter as “secretary of combat” and a no-bid contractor helping renovate The White House. The aim is to piece together enough “Big Brainpower” to figure out how to distract voters from the oil crisis. After Trump accidentally hits on his own daughter, Ivanka, and speaks to enough advisers to collect enough partial ideas to make one “big beautiful idea”, he decides to invade Greenland.

For The Secret Handshake, the video game as a medium helps people take in “the insanity” of what’s happening, which the collective believes may be hard to ascertain from just headlines. “When you are using a medium that’s very familiar, like a video game, and you’re going through these actions, it allows you to experience the headlines in a different way,” a spokesperson says. “This game is meant to be a caricature and satire, but it’s full of things in there that aren’t. Trump calling a woman a maggot felt very intense to experience in the form of a game.”

The Secret Handshake had to learn how to build a game on the fly for Operation Epic Furious. “We had no idea what we were doing,” a spokesperson explains. “It was a lot of trial and error, and figuring it out as we went along. We did have someone helping that understood this world and could actually make it happen, but no one was a game designer.” They describe the games as, “held together with duct tape”.

Still, there are avid gamers in the group, and they pulled inspiration from Japanese role-playing adventures, particularly the early Final Fantasy titles, while the invidious, scatalogical tone is similar to South Park games such as The Stick of Truth and The Fractured But Whole. The aim was for the games to be funny and to properly satirise the absurdity of the current administration. So far, more than 350,000 people have played them online.

Two further anti-Trump games mimic the iconic arcade shooter Space Invaders, and they couldn’t have been made in more different ways. This summer, game developer Richie Branson partnered with nonprofit All for America to create Tax Evaders, in which you choose one of four playable pilots (President Trump, vice-president JD Vance, House speaker Mike Johnson, or Senate leader John Thune) before jumping into the first level, destroying healthcare and lining billionaire pockets.

“There’s something a bit unsettling about playing as the ‘villain’,” says Branson, who created Tax Evaders using the free and open-source game development engine, Godot. “The intent here is to drive home the point that these officials are destroying beneficial programmes with the same combination of enthusiasm and indifference as someone blowing up enemy space ships in an arcade game.”

The Trump administration’s aggressive push into online culture is working, according to Branson, who said the White House team is, “on a rampage” with its memelord and gaming culture posts. “It’s a very cunning way of spreading whatever message they’re trying to spread,” he says, before referring to the White House Arcade as “gamified propaganda”, and “garbage, [with] no love for the art”. Tax Evaders has had over 50,000 players and over 2m page impressions since July.

Alfie Souter and Carlota Real work in advertising together. They often chat about breaking news and trending topics, so when they saw the White House release its propaganda arcade, they decided to do something about it. “The craziest thing is the oversimplification of such a complex issue, like immigration,” says Real. “What they’re trying to do is boil this down to the minimum that people understand. A Tetris game; everyone on the planet has probably played it once, and they apply it to the shitshow that they’re doing.”

Angered by the administration’s trivialision of the issues and its demonisation of immigrants, the duo started brainstorming their own version of a simplified game with a political message. With no background in game design, they decided to build it in ChatGPT, which itself is perhaps a satirical message: many believe the Trump Arcade games are “vibe-coded”, or built using plain language to describe a game to a generative AI program, which then codes it.

The result is Corrupt Invaders. Essentially a homage to Space Invaders with an anti-Trump filter, the game tasks you with moving Trump’s “$400m Qatari gift” (his aeroplane) to “collect another $1.4bn in crypto.” Your final score is subtracted from Trump’s reported cryptocurrency earnings. According to Souter the duo wanted the game to be focused on something that felt inarguable about the Trump regime and settled on corruption, using the $400m Boeing 747-8 luxury jet gifted by Qatar. Federal law says US officials can only accept gifts under $480, but the Trump White House insisted Trump accepting the aircraft was legal. “We thought about that jet, and also the $1.4bn earnings in crypto last year – those numbers are so ridiculous,” says Souter. “That’s why when you play the game, you subtract it from the score, because it’s such an unfathomable number”.

The two wanted to focus on the money that President Trump and his close allies have earned since his second presidency and juxtapose that against Americans’ consistent concerns with the cost of living crisis. The games are designed to makes the dichotomy crystal clear. Recently, the duo launched Diesel Kong, a parody of the classic Nintendo platformer Donkey Kong in the context of rising oil prices due to the continued war in Iran. “Prices are going up. Putin’s throwing useless barrels, can Trump be saved?” asks the starting screen. Trump stands in place of Princess Peach, while a nondescript Maga supporter wearing an American flag shirt and red hat tries to make his way up the ramps and ladders.

The developers and activists behind these games are pushing back against the Trump administration’s gamified propaganda while looking to subvert the gaming subcultures the president has co-opted. “Our current administration runs the country as if were a video game, with no real sense of sympathy for the people affected by the losses incurred by their policies,” said Branson. “Gas prices are crazy right now, people’s lives are being affected, but to our nation’s leadership, we’re just NPCs.”

items.title: Love for pumpkin spice – level 1
paragraphs: People love pumpkin spice. The spice is a mixture of several spices. For example, they are cinnamon, nutmeg, or ginger. It smells very good. It brings happy feelings.
No pumpkin is in the mixture. Some people think that Starbucks makes pumpkin spice. The recipe is much older.
American settlers use the spices to keep food fresh during the winter. The foods are meat, fruit, and vegetables.

In 1976, Amelia Simmons writes a pumpkin spice recipe. She puts pumpkin spice in the first American cookbook. In the 1990s, Starbucks creates the pumpkin spice latte. Many people love it. The drink helps them welcome the fall after a hot summer.
Difficult words: mixture (several things put together), nutmeg (a hard seed of a tropical tree), settler (a person who lives in a new country).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Love for pumpkin spice – level 2
paragraphs: Many people love pumpkin spice because it gives them warm cozy feelings. They love to drink to welcome the fall when the hot summer ends. Pumpkin spice has many spices, including cinnamon, nutmeg, and ginger, and its smell is very popular.

In the 1990s, Starbucks created with the first pumpkin spice latte, and millions of people loved it. Since that time, Starbucks sold more than 420 million cups of pumpkin spice latte in the US, and the company offers it to customers in the fall and winter.

The history of pumpkin spice is much older than the 1990s. Hundreds of years ago, American settlers used the same spices to preserve meat, fruit, and vegetables for the winter months. In 1976, author Amelia Simmons wrote a pumpkin spice recipe which she put in the first American cookbook.
Difficult words: cozy (something that makes you feel warm and relaxed), settler (a person who moves to survive and live in a new country or area), preserve (to keep food fresh).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Love for pumpkin spice – level 3
paragraphs: The average pumpkin spice blend has cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and allspice, and for many consumers, it gives the warm, fuzzy feelings.

For centuries, people have associated the pumpkin spice flavor with fall. Early American settlers used the same ingredients to preserve the fall harvests of meat, fruit, and vegetables. In 1976, Amelia Simmons wrote a recipe for the flavor in the first American cookbook. In 1934, McCormick made the flavor official with the name pumpkin pie spice. The company gave an easy method to get all the spices needed for pumpkin pie in one shake.

In the early 1990s, Starbucks capitalized on the flavor, and the company added the pumpkin spice latte to its repertoire of seasonal drinks. Since then, Starbucks has sold more than 420 million cups in the US alone.
People love pumpkin spice as its smell evokes memories. Some experts say the words pumpkin spice can spark cozy fall feelings which people crave at the end of a hot summer.
Difficult words: blend (a mixture of different substances), capitalize on (to make profit from something), repertoire (all the items on stock).

items.title: Russell Brand's social media accounts disabled by Meta
paragraphs: Russell Brand's social media accounts on platforms owned by tech company Meta have been disabled.
It comes after the 51-year-old former entertainer was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in jail for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault earlier this week.
He was found guilty of the charges involving four women and relating to offences between 2004 and 2009.
Meta owns social media platforms including Instagram and Facebook.
Brand is currently in prison and is expected to serve seven years of his sentence behind bars before being released on licence.
On Wednesday evening, a post appeared on his X account, which remains active. "There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read.
"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner. "Stay tuned," it concluded.
The post included what appeared to be screenshots showing Brand's Instagram account having been disabled.
Meta's community standards policy says that "in order to maintain a safe environment and empower free expression" it restricts or removes accounts that are "harmful to the community".
That includes accounts owned by convicted sex offenders.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand's behaviour - which he denies - YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy".
At the time, the video platform said it was taking action "to protect" its users.

items.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
paragraphs: The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

items.title: Two men found guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target UK-based journalists
paragraphs: Two Iranian men have been convicted of spying for an Iranian intelligence service by carrying out surveillance on journalists and a lawyer in the UK.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted of "assisting a foreign intelligence service" at Woolwich Crown Court on Thursday.

They were tasked by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) with monitoring the targets. Sepahvand intended to carry out a "violent attack" against at least one of them, while Manesh helped with planning.
A third man, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was cleared of the same charge.
Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.

Police seized 534GB of data that showed Sapahvand and Manesh were given documents that included pictures of targets, their work addresses, the make and colour of their cars and the names of pets. They then used ChatGPT to carry out further research.
The pair, from west London, are asylum seekers who had been granted temporary leave to remain. Sepahvand arrived in the UK in a lorry in 2016, and Manesh arrived via small boat in 2019.
Sepahvand conducted surveillance and reconnaissance in preparation for inflicting violence on several "subjects" in the UK.

These included journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, who worked for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran international, Jonathan Turner, a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, as well as a media production professional.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, the senior national co-ordinator for Counter-Terrorism Policing, said it was the first time ChatGPT case search history had been presented in a state threat case.
She added: "It's something we're beginning to see more of as AI tools become more widely available and people become more aware of them."
It was clear from the evidence at the trial that at times Sepahvand felt he was being mistreated by his Iranian handlers, who had not paid him.

Evans said: "This is a trend we see in these types of cases where people get involved in work on behalf of foreign states and they're often promised money and lots of other things but they rarely receive what they've been offered."
Sepahvand had claimed he participated in the spying out of fear of the consequences of refusing but the prosecution described this as "entirely bogus".

In voice notes sent to an Iranian contact, he said he had been promised that a conviction for theft in Iran would be "sorted out" - which prosecutors said was part of his motivation for conducting the surveillance.
Sepahvand also asked for £150,000 in exchange for "finishing off" a target, stressing that he would "do it".
Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service's counter-terrorism division, said the two men had been promised rewards for sending intelligence back to contacts in Iran.
"Sepahvand himself was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit serious violence against their targets," he said.
"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place.
"Cases like this show Iranian intelligence's willingness to use proxies to target the regime's critics abroad."
Sepahvand and Manesh will be sentenced at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

items.title: Four video tracks and a doughnut shop – how Dispatch got its start
paragraphs: A year ago, Dispatch released a game that surprised many people, including me. It's a superhero game about managing reformed villains from behind a desk, launched on PC and PlayStation 5. It has since sold five million copies, and a mobile version arrives on iOS and Android on 9 December, following October's Dispatch anniversary Deluxe Edition.

Dispatch was made in Unreal Engine and stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. It's an animated, episodic workplace comedy that plays like a TV series, but it wasn't always a game, and that's perhaps why it feels so unique. AdHoc was founded in Los Angeles in 2018 by Telltale Games alumni who planned to make interactive experiences with real actors on screen, and Dispatch began that way.
I asked co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors, what survived the jump from live-action series to animated game, and what had to change.

One piece of the original script made it through every draft: the doughnut shop scene in episode two. Lenart says it was "one of the pieces from the early script that just kind of kept hanging around through every draft all the way from live action into the animated game".

The set-up was different back then. You watched a camera feed as the hero Invisigal dealt with a thief, and your job was to feed her the information she needed to succeed. In the live-action version, that meant switching cameras and pulling information from what each camera showed. Herman says the scene was "purely built around the technology" AdHoc was using to create its interactive live action. It ran in a browser and had hard limits, including, as Herman recalls, “I think it was like four simultaneous tracks of video”.

The team turned that restriction into a mechanic. Watch the alley behind the shop, and you couldn't see what was happening inside the front. "By choosing where you were going to give your attention, the game would adjust, and you'd learn different things based on where you were looking," says Herman, calling it the perfect place to test the idea.

Because they'd spent so long on it, they carried it forward. In the game, Lenart says, they wove in mechanics from the final design, such as hacking, "to make it feel a little bit more like Robert was helping out Invisigal".

The original story was a mentorship, centred on the one-on-one relationship between Robert and Invisigal. Pivoting it into a game changed that. AdHoc wanted a dispatch mechanic, with the player sending heroes out on calls, and that needs a roster. "So the Z-Team was created to support the gameplay," Lenart says, "which then informed the story, and then changed the overall arc of the season, which brought a whole team into it as opposed to just a one-on-one mentorship with Invisigal."

It's a neat illustration of how the studio works. "Everything at AdHoc starts with story," says Herman, contrasting that with studios that pick a genre first, polish the mechanics and the game-feel, and only later ask what the story is. AdHoc begins with the world, the characters and who the player is, then asks what that means for gameplay. "Oh, well, you're a superhero dispatcher, so maybe we should have some sort of dispatching mechanic, right?"

Once there's a script, it moves on to storyboards, animatics and animation. That storyboard stage is now part of the product: the anniversary Deluxe Edition update adds Storyboard Mode, which plays the whole game through its original animatics. It's a new mode that offers genuine insight into how a scene was planned, scripted and animated.

The move to animation was driven by budget constraints, to an extent, because they could do more with a little extra, and it also changed the game's scale, given Dispatch's live-action origins; Lenart says the team knew they were "severely limited from a budget standpoint compared to big-budget superhero tentpole movies". For budgetary reasons, the story was largely set in an office with a small cast.

Animation flipped that constraint and aligned with trends like Mixtape's hand-made animation, giving the team room to grow and aim higher within the new art form. "We're able to have a giant action scene because it doesn't cost that much more than having a bunch of characters walking around talking," Lenart explains. That let AdHoc expand the moments that deserved spectacle: "Let's really go all out and try to compete with some of the other best-in-class versions of these scenes in animation."

Ask whether players have done anything that made AdHoc rethink how interactive stories should work, and Herman is refreshingly honest. “I don’t know that there have been any major epiphanies,” he says, before steering to a different answer: launching Dispatch “was a labour of love”, the culmination of a lot of work distilled into one experience the team felt was exciting and high quality.

He adds: "The success of the game has just really injected a lot of confidence into us and other developers making similar types of games. For a long time, there hadn't been a really clear or recent example of something like this reaching a level of success that a developer could go out and raise funding for."

He's proud of who found it, too. Dispatch "was able to pierce a new audience who perhaps thought gaming wasn't for them". Lenart agrees, saying the success feels like "motivation to keep making these types of games and expand our possibilities even more".
The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Bond producer first female president of film school
paragraphs: A producer whose credits include the James Bond movies has been announced as the first female president of a film school.
Barbara Broccoli will take over the role at the UK's National Film and Television School (NFTS) in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, in February, succeeding Oscar-winning producer David Puttnam.
She has produced nine Bond films with her half-brother, Michael G. Wilson, before it was announced in February that Amazon MGM Studios had gained creative control.
Puttnam, whose credits include Chariots of Fire, The Killing Fields and Midnight Express, said he was "over the moon" that such a "hugely respected figure" was succeeding him.
The National Film School was established in 1971 by director Colin Young, taking over the Beaconsfield site with an initial intake of about 25 students.
In 1982 the institution was renamed the National Film and Television School to reflect its expanding curriculum.
Puttnam, who has been involved with the school for over 50 years, said it was a "lovely job" to have and that he had tried never to interfere.
He added that Broccoli's decision to take up the role was a "wonderful thing for the school".
Puttnam will take on an honorary role as president emeritus.

items.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
paragraphs: Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".
Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.
The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.
Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.
"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".
"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."
The Department for Education has been asked for comment.
Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September.
Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books.
Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff".
Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils.
Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries.
"The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said.

"Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock."

A Telford and Wrekin council spokesperson added that after the "recent media coverage and allegations published in the press" they had taken the decision to "remove all Walliams' books and audio books from their library catalogues".
Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow".
Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage.
A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships.
"Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display."

On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.
In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

items.title: Resident Evil Requiem sweeps Golden Joystick Awards
paragraphs: Resident Evil Requiem and its makers have won big at the Golden Joystick Awards, which celebrate the year's most popular games.
Released in February, it was the latest instalment of the global survival horror phenomenon, which has also spawned books, films and TV programmes since it was first released 30 years ago.

At Wednesday's awards ceremony, it scooped ultimate game of the year, console game of the year, best game trailer, and best lead performer for the game's star Angela Sant'Albano, who plays protagonist Grace Ashcroft.
Meanwhile its makers, Japanese studio Capcom, was named studio of the year and was also recognised for other games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword and Pragmata.

FBI agent Grace Ashcroft was a brand new lead character in Resident Evil Requiem who, along with returning fan favourite Leon S. Kennedy, explores old haunts, such as Racoon City's police department as they investigate a series of mysterious deaths.
Securing 17% of the public vote, it was named ultimate game of the year ahead of other contenders Phantom Blade Zero, Crimson Desert, Control Resonant and The Blood of Dawnwalker.

items.title: CMAT joins Philomena Begley on stage in surprise appearance
paragraphs: CMAT and Philomena Begley celebrating Begley receiving the Lifetime Achievement Award
Irish star CMAT made a surprise appearance at an award ceremony in Belfast on Wednesday.
The pop-star joined Philomena Begley, one of Irish country music's most loved and celebrated entertainers, on stage at the NI Music Prize.
Begley was honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of her 64-year career.
The country music legend performed the hit Blanket on the Ground alongside CMAT.
The NI Music Prize, an annual event celebrating music in Northern Ireland, was marking its 15th anniversary on Wednesday at Ulster Hall.
Begley's award was presented by BBC broadcaster Hugo Duncan, a longtime friend of the musician.
When Begley went on to perform Blanket on the Ground she invited CMAT, who had made a surprise appearance at the ceremony, to join her on stage.
At a concert in Belfast earlier this year, CMAT, whose real name is Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson, gave a shout-out to Begley, thanking the country legend.
Reacting to the shout-out in October, Begley told the Good Morning Ulster programme that she had never met her but had "heard so much about her".
"It's hard to beat the new generation, it's great to see them all doing well."
The pop-star joined Begley, one of Irish country music's most loved and celebrated entertainers, at the NI Music Prize
Begley added that she was "over the moon" to win the award.
Begley said she did not know what reaction to expect at the awards ceremony, but that she was "looking forward to it".
Charlotte Dryden, CEO of Oh Yeah Music Centre, who were the organisers of the NI Music Prize, said that seeing Begley and CMAT together "was something really special".
"We've had some incredible moments at the NI Music Prize over the years, but I don't think we've ever experienced an atmosphere quite like that," she said.
Philomena Begley is one of the island's most loved entertainers.

An unrivalled interpreter of country music, she has delighted audiences on stages all over the world and collaborated with country greats like Porter Wagoner and Billie Jo Spears, who first released Blanket on The Ground.
From humble beginnings in Pomeroy, County Tyrone, Begley had a simple, but happy childhood as one of eight children in a close-knit, traditional and musical family.
She always loved to sing, but had no plans of pursuing a career in music.
Begley accidentally entered the world of country music at a local dance, when she was called on stage as a dare to sing a song with the Old Cross Céilí Band.
An instant hit, she was asked to fill in as cover for someone who had taken ill in the band and suddenly became swept up in the 1960s dance-hall circuit.

In 1975, Begley was granted permission to record her own version of Blanket on the Ground from US country music star Billie Jo Spears who had released it earlier that year as the title track from the album of the same name.
Begley's version went to number five in the Irish charts and sparked some friendly rivalry between the pair.
Over the years, they became close friends, sharing many of the same hits and performing together on several occasions.
Blanket on the Ground remains one of Begley's most popular songs to this day.
Begley has captivated crowds on stages all over the world, performing everywhere from Wembley Stadium to Nashville, Tennessee.
In 1978, she was invited by Porter Wagoner, the man who introduced Dolly Parton to the world, to perform at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville's legendary home of country music.
Here she rubbed shoulders with the stars of global country music and even received a standing ovation for her performance of Blanket on the Ground.
It was fitting recognition for her contribution to country music in Ireland and beyond.
Philomena Begley put on a special performance for Dungannon Swifts' fans and players
Speaking to BBC News NI ahead of the Irish Cup final, Ms Begley said she was "shocked, but delighted" with the response.
The Swifts went on to win the final, holding their nerve against Cliftonville to secure a 4-3 penalty shootout win after a 1-1 draw after extra time.
Country star Philomena Begley joined in the celebrations on stage
There were a number of other artists honoured on Wednesday, including Joshua Burnside, who won the PPL Album of the Year award for It's Not Going to Be OK.
Belfast band Chalk, meanwhile, celebrated a double win: the group was awarded Single of the Year for Pain, as well as MCD Live Act of the Year.
Joshua Burnside won the Album of the Year award
Kaidi Tatham was named PRS for Music NI Creator of the Year.
