items.title: EMBT shelters Naples metro station beneath "natural and welcoming" vaulted timber roof
paragraphs: Spanish architecture studio EMBT has completed the Naples Underground Central Station in Italy, contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof.

The station, which is shortlisted in the Infrastructure and transport category of Dezeen Awards 2026, sits within the Centro Direzionale, a business district in Naples designed in the 1970s by Japanese architect Kenzo Tange.
The 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

As EMBT founder Benedetta Tagliabue previously told Dezeen during the station’s construction, the curvilinear timber canopy was designed in direct response to what she called the “artificial” feel of the modernist Centro Direzionale.
“Kenzo Tange designed Centro Direzionale, and he built a very Kenzo Tange-type of city with reflective skyscrapers and a piazza, very 1970s, very clean,” she told Dezeen in 2021.

“It didn’t work because it’s so different from the rest of Naples,” Tagliabue continued. “So the idea of making a new station there and connecting with the new subway line was also to try to introduce a piece of nature and a piece of the original part of Naples into this artificial piece of the city.”

The roof of the station was constructed from arches and beams of glue-laminated (glulam) timber, which are partially supported by the existing concrete structure and shelter a floor finished in local Etna and Trani limestone.

According to Tagliabue, the branching columns and supports of these arches were designed to evoke the feeling of “walking through a forest”, while referencing the arched roofs of historic railway stations.
“We wanted the everyday experience of catching a train to feel more natural and welcoming, giving people a sense of being at home in the middle of the city,” she told Dezeen.

“We were also interested in what wood could bring to this particular neighbourhood. There is so much glass and concrete here; introducing timber was a way of bringing back a connection with nature, through its warmth and texture,” she added.
“The roof follows the geometry of the tracks, so something that is normally hidden underground becomes visible in the shape of the building.”

The vaulted canopy not only shelters the station’s ticket barriers and access routes, but extends towards the new surrounding paved plaza on either side, which faces a church to the north and incorporates new planting to the south.

Below ground, the station platforms are lined entirely with striped panels in bold shades of red, orange and yellow informed by Pompeian frescoes. This theme is continued above ground in the form of colourful silhouettes.

“Our station is not directly above archaeological remains, so we introduced our own references to that history, with a little humour. The reds and yellows recall Pompeii, and figures appear and disappear across the surfaces,” Tagliabue explained.
“I like the idea that a station can offer these unexpected encounters: along the way, you discover something about the city and feel more connected to it,” she added.

Elsewhere in Naples, sculptor Anish Kapoor and architecture studio AL_A previously designed two sculptural station entrances – one in weathered steel and the other in aluminium – as part of a project to connect the underground to the city’s Traiano district.

Other metro station architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the mirrored Qasr AlHokm Metro Station in Saudi Arabia by Snøhetta and the series of buildings created for Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel by studios RSHP, Hassell and WW+P Architects.

items.title: King Charles appears on Sir Elton John's radio show
paragraphs: King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.
During the Rocket Hour show, the King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years", to which the singer joked: "I'll be on the Antiques Roadshow."

The pair discussed some of their favourite musical performances, as well as the role music has played in the King's charity, the King's Trust. The show was recorded in secret last month and will air this Saturday.
Sir Elton has long been a supporter of the trust, most recently donating a pair of his rose-tinted glasses to its 50th anniversary auction this year.
In a trailer for the upcoming episode, the King and Sir Elton are seen laughing together as they chat.
In a voiceover, the singer said he was "excited to hear what he's got to say about music, about the King's Trust and memories that we both share".

The King's Trust - previously known as The Prince's Trust - was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people from disadvantaged backgrounds overcome challenging situations, become employed or launch their own businesses.

During the radio episode, the King called it "an opportunity too good to resist" when he was asked to showcase music from the "talented performers who have so generously supported us over the years, together with some of the newer artists the trust has helped to launch".
The full list of their chosen tracks is under wraps until the episode airs but Skye Newman's Hairdresser, Raye's Joy and Muse's rendition of Feeling Good are said to be among them.

The pair will reminisce about some of the most memorable performances for the trust, from the Wembley Arena rock galas of the 1980s - which Sir Elton participated in - to charity shows at the Royal Albert Hall and pop concerts in Hyde Park.
The episode was recorded at Apple Music Studios - which hosts the show - in Battersea Power Station when the King and Sir Elton visited for the launch of the Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs.
The mentorship programme aims to help young people explore careers in creative industries.

items.title: Faulty Wedding Cake pavilion to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor
paragraphs: A 12-metre-high pavilion shaped like a wedding cake is set to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor in Buckinghamshire, UK, after it was closed over health and safety concerns.
A spokesperson for the Grade I-listed country house told the BBC that the pavilion, which was installed in 2023, was not “open for quite as long as hoped” due to faults in its ceramic tiles.
The sculptural pavilion, simply named Wedding Cake, was designed by Portuguese artist Joana Vasconcelos as a permanent garden pavilion for the grounds of Waddesdon Manor.

Its three tiers are wrapped in glazed, pastel-toned ceramic tiles made by the historic Portuguese tile manufacturer Viúva Lamego and intended to look like cake icing. They are now faulty, forcing the structure to close because of concerns about their safety.
A report including photos of the damaged tiles was shared on Buckinghamshire Council’s online planning portal, but the root cause has not been publicly stated.
According to the BBC, a Buckinghamshire Council officer found that no viable solution to repair the faulty tiles had been identified.

As such, the council has approved a change to the listed building consent, allowing the sculpture to be removed. As the manor and its grounds are protected sites, permission must be obtained to carry out such work.
The structure must now be removed no later than January 2036. However, the Rothschild Foundation, which manages the estate, wants the sculpture removed as soon as possible, according to the BBC.
The revised consent also requires the surrounding landscape to be returned to grass within six months of its removal.
When the pavilion was completed, its designer Vasconcelos told Dezeen it was her “most ambitious project to date”.
Her use of tiles reflected her ambition to use ceramics and textiles to challenge traditional hierarchies of what she called “noble materials”, such as marble, in grand architectural settings.

The manufacturer Viúva Lamego’s standard 14-by-14 centimetre tiles determined the size of the overall structure. It has an 11-metre diameter, which was the smallest that could be achieved using the tiles.
The pavilion is the fourth project by Vasconcelos created for the estate, which was built in the 1870s by Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild to entertain guests and showcase his ceramic collections.
A spokesperson for the manor said it plans to continue to commission artwork for its grounds.
“We are hoping to continue to showcase art in the landscape, including plans for a new contemporary sculpture trail in the grounds of Waddesdon Manor, which will open in July 2027,” they said.
Other projects by Vasconcelos featured on Dezeen include a 24-metre-long textile installation for Dior’s Autumn Winter 2023 catwalk show.

Elsewhere, we recently reported on the dismantling of Rike Concert Hall, designed by Italian practice Studio Fuksas. It is being demolished less than 15 years after it was completed, and before ever opening to the public.
Photography by Chris Lacey and Merriman Photography

items.title: DJ Tim Westwood denies two more sexual offences
paragraphs: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has denied two more sexual offences during a court hearing.
His latest pleas of not guilty mean he now denies a total of 17 charges concerning allegations by nine women between 1983 and 2016.
The 69-year-old pleaded not guilty to indecently assaulting a teenage girl aged 16 or 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham, west London, in 1991 at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday.
At the same hearing, Westwood also denied sexually assaulting an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth, south London, in May 2004.
Westwood, of Fitzrovia, in London's West End, was charged in October last year with offences against seven women, which he also denies.
He is accused of four indecent assaults in the 1980s in London, as well as three indecent assaults while at the BBC in the 1990s.
The defendant is also alleged to have raped a woman in a hotel in 1996.
Westwood is further accused of two indecent assaults and one count of rape from the early 2000s at a London address, and two counts of rape at a London address in the 2010s.
He is also alleged to have committed a sexual assault at a nightclub in Stroud, Gloucestershire, in 2010 and at a London music festival in 2016.
Westwood has been granted conditional bail and is due to face a seven-week trial at Southwark Crown Court starting on 27 January.

items.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
paragraphs: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.

In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.
Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.

"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.
On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.
He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.
But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.
"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.
Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.
And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.
Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.
Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target, external.
Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.

"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need.
"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."
Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.

In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."
Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.

For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.
Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.
The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.

As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

items.title: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools
paragraphs: NHS England has deleted a claim from its website stating 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system after the Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial technology.

Health bosses had published a list of all the NHS bodies “live” with and “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP), a system set up to improve patient outcomes, boost operating theatre efficiency and speed up bed discharges. But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down.

The move comes as ministers weigh up whether to extend Palantir’s £330m contract to 2029 and after the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) said it was examining the NHS claims about the extent of the system’s use, which critics say make it appear more embedded in the health service than it actually is.

A less detailed page now says early users were “already seeing real results – reduced admin, faster patient pathways, and more time for care”. A senior Labour MP, calling for the contract to be scrapped, warned the move threatened public trust.

Palantir was hired to help manage vast quantities of medical data held by NHS England but campaigners, MPs and doctors’ unions want the deal scrapped – often arguing its effectiveness has been overstated. NHS England was previously warned by the OSR that it has no evidence to support a claim that the technology has helped deliver more than 100,000 extra operations.

Some Palantir opponents also object to the presence in the health service of a company, founded by the Donald Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, which also works for the Israeli military and the US administration’s ICE immigration crackdown.

The Labour MP Ben Coleman, a member of the Commons health and social care select committee, said it was “troubling” that NHS England had listed the 137 trusts as benefiting from FDP, but then “apparently pulled the list when 29 said they weren’t using all or most of it”.

“When NHS England makes claims like this without checking them, it destroys trust – and it has happened before,” he added. “The statistics watchdog warned there was no evidence for the NHS’s claim of 117,000 extra operations due to the FDP. This latest overclaim could put more hospitals off using the FDP and threaten its viability.”
Coleman wants the NHS to drop Palantir and develop an open platform for health data on which NHS trusts and British tech companies can build tools instead.

The decision to take down the list of NHS trusts came after the Medact campaign group researched the use of Palantir’s technology by sending freedom of information requests to every hospital and integrated care board in England.

“It’s a relief to see these webpages taken down, but this has only happened after multiple investigations exposed the misleading nature of NHS England’s claims,” said Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, an NHS doctor and Medact spokesperson. “The question remains, why did NHSE [NHS England] spend years using shaky evidence to promote the alleged ‘benefits’ of Palantir software?”

Last week it was reported ministers planned to extend Palantir’s deal, amid intense lobbying. The US company has hired the Labour peer Tom Watson as a full-time lobbyist and he recently wrote to Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, saying Palantir wanted to help “build Britain’s sovereign technological capability”.

Meanwhile, the health workers’ union Unison has called on ministers to instead end the contract with its general secretary, Andrea Egan, telling the Guardian any decision to extend the deal would be “completely unacceptable and a betrayal of staff and patients”.

Palantir has said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients”, but Egan called it a “sinister American surveillance firm”, and said that allowing it to hold a vital NHS contract “surrenders sovereignty over our most sensitive data and poses security risks”.

Groups including the Doctors Association UK, Medact, a health justice campaign group, Amnesty UK and Just Treatment, a patients’ group, have also this week written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and Cooper opposing Labour’s reported plan to give Palantir a further two years to allow time for a transition to UK-based technology.
They say the deal could be safely ended in 2027 using an aspect of the contract called the “termination assistance period” to allow NHS trusts to transition away from Palantir’s technology.

“Ministers could risk looking as if they were saying one thing and doing another if they said they were planning for a future without Palantir while simultaneously handing it two more years to embed itself further into our health service,” the group said.
NHS England did not respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
paragraphs: ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.

One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”.

Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much.

There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies.

What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee, built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik.

For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29%, in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid.

Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”.

Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report.

The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free.

The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik. The Swedish climate means less cooling is required, and there is plenty of water around (they get most of theirs from a nearby lake that was once used for drinking water). On a dreary, rainy day, no water is needed: the air is cold enough already (15C – anything below 20C will do). They simply have to pipe it around the building. On days when it is hot, or there is surplus electricity to use, there are electrically powered chillers on the roofs that cool air using a mist of water before it is circulated around the buildings.

The future, however, lies in liquid cooling – where the heat from the chips is transferred directly to liquid, rather than through the air. The latest generation of chips require this, Wernvik explains, as we walk through a spotlessly clean room containing several fridge-sized racks of chips, arranged in two parallel rows. They take up about the same amount of space as a bus. The noise is deafening (but inaudible outside), the chips themselves are barely visible behind a spaghetti of cables and cooling tubes connected to the backs of the server racks. It is a closed-loop system, so it does not use any external water, he says. “Each rack here is basically 25 saunas that we need to cool away and keep at about 27 degrees for it to not burn up inside,” says Wernvik. “That’s the whole engineering challenge we’re trying to solve.”

These particular Blackwell chips are powering DeepL, the German-based AI translation platform. Some of EcoDataCenter’s clients are confidential; declared ones include US cloud computing company CoreWeave, French AI firm Mistral, and research institutes including the universities of Hull and York. Supporting sovereign European tech is one of their key aims, Wernvik says.

The final part of the energy equation is excess heat, which EcoDataCenter reuses as much as possible. Much of it is used to dry wood pellets – a byproduct of the timber industry. The pellets go into incinerators in populated areas to provide heating. There is one right next door, which is no coincidence. (Admittedly, burning them emits CO2, but given the circular nature of the timber industry, they are arguably carbon-neutral.)

The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun. Since the 1950s, Sweden has been building district heating networks across the country, where water is heated at large, centralised boilers, rather than in individual homes, then piped around towns and cities in underground pipes, typically at 60C to 80C. Homes and businesses extract the heat via a heat exchanger on their property. Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.

There’s another aspect of EcoDataCenter’s operation that stands out. While datacentres are being imposed on many communities from the outside, in Falun it was practically the opposite. The project was initiated by local government, says Wernvik, “so the idea from the beginning was very much based on, how do we integrate a datacentre in the local community in order for it to fit the municipality?” This was in 2010, long before the AI revolution. The municipality (like a local council) decided the project would be better handled by a private company, which led to the formation of EcoDataCenter in 2014. The first part of the Falun site was up and running in 2019. The final phases are still under construction.

Local benefits were built in from the outset: 90% of its suppliers are sourced locally and 60% of its capital expenditure is spent locally, Wernvik says. It invests in local education and training, including sponsoring local sports teams and youth activities.

Local integration is even more evident at EcoDataCenter’s second site, in the industrial city of Borlänge, about a 20-minute drive away. This facility, the first phase of which will open in 2027, has a capacity of 240MW – three times larger than Falun. And the site is enormous: 200,000 sq m. In Borlänge, by contrast, they are building on a brownfield site. Poetically, perhaps, it used to be a paper mill, which closed in 2021. A datacentre is a good replacement: it can plug into the existing industrial infrastructure in much the same way – the power grid, the nearby water supply, the district heating. It will also employ 200 to 300 people, roughly the same number that worked at the paper mill before it closed, says Wernvik. “The discussion that datacentres don’t generate that amount of jobs, that needs to be put in context. There are a lot of different datacentres.”

In Stockholm, the datacentre strategy is different, but no less joined up. Sweden’s capital has become something of a European tech centre in its own right, and demand for datacentres is high. Stockholm Data Parks – a joint initiative by the city council and the city’s energy, power grid and fibre optic companies – was founded in 2014 as “a one-stop shop in order to make it easier to attract datacentre operators,” explains Michael Gullberg, product manager at energy company Stockholm Exergi. They free up suitable land, and again, the emphasis is on sustainability, including clean power (the city hopes to be net zero by 2035) and recycling waste heat. Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital. There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating. They contribute about 1.5% of the city’s annual heat demand, which might not sound much, “but 110 gigawatt-hours of recovered heat is still a decent amount, because the system is so vast,” says Gullberg.

I visit one such facility in Kista, a suburb north of the city centre that has become Stockholm’s tech hub. It is an unobtrusive shed on an industrial estate, with a capacity of 12MW. Crucially, it is right next door to a district heating plant, so the datacentre basically pipes its heated water over the fence. It’s a win-win, says Sandra Karlsson, senior public affairs manager: “When they need to do district heating, they don’t need to boil the water from six degrees, they get it at 30 degrees from us, so they save a lot of energy.” In return, it takes in cold water from the district heating plant, which it uses for cooling.

This datacentre is run by atNorth, a company that began in Iceland, and now has 13 datacentres running or under construction across Sweden, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Conditions are similar to Sweden in all these countries, says atNorth’s CEO, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson: renewable power, reliable grids, district heating, “as well as the crappy weather that we have. We barely can live there as human beings, but datacentres love it.” As with EcoDataCenter, it claims to put sustainability and community engagement to the fore, investing and employing locally, using resources efficiently.

In terms of heat recovery, it’s a bit of a catch-22, Kristinsson points out: larger datacentres must be built in more remote areas, where there is less need for district heating, and vice versa. So they have been thinking of other ways. At its “mega site” in Varde, Denmark, with an initial capacity of 250MW, as well as district heating the plan is to channel excess heat into a 20 ha complex of greenhouses. “That means that Denmark can be self-sufficient with tomatoes during the six months of winter,” says Kristinsson. In turn, that means fewer imported vegetables: “that also saves a lot of carbon footprint, creates local jobs, and increases energy efficiency.” In Rjukan, Norway, Green Mountain’s datacentre channels excess heat to the fish farm next door.

Could other countries replicate this model? Yes and no. For one thing, the AI “hyperscalers” – such as Google, Meta, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft – dwarf Europe in terms of demand. Currently Europe’s datacentre capacity is estimated to be between 15% and 25% of that of the US. In addition, the renewable energy infrastructure in countries like Sweden has taken decades to establish; it is difficult to see the US catching up quickly. Added to which, European countries are relatively strict, both in terms of building and environmental regulations, and in areas like data privacy and protection. Elon Musk would never get away with trucking in some gas generators without permission in Sweden. To many critics, tighter regulation is exactly what the US datacentre landscape is crying out for. In July 2025, the Trump administration announced its AI Action Plan, which dismantled environmental and planning protections and rejected “radical climate dogma” in order to win the AI race.

Having said that, the US is building big in Nordic countries, to service their European users. In Sweden, Meta is building a 723MW facility in Lulea, Canadian-American firm Brookfield is planning a 750MW datacentre in Strängnäs, and Google broke ground on a 150MW plant in Horndal this June. These companies profess to be adopting the Nordic model, including building their own renewable energy supplies, although last month, the Guardian reported that Google had illegally felled 250,000 trees in Muhos, in northern Finland, to clear a site for its datacentre, leaving a barren 330 ha landscape. Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time” and planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Contractors building Microsoft’s datacentre in Gävle, Sweden, have been accused of housing their mostly foreign workers in poor conditions and subjecting them to long hours. Microsoft said of its contractors and suppliers, it “set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining” and had “robust processes in place” to ensure contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies. The community engagement has not gone so smoothly for Google in Sweden, either. In 2021, a local metal band, also named Horndal, released an album railing against Google’s imminent arrival, called Lake Drinker (sample lyrics: “The digital devil shivers of thirst … First you took our trees / Now you drink our lake”).

Both atNorth and EcoDataCenter avoid importing cheap foreign labour, they say, but Kristinsson acknowledges that opposition to datacentres in the region has been growing, largely fuelled by the backlash in the US: “It’s probably not as strong [here], but Nordics are early adopters of everything that is new. We adopt, also, the same TikTok propaganda that is showing now in the US.”
Wernvik is more measured: “The American companies and the hyperscalers are definitely needed in the ecosystem as well because they possess unique competitiveness and capabilities.”

Could Sweden become a victim of its own success? The prospect of more and more of these gigantic facilities eating up the landscape is pretty dystopian even in a large country like Sweden. Wernvik is not too worried, though: “Our core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.” Exactly how many datacentres the world needs is largely a question of demand: how much more AI we require, and how much the benefits offset the harms. That’s really a separate conversation, but at the very least, Sweden’s joined-up, long-term approach to tech, energy and communities shows that there are better and worse ways to build our digital future.
This article was amended on 12 November 2026 because an earlier version said the site covered by the EcoDataCenter in Borlänge is 200 sq km. In fact the figure is 200,000 sq m.

items.title: 5 Canadian Universities for Indian Students Who Prefer a Smaller City – level 1
paragraphs: A student moving from India to a smaller Canadian city may look forward to finding a few favourite places around campus. As the city will be home during term, a campus tour can help them picture where they would spend their time between classes. They can look for nearby outdoor space or ask about a college community and regular activities they could join.

At Queen’s University in Kingston, Campus Life provides information on student clubs, intramurals, recreational activities and volunteering in the city. Students can find activities on campus and ways to meet local people beyond it.
The university has broad undergraduate and graduate choices. Applicants still need to choose the level and degree they want and meet its admission requirements.

Queen’s offers incoming international first-year undergraduates early move-in access and dedicated academic and career advising. A recurring activity can give students somewhere to return after orientation.
Student Academic Success Services provides writing and learning-strategy support. Students can discuss unfamiliar academic expectations there as assignments begin to require more independent work.

Students considering residence should check the conditions in their offer. Residence has Living Learning Communities and interest-based options, but a bed-space commitment does not promise a particular room or building. Those conditions belong alongside the decision to study in Kingston.

The campus is in Guelph in southwestern Ontario, with organized activities and nearby outdoor space students can use during the week. The Arboretum connects to campus through trails and forest. Outdoor space is another part of the setting to consider alongside the city’s size.

At the University of Guelph, GryphLife brings together clubs, events, workshops and co-curricular opportunities. Student Volunteer Connections helps students find community volunteering that suits their interests and availability. A regular activity offers contact with people beyond orientation.

International applicants from India can contact an in-country representative with admissions questions. Global Pre-Arrival Support advisors help new students with registration, housing and arrival matters.
GO Transit serves the campus and provides a connection with the Toronto region. Students considering visits or commuting can check the current timetable from the intended starting point.

The University of New Brunswick has campuses in Fredericton and Saint John. The Fredericton campus is the option here. Applicants considering Fredericton need to confirm that their intended degree is available there.

The International Student Advisor’s Office serves undergraduate and graduate students as well as exchange and other international students. Its transition support includes pre-arrival virtual sessions, in-person workshops and individual advising. Mentorship, cultural activities and social events connect students with peers and New Brunswick communities.

items.title: RooMoo transforms abandoned mountain cabins into hotel in China
paragraphs: Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins have been repurposed for a 24-room retreat by Chinese studio RooMoo on Jinfo Mountain in Chongqing, China.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Located at an altitude of 1,200 metres on the mountain’s northern slope, the building has a white-rendered facade punctuated by eight projecting white frames that extend vertically across its elevations.
Bamboo panels and stone slabs fill sections between the frames, while timber detailing and sloping tiled roofs reference traditional buildings in the region.

Rather than using new materials, RooMoo visited local abandoned wooden cabins and furniture workshops to identify resources that could be reused. The studio ended up using timber from the cabins for the project.

“Instead of relying solely on research, we planned most of our conceptual design time to explore the mountains for locally available materials and resources to respect the local environment,” the studio said.
Among the most unusual interventions are walls made from concrete cores extracted during structural renovations, which have been stacked vertically and separated by dark metal supports.
Demolished red bricks were reused in the restaurant, while discarded bamboo scaffolding treads were cut into strips and transformed into ceiling panels and outdoor paving.
The restaurant occupies an expanded podium at the building’s lower level, with indoor dining areas leading towards outdoor terraces.
Its interiors combine stone walls, timber furniture and woven seating, while reclaimed bricks and bamboo offcuts feature in the finishes.
Visitors enter the hotel via the reception on the building’s uppermost floor, which is accessed from an entrance courtyard and connecting bridge.
A timber reception desk sits in front of a wall covered in bamboo panels, woven surfaces and discarded bamboo-shoot shells, which had been harvested locally in the mountains.
Above the lobby, an exposed pitched roof was lined with bamboo and supported by substantial timber beams.
A large woven bamboo installation hangs over the lounge, where black sofas and tan leather chairs were arranged beside full-height glazing overlooking the forested mountains.
Guestrooms were arranged in a fan-shaped layout facing the mountain landscape.
The hotel offers several room types, including courtyard rooms, suites and standard king rooms, with interiors featuring earthy colours, salvaged timber and locally made furniture.
Founded in Shanghai in 2017 by Tao Zhang, Ray Zhang and Marine Bois, RooMoo works across hospitality, restaurant, commercial, office and residential projects.
Other recent interior projects in China include a Linehouse-designed hotel with an industrial feel and a Shanghai tea shop that draws on Rockbund’s historic buildings.

items.title: Renovation delays pose "Notre Dame-like" fire risk for Houses of Parliament
paragraphs: A government report has found that risks of a major fire at the Palace of Westminster are rising as health and safety incidents increase at the UK parliament building in London, amid continuing delays to its renovation.

Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report said that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken. According to the latest report on the restoration, the overall cost of the renovation will rise by £420 million for each year the project is delayed.

Parliament voted in 2018 to vacate the Palace for restoration, however this has been delayed by ongoing disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the anticipated decades-long renovation.
“Political allergy” to updating the building

According to Public Accounts Committee chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the parliament building, which in 2023 was reported by the committee to be at “constant risk of fire”.
“There has long been a political allergy to gripping the nettle that is R&R [repair and renovation],” Clifton-Brown said.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he continued.
“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks which our committee identified three years ago.”
Renovation strategy to be decided by 2030
The report outlines four strategies for the renovation of the building laid out by the R&R Client Board, with one needing to be selected by parliament by 2030 for the programme to progress.

Two of these strategies have been recommended by the board in a bid to speed up the decision-making process. These are fully leaving the building, which is estimated to cost between £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion and take 19 to 24 years, and the partially vacating the building, which is estimated at £19.5 billion to £39.2 billion and could take up to 61 years.
Approving either of these recommendations would require parliamentary approval.
“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very big ranges,” Clifton-Brown said.
“At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”

The PAC’s report also found that there are areas that still need costing, including aspects like decommissioning, relocation of the building’s services, and the restoration of the medieval cloister court.
The cross-party committee has urged the clerks of both House of Commons and House of Lords to set out remaining cost estimates and provide a detailed schedule for the works.
“It is crucial that we preserve the palace as a symbol of our democracy,” the report said. “A failure to act would have serious consequences for taxpayers and future generations.”
The renovation of the adjacent Elizabeth Tower was recently completed by architecture studio Purcell, and last year was awarded a RIBA London award.
Image by Pandora Pictures courtesy of Shutterstock

items.title: Steven Holl designs The Sculpture Watch as a tribute to Álvaro Siza
paragraphs: American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny that was informed by conversations with Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza.
Named The Sculpture Watch, the timepiece has a dial that includes four intersecting blocks of colour within a circular case that resembles a watch designed by Siza for Cauny.
According to Holl, his watch was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects and was directly informed by a compliment the Portuguese architect once gave him.

“On July 25, 2018, I gave a summer lecture in at the Porto Academy,” Holl told Dezeen. “Siza came to my talk and came up to me after and said ‘Steven, you use colour like Matisse, I must try in my next project’.”
“Siza is the greatest living architect,” he continued. “I will never forget that afternoon. This watch is an homage to Alvaro Siza,”
The Sculpture Watch has a three-dimensional dial with the red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks raised on top of each other.

It was intended as a direct translation of Holl’s watercolour paintings that were complimented by Siza. Holl is well known for his painting and begins the majority of his architecture projects with a small watercolour sketch.
“Watercolor painting, integral to my design process for architecture, inspires this timepiece,” said Holl.
“The colour volumes on the dial are made of brass; well-tested in watchmaking and best to allow Cauny to reproduce the watercolours.”
“My approach to colour is conceptual,” he continued.

“I try to engage colour in the idea driving the design, like the ‘projected colour’ from unseen surfaces in the DE Shaw trading floor, or the complimentary colours in the ‘seven bottles of light’ in our Chapel of St. Ignatius, which is analogous to the Jesuit spiritual exercises.”
Holl also reflected on how colour can reflect the passing of time.
“Time is marked in a personal way, with each moment its own polychrome experience,” he said.
“Colour turns time’s passage into both a visual and temporal experience. The fragility and variation of colour remind us that time is a human experience of duration.”

The Sculpture Watch is the fifth piece created for Cauny in its The Architects of Time Series. Following Siza, who designed the first timepiece in the collection, architects Rafael Moneo, Eduardo Souto Moura and Tadao Ando have designed watches for the brand.
Numerous high-profile architects have turned their hands to watch design and we recently rounded up six watches designed by Pritzker Architecture Prize-winning architects.
Photography by Nuno Sousa Dias unless stated

items.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?
paragraphs: Nvidia is facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.

The chief executive and co-founder of the AI chip-making giant is at the centre of a major scandal over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia's board is reportedly meeting to discuss whether to replace Huang.
But finding the right person to lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into the world's second most valuable company - after Apple - is a challenge.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
Colette Kress is chief financial officer at Nvidia
Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, has been tipped as someone who could steady the ship in the interim, and possibly stop its share price from plunging.
An industry veteran for more than 30 years, Kress previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She "fronts every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
Chris Malachowsky is one of Nvidia's three co-founders
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.

"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young.
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.

She said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Apple's Tim Cook (R) with Jensen Huang (L) and his wife Lori Huang at the White House
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.

items.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
paragraphs: Arriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together.

It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country, except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it.

At the heart of it all is a sense of daily ritual. To pay for the shrine’s restoration, you’ll be taking a job at the local post office, which means that every morning – except Wednesdays and the weekend – you’ll bike over to collect your packages, and then spend the rest of the day riding around the snug open world making sure they all end up in the right places.

Your reward for a delivery is often a bit of cash and some local gossip. Sometimes, though, you’ll be roped into a mini game: fishing for an impatient sushi chef, say, or chopping down trees and then sanding the logs. These games can be somewhat clumsily implemented, particularly if they involve aiming, since there’s no on-screen reticule. Regardless, they provide a little bit of variation to the gentle flow of each in-game day, while reminding you of the richness and variety of the little town you’re starting to call home.

This process of coming to understand the town better each day carries the game through to the end. While it’s nice to level up and earn money, all while restoring the shrine’s big ticket items, the truest sense of accomplishment here comes when you discover that you can stop using the in-game map because the paths to and from the post office have started to become genuinely familiar.

And once you feel comfortable in the world, you can step away from your objective, thin as it is, and simply explore the space, unlocking new shrines, enjoying the local architecture and performing stunts on your BMX. (The BMX, incidentally, is one of the game’s secret stars, not just providing enough joy in its movement to keep you from fast travel, but also connecting to the wider environment with jumps and grinds, and showing you fresh opportunities for path-making in the landscape all around you.)

Whether you’re fiddling with the escapement and crystal of an old mechanical watch in Assemble With Care or rebuilding a gloriously seedy business in Promise Mascot Agency, it’s astonishing how much magic games can find in the disparate aspects of restoration and reinvention. Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a reminder that, for all the destructive powers of video games, some of the medium’s greatest potential lies with the pleasing business of putting things back together again.

items.title: Minimal merges small van and electric bike in Pedal 4 delivery vehicle
paragraphs: British start-up Minimal has designed an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van in the Pedal 4, now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.
Shortlisted in the consumer product design category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, Pedal 4 was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle has a footprint not much larger than a bike – three metres by one metre – and is able to go down pedestrianised roads and use cycle infrastructure, according to Minimal.
At the same time, it boasts 2.5 cubic metres of cargo space and in London trials made 36 per cent more deliveries per hour than vans.

“Electric vans solve the emissions problem, but not the access problem,” said Minimal CEO and co-founder Patrick Bion. “They still sit in the same traffic, fight for the same kerb space and need a driver with a licence.”

“They weren’t built for the job they’re doing,” he added. “We designed Pedal 4 around that job: a full round of deliveries, through streets a van can’t get down, ridden by anyone who can ride a bike.”

Minimal considers the Pedal 4 to be not just an electrified van or scaled-up bicycle, but a vehicle engineered specifically for delivery with an aesthetic drawn directly from its functional architecture.

It has a four-wheeled base for stability and independent double-wishbone suspension at the front and a rubber torsion axle suspension system at the rear to help keep it level around corners, even when its cargo box is full.
The team removed the traditional bike chain, minimised fasteners and reduced part counts with the aim of making the vehicle both rugged enough for its task and easily serviceable.
They wanted the vehicle’s aesthetic to come directly from its functional architecture – an exposed zinc-coated carbon steel frame with satin black metal covers.

“Pedal 4 has to do a van’s job every day for years, so it can’t be fragile, fussy or expensive,” said Minimal product design engineer Sean Heany. “Our biggest wins came from deleting parts, not adding features.”
“By rethinking the geometry, we cut part count and fastenings, which made the vehicle tougher, quicker to fix and cheaper to build in our London microfactory.”
The Pedal 4 includes two slots for swappable batteries, which lift out to charge outside of the vehicle and together give a range of 60 kilometres.
In the UK, the vehicle is classed as a heavy-duty electrically power-assisted cycle (EPAC) and can be driven without a licence, which Minimal says widens the pool of people who can do the job.

However, Minimal believes that the future of logistics lies in autonomous and worker-driven vehicles working side by side. To that end, each Pedal 4 is equipped with the company’s FleetOS fleet management software, which tracks its route and vehicle performance.

Minimal says that the data collected will be used to make the next round of design changes and inform the company’s autonomous vehicle programme. Recently, it has launched Bot, a UK- and EU-focused delivery robot.
“Pedal 4 is where our autonomy work starts,” said Heaney. “Every vehicle is connected, and more than 100,000 kilometres of real delivery data has taught us what city logistics actually demands.”
“The same principles carry over: fewer parts, lower cost, built for uptime. They are what make autonomy work economically, not just technically.”

Pedal 4 has been engineered for, tested on and now launched on London’s streets through partners Royal Mail and Evri, but Heaney says the same vehicles and software are built to scale across Europe. The company plans to launch in the US in 2027.
“London is one of the hardest places in the world to deliver, which makes it the best place to start,” said Heaney. “If Pedal 4 works on London’s streets, it can work anywhere.”
“Cities can’t keep moving goods the way they did last century,” he continued. “We need new ways of moving things that make our cities, our environment and our everyday lives better.”
Other recent new electric vehicle typologies include the Amble One – a doorless electric buggy in the vein of a golf cart – and a three-wheeler called Trinity designed for urban travel.

items.title: Access to Shanghai Grand Opera House staircase restricted to paid ticket holders
paragraphs: The Snøhetta-designed Shanghai Grand Opera House has introduced a paid ticketing system for visitors wanting to access the signature spiral staircase and rooftop viewing platform at the recently opened building in Shanghai.

When Dezeen visited the site, we observed a temporary barricade separating the free-to-access ground-level public space from the spiral staircase leading up to the roof. Access to the staircase and roof now costs 50 yuan (£5.60) per person.

Since opening, access to the architectural feature has been restricted, with visitors now required to pre-book tickets online to access it between 10:30 am and 2:30 pm. According to the booking site, people with tickets to see a performance inside the opera house are still required to purchase a ticket, and the fee includes accident insurance.
Asked about the apparent change in access requirements, Snøhetta said that demand meant that “visitor management is necessary” and that “access arrangements will continue to develop”.

“As with any major cultural institution, operational procedures continue to evolve during the opening period as the Opera House team gains experience with visitor patterns, capacity needs, and the building’s day-to-day use,” the studio told Dezeen.
“Given the exceptional public interest and the limited capacity of the roof and public stairs, visitor management is necessary to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience for everyone,” it continued.

“Access arrangements will continue to develop with operational experience, but the intention remains the same: to create a building that can be widely enjoyed by the public while balancing accessibility, safety, and the visitor experience.”
Following news that a fee had been introduced, the phrase “is it worth spending 50 yuan to visit Shanghai Grand Opera House” trended on Chinese social media.

Some commenters questioned whether charging to visit the attraction was justifiable, while others sympathised with the need for crowd control. Others shared tips on how to take the best photos of the building without paying the entrance fee.
Visitors Dezeen spoke to at the site were concerned about both the fee and the temporary barriers.

“I don’t think it’s worth the money,” Mr Qiu, who paid to climb the stairs, told Dezeen. “Basically you pay to climb a giant stair. If you want good photos of the stairs, best to take from afar, which you can do for free,”
Ms Ye, who didn’t pay the entry fee, told Dezeen that she was really disappointed that the barricade was in her photos.

“I don’t know what the point of the barricade is – to separate the paid and unpaid? Or for better crowd circulation? But at least they need to put some effort into designing it to match the beauty of the building,” she said.
“It really is an eyesore for the photos.”

The building, and its accessible roof, are often compared to Oslo Opera House, which was also designed by Snøhetta and is topped with a walkable roof. According to the studio, both projects were designed to “reduce thresholds wherever possible”.
“Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs,” said Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen at the time of the Shanghai Grand Opera House opening.

“We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue. People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” he continued.
“A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.”
Several other cultural projects in China have been built with publicly accessible roofs. However, the accessibility presented in concepts has often been restricted when the buildings open.

Also in Shanghai, the Start Museum, designed by French architect Jean Nouvel and opened in 2022, features a public roof that can be used for displaying large-scale artwork. However, the space has rarely been used.

The Amateur Architecture Studio-designed Fuchun Cultural Museum Complex is defined by a continuous undulating roof to resemble the experience of climbing the local Fuchun Mountain. However, the roof didn’t open to the public for four years and is now only open to public visits for one hour a day, three days a week.
Photography by Kaia Wang, Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao

items.title: Logitech MX Master 4 Special Edition review: Still the productivity mouse to beat, but should you upgrade?
paragraphs: A brilliant, comfortable productivity mouse. The haptics and Actions Ring reward creatives who’ll map shortcuts, but Options+ takes work, and for most MX Master 3S owners or non-creatives, it’s a marginal upgrade.
Comfortable, well-judged weight with real desk presence
Special Edition colourway offers a touch of personality
Haptic feedback adds useful tactile confirmation
Actions Ring speeds up app switching and folder access
MagSpeed scrolling is still class-leading
Needs time in Options+ to get the best from it
Marginal upgrade over the MX Master 3S unless you map shortcuts to the Action Ring
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Product: Logitech MX Master 4 (Special Edition)
Sensor & Tracking: Darkfield high precision, 200-8000 DPI
Scroll: MagSpeed electromagnetic wheel plus thumb wheel
Connectivity: Bluetooth and Logi Bolt receiver
Software: Logitech Options+ (Windows and macOS)
Best for: creatives, office workers and anyone with long desk sessions

The MX Master 4 Special Edition takes Logitech's excellent black mouse and spruces it up with a new white colourway and red-and-grey accents. Inside, it's the same MX Master 4, and like the 2025 version, it has a tough act to follow. Its predecessor, the MX Master 3S, is already one of the best productivity mice you can buy, so Logitech never intended to reinvent the wheel. Instead, we get more customisation, haptic feedback, and a handful of design tweaks, and in this Special Edition, a more personalised colour choice.

These are all the developments I’d expect from a follow-up to the excellent MX Master 3S, one of the best mice you can buy, but they make this a nicer-looking version of a mouse that was a smart evolution rather than a must-have upgrade, unless, I'd argue, you're a creative; then the Actions Ring becomes a bigger thing than you may expect and is new to MX Master 4, Special Edition or not.

The shape is the same as the MX Master 3S, with its sculpted ergonomic design, deep thumb rest, and plenty of controls to keep your hands off the keyboard. It’s comfortable for long workdays, and the weight is spot on. It has enough heft to feel planted on the desk without feeling clumsy. It’s big, though, and it won’t suit everyone. This is a mouse for your desk, not your laptop bag.
• For more control consider one of the best drawing tablets

The MagSpeed wheel is as good as ever. Flick it, and it free-spins through a long spreadsheet or a 40-page document, then ratchets back to click-by-click scrolling when you need precision. Switching between the two is automatic, which is why it’s so easy to take for granted.

The finish is where things have changed. This is the Special Edition of last year’s MX Master 4 release, so the design changes over the MX Master 3S remain. Logitech has swapped the soft, rubberised coating of older models for something harder, but it’s not slick or glassy. The cover has a nice bit of tooth, and different areas have subtly different textures, so your fingers always know where they are without you looking. It feels different from the old MX Masters. A colleague wasn’t keen on it when they tried [2025’s MX Master 4], but I got used to it quickly, so your mileage may vary, and existing owners may need a few days to adjust.

Those alterations aside, the Special Edition replaces flat blacks with a soft grey-white colour and red accents. The dark grey Actions Ring thumb rest pops in this colourway, and I far prefer it to the faceless black PC-mouse aesthetic of the base model. There’s no price difference between black and Special Edition.

The thumb rest gets the biggest rethink. It’s usually the most wasted area of a mouse, a bit of plastic to rest your thumb on. Here, it’s the way into the new virtual dial, called the Actions Ring, which makes it feel like part of the design rather than an afterthought.

The haptics are a lovely touch. They kick in when you make a selection and when you open and cycle through the Actions Ring, so I can keep my eyes on the screen, click and scroll, and still feel a little resistance and feedback. This also helps with gesture control, too, if you go as far as needing that kind of input. It’s subtle, but it makes the mouse feel more connected to what you’re doing.

As you may have guessed, the Actions Ring is the real star of the new features. It’s an on-screen dial that expands what the mouse can do, making it easy to open folders or switch between apps without dropping into the Windows menus. You can tailor the ring to the job, from something as basic as Google to Photoshop or DaVinci Resolve. Support isn’t universal, though. The best digital art and design apps like Krita, Affinity Photo and CorelDRAW are covered, but smaller apps like Escape Motions Rebelle aren’t a default option, so you’ll need a workaround: assign function keys in Options+, then match them to the app’s own shortcuts for undo, clear layer or brush toggles. It works, but you need to know your keys or set them up ahead of time.

This also means getting to grips with Options+ and its app features, which is a lot of learning for a mouse. I’d like it to work more without that software running in the background. But if you persevere, it adds real depth and makes the mouse faster to use and more flexible. Once it’s set up, you’ll love it. You can tweak everything from haptic strength to scroll speed, and I’d probably be moaning if I couldn’t fiddle.
The haptics, gestures, and Actions Ring are a step beyond the MX Master 3S, and creatives who map shortcuts to the ring will get the most from this mouse.

So, should you buy the MX Master 4 Special Edition? If you’re coming from a basic mouse, absolutely. The ergonomics, scrolling and customisation make it a brilliant tool for anyone who works at a computer all day, whether in creative apps or simply navigating menus and Google.

If you already own an MX Master 3S, it comes down to how you work. The haptics and Actions Ring are genuinely useful and, for creative apps, a new, easier way to work, so it’s worth it if you’ll map shortcuts to the ring or, like me, hate sorting through Windows menus and would rather one-click into the regular apps and files. For everyone else, they’re not enough to make a perfectly good mouse obsolete.

items.title: ‘I railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian’: the cheeky, feminist photography of Jill Posener
paragraphs: If it were a lady it would get its bottom pinched. If this lady was a car she’d run you down.” These are the words that Jill Posener immortalised in November 1979, when she picked her way through traffic on London’s Farringdon Road to photograph something most would have overlooked: a graffitied billboard. The first sentence was there by design – a sexist attempt at wit intended to promote a new Fiat. The second she has since been repeatedly accused of adding herself.

In reality, the image-maker, playwright and nonprofit founder explains from her home in California, the now infamous phrase had been daubed by two women working at the nearby offices of the socialist newspaper Morning Star. “They had seen the billboard go up and were so incensed that they came up with this solution,” Posener recalls. “They didn’t think anything of it until they saw the postcard. I sent them a whole bunch and we all had a good laugh.”

It was in a small West End print shop that Posener first produced about 100 postcards featuring her image of the defaced – or, to use her preferred term, refaced – Fiat advertisement. In the years since, she estimates that more than 1m have been sold. Although, she hastens to add, she has never made much money from them.

Not that profit was ever Posener’s goal: the postcards were simply a way to disseminate what would become her signature brand of political satire. They were created at a time when the women’s liberation and gay rights movements were at odds with Margaret Thatcher’s socially conservative vision for Britain, and explicitly railed against the stereotype of what Posener describes as “the humourless lesbian or humourless feminist”. As with much of the photographer’s work, they also carried another message: “a big fuck you to the establishment”.

More than 40 years after it was taken, in 2023 the Fiat image enjoyed a somewhat unexpected revival when it featured in Tate Britain’s landmark exhibition Women in Revolt. For Posener, who had shifted her professional focus to animal welfare more than a decade earlier, the experience was cathartic. “I had absolutely walked away from photography,” she recalls. “So I do credit the Tate show with – and I don’t mean to sound dramatic – giving me my old life back.”

The show also sparked renewed institutional interest in her work, and eventually led to a new Glasgow School of Art retrospective, Jill Posener: Stage and Street. The exhibition looks far beyond that one well-timed photograph, traversing the image-maker’s years as a member of Britain’s first professional gay theatre troupe, Gay Sweatshop, exploring her time photographing party conferences for the Daily Mirror, and re-examining her influential 1987 series, Dirty Girls Guide to London. It also features several less famous – though equally deserving – examples of wry billboard graffiti.

Together, these works make Stage and Street Posener’s most significant UK solo show to date, and the first to recognise, in its entirety, a 50-year career dedicated to cultural production and social justice. Now 73, she is stoic about the overdue nature of the honour. “I think part of it is that I’m not a particularly gifted photographer,” she says, “and I’m not being self-deprecating. But I am somebody that sees things, and it’s possible that I can see things others don’t.”

This was certainly the case in November 1979, when Posener first caught sight of the graffitied Fiat billboard. Does she worry that, even now, this remains the defining moment of her photographic career? “I think, if you have one image that so encapsulates a moment, a movement, then embrace it,” she says. “I have no problem being a one-hit wonder.”

Join Lesbians United, London, 1981 (main picture) “I’m not sure how I came upon this one, but I think it was in north London. You can’t help but laugh when you see it. Maybe because I’ve lived with a lot of anger in my life, I loved that we could respond to these things with humour, and that other people could then recognise and take pleasure from that.”

Promotional photo for Posener’s play Any Woman Can, performed by the Gay Sweatshop theatre company, 1976 “At the time, there was a lot about it that resonated with people,” says Posener. “The last line was: ‘You’re looking at a screaming lesbian, and I’m looking right back at you.’ For me, as a young woman, this was both a reflection of my own coming out and my confrontational nature toward the world.”

Margaret Thatcher at the Conservative Women’s Conference, London, 1987 “I took some photographs at the Tory party women’s conference that really made fun of that audience, and sometimes I feel embarrassed that I did that. On the other hand, they were showing who they were, and I was identifying that and photographing it. Thatcher in the creche was just the most hilarious thing I could possibly imagine.”

From A Dirty Girls Guide to London, 1987 “It’s called A Dirty Girls Guide to London because it was like a tourist brochure. But instead of just icons of British culture, there’s two women kissing, basically saying: ‘We can do this right here, in front of everybody.’ It’s about not hiding, and it’s about saying: ‘You cannot control our lives and you cannot control our bodies.’”

Drew Griffiths performs in Jingleball, a Gay Sweatshop production, eight years before his murder, which remains unsolved, 1976 “When Sweatshop had its first press conference, Drew actually couldn’t face the press. He was too ashamed to face the media, so he had his back to them, even though he’d started the group. And I think that’s what we all felt: this terrible fear, and yet this hope and possibility of something new.”
Jill Posener: Stage and Street is at Glasgow School of Art to 9 January.
