items.title: YSG creates Bali wellness hotel with DJ station
paragraphs: Australian studio YSG has converted a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture.
The Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

According to its Australian hoteliers, the hotel was inspired by “our feverish obsession with Indonesian music and culture” and its offerings include an all-day spa and a “DIY DJ station” stacked with Indonesian and Japanese city pop records curated by DJ Midnight Runners.
YSG was similarly influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“Once a private vacation residence in severe disrepair, the concrete bunker was radically transformed into a modern-day Babylon infused with cosmic references and hybrid Japanese architectural elements, including the spa’s sliding bamboo doors depicting lunar phases,” the studio said.
The hotel is only accessible via motorbike or on foot, according to the team, and is located along an alleyway.
Guests enter on the far side of the courtyard pool, while the suites and common areas enclose the space on three sides.

The suites were designed with “dreamers, misfits and wanderers in mind”, according to the hotel, and each is outfitted with an assortment of objects by local studios set against walls clad in recycled earth-based finishes.

Locally made objects throughout the hotel include counter and stools manufactured from recycled plastic bottle tops by Weedoo Plastics, pool lounge chairs handwoven from upcycled materials by BYO Living and wall sconces made of local seseh wood and green-coloured resin by AA Practice.
YSG also made efforts to source construction materials locally while working on the project, as the studio noted it was difficult to transport them to the secluded site.
This included crushing terracotta tiles and breeze blocks and repurposing them as flooding riffraff to help with drainage, and joinery designed to be assembled on site.
The studio also addressed significant water damage to the complex and replaced rotten wooden walls, portions of the roof and concrete flooring.
The project also included adding a second-storey suite made of bamboo with an oversized skylight.
Other details include a black-and-white checkered tile relief that surrounds the pool’s edge, as a nod to the Saput Poleng cloths wrapped around holy objects as part of local customs.
YSG previously converted a warehouse into a co-working space in Sydney and brought 1970s elements to a local cafe.

items.title: The Boulies EP600 office chair gave me an existential crisis
paragraphs: The Boulies EP600 is a conundrum of an office chair that gets something wrong for everything it does right. The lumbar support is one of the best, but the backrest doesn't seem to be in the right place; the armrests are mind-bogglingly adjustable but also rock-hard. The result is a chair that fails to deliver on the comfort it promises.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Am I doing this wrong? As a chair reviewer, I’d like to think I’m better at sitting on chairs than most people. I put a lot of thought and effort into how I position myself on a chair. But the Boulies EP600 has made me question how good I am at sitting on things.

On paper, the Boulies EP600 can be adjusted to a ridiculous degree. It has an innovative floating lumbar support that slides up and down depending on your fore or aft position, which would make it one of the best office chairs for back pain. In reality, it’s just not that comfortable.

The real highlight of the Boulies Ep600 is the lumbar support, a really smart piece of counterbalanced engineering that tracks up and down with your lumbar as you move forwards and backwards on the chair. It achieves mechanically what the Hbada X7 failed to do electronically, with none of that chair’s irritating motor noises and intrusive micro-adjustments. It can be locked in place, too, but I found the floating mode suited me really well.

While the lumbar support is the best feature here, it’s coupled with the absolute worst: the back support. There’s nothing wrong with the support itself, but it’s positioned too far back in relation to the seat pad. If you want back support, then you have to lean right back in the seat, and you’re then an unfathomable distance away from your screen. The headrest is fine, but its bracket either goes higher or more forwards, but never both. As a taller person, I found that the chair was conspiring to position my head as far away from the monitor as is physically possible.

This distance is what got me questioning whether I’ve been sitting properly for all these years. Are you meant to sit like your computer screen is repulsive? It's something that I’ve been aware of in other chairs, but here it’s really noticeable: ideally you should be able to touch your screen with a fully stretched arm when your back is supported, but the Boulies EP600 puts a good few inches between my fingertips and Reddit.

When you want to relax, the chair does lean back further, and while the pull-out leg rest is appreciated, it’s made of rock-hard plastic. I’d sacrifice the leg rest for a chair that leans forwards to offer back support when you’re in those intensely focused sessions — it was a feature I really appreciated when I reviewed the Titan Evo NanoGen.

Elsewhere in the Boulies EP600 it’s business as usual. The armrests flex and pivot all over the place, and even tilt upwards or out of the way completely, but they’re coupled with very, very firm cushions that make you painfully aware of your elbow bones. The seatpad also moves backwards and forwards to accommodate different leg lengths and preferences.

From the front, the Boulies EP600 tends towards the uglier side of office chairs, with its curved back panels resembling an insect: thorax, abdomen, and. It looks better from behind; its curved central column gives it an aesthetically pleasing structure, and its chunky armrests make it feel like the captain’s chair on the U.S.S. Enterprise.

One thing I like about mesh chairs (and this is mesh throughout) is that their transparency helps negate some of the weightiness of the design, and this is the case here. The grey colour scheme Boulies supplied has a slightly Y2K feel, especially in the silver plastic under the armrests and the metallic accent on the rear column. It’s also available in black, which looks even more insectoid.

I almost forgot to mention the pull-out leg rest, because I’d blanked it from my mind, but it’s really hideous; a single piece of plastic that wouldn’t look out of place in a 1970s hospital, which was truly the worst time for healthcare implements.

The Boulies EP600 is never going to win a good-looking chair contest, but this bug-like design language has become fairly standard in mid-range ergonomic chairs, and I don’t think it’s better or worse than any other.

One thing I’ve come to loathe in chair construction is bases that need to be screwed together. I get that it saves packaging, but it’s such a chore! Thankfully, Boulies has overcome this with arms that lever themselves into position when you stand on the centre and, oh my gosh, it’s one of the most satisfying things I’ve ever experienced. More of this, please!

The manual is a little basic, and there are a few bolts that are fiddly to get in the right place, but overall it’s a 15-minute process with very little that can go wrong. The fully built chair feels solid and well-made; there are no creaking parts and nothing wobbles.
At 21kg, it’s reassuringly heavy, and its wide dimensions make it tricky to move through my Hobbity Victorian English home, so this is one that you won't want to move around too much.
The Boulies EP600 carries a retail price of $489.99 / £429.99, but at the time of writing it’s $409.99 / £339.99, placing it firmly in the mid-range of ergonomic chairs.

For around the same price, you can pick up the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro, which includes a similar range of features. It lacks Boulies’ dynamic lumbar support and built-in leg rest, but it’s still a supremely comfortable chair with those all-important adjustable armrests.

If you want even more adjustability in a similar form factor, look no further than Hinomi’s H2 Pro. While its price point is a bit higher (it’s currently $569 / £569), it has adjustable points just about everywhere, and I found it really comfortable and supportive once I got the fit dialled in.

Boulies primarily makes gaming chairs, and it feels as if the EP600 hasn’t quite shaken off its specialisation. It could work well if you’re primarily into gaming or watching movies and occasionally delve into more focused tasks. The flip-up armrests make it good for people who like to draw at their desks or noodle on a guitar to get those creative juices flowing. But designers, editors, and chair review writers who like a more upright position for focused work just won’t find enough support here.

It’s a shame because the lumbar support is smart, the armrests are versatile, and the mesh design is comfortable and cool. It’s also one of the easiest chairs to assemble. A few tweaks, such as better back support and plusher armrests, and the Boulies EP600 would be an instant classic. But as it stands, it’s hard to recommend, and I'm confident that the problem is with the design, not the person who's sitting on it.

With over 20 years of experience in journalism and content creation, Henry has covered everything from gaming and digital art to VFX, new tech and film. He loves to translate the complex into accessible, whether that with text or video. When he’s not thinking about what creatives need to do their jobs properly, he’s busy discovering new and creative ways to fall off his bicycle.

items.title: Argentinian lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case
paragraphs: Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.

Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.

Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet on Tuesday a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.

Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.

“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici,” he said. “We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”

Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.

She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.

Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.

The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.

Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.

In his closing remarks to the panel of 20 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.

He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”

Sam Wordsworth KC, responding for the UK, said there was nothing in the convention on the law of the seas, over which Itlos has jurisdiction, which obliged a state not to “aggravate” a sovereignty dispute and that the UN resolution cited by Kohen as the “elephant in the room” was not legally binding.

The UK further claims there is no need for urgent suspension of drilling as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an Itlos arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on Argentina’s wider claim that its rights have been breached.

During his recent speech at the UN general assembly, Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause”. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
Itlos is expected to make its ruling on Argentina’s case on 28 November.

items.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
paragraphs: This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad.

In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life.

That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air. We put on a brave face but secretly I was thinking: “Wow, the risks are no longer theoretical. I could have been on that.”

The dust cloud in the image emerged from the concrete launchpad and tower – obliterated by the power of the raptor engines. The debris ended up all over the local houses and SpaceX closed the launch facility for reconstruction for four months while they conducted a huge clean-up operation. Going to space feels futuristic and grandiose but there are still the practical problems – like people wiping dust off their windows.

Unbeknown to me, this photograph marked the beginning of the end of dearMoon. We didn’t know at that time there was trouble in paradise and a loss of faith in the project and its viability. Maezawa had gone back to Japan after the first launch attempt had been scrubbed the day before, and so missed this launch. Eventually, in mid-2024, we all received an email invite to a Zoom call. We were told that they were not continuing the project, but it was made to sound like the disappointment should be only equal to finding out your favourite TV show was cancelled. But it was completely flooring. This wasn’t just a project – it had become my whole identity. I still dreamed about it every night. It was a poisoned chalice and it obliterated my career as I knew it.

This photograph is now part of my Rhi-Entry project, which is my version of a modern-day tragic cycle. I am Icarus, who flew too close to the sun and my wings melted. It is both tongue-in-cheek and deadly serious, moving through bathos, pathos and hamartia. The exhibition combines the visual tropes of the space museum, brings together facts and fiction, a reflection on the past and my fears for the future, with my personal story as its spine. The irony is, all of my work is about calling out structural abuses of power, and I was blinded by the wild promise of an almost impossible dream.

I wanted to change how we collectively feel about who is selected to go to space. I’m a 5ft 2in, gobby, messy queer who grew up on a sailing boat. Living in a tin can floating with blackness above and below, surviving with what you have – it was the closest thing on Earth to going to space, and uniquely prepared me for potentially leaving our planet. We still think of people who go to space as untouchable superheroes. The chiselled-jaw GI Joe lookalike with a wife at home. I wanted to break that mould. It was also about exploring ideas and debates around the colonisation and ownership of space, and who has the right to explore it – and to craft our collective future.

Rhi-Entry is at the International Centre for the Image, Dublin, until 23 December. Rhiannon Adam’s work is also part of Space @ Fotografiska Tallinn until 17 January. Her book Polaroid: The Missing Manual is published by Thames and Hudson. See more @rhiannon_adam

Born: Cork, Ireland, 1985 High point: Being selected for dearMoon. Strangers coming up to me to tell me that my book Big Fence changed the way that they move through the world Top tip: It never gets easier, so don’t expect it to! Remember that we’re all in the same boat; you can win the biggest award at 20 or at 85, and whichever way it happens, don’t count your chickens. Be nice to everyone, be generous with your time, treat others as you want to be treated – being a diva isn’t a good look. No matter how much success you have, remember half of it was luck and being in the right place at the right time. Listen to Baz Luhrmann’s Everybody’s Free to Wear Sunscreen at least once a year

items.title: The 37 best Christmas gifts in the UK for tweens – chosen by 10- to 12-year-olds
paragraphs: Buying for someone in the tweenage years can be a balancing act: while some kids are still crafting, enjoying board games and deep into Lego, others have moved on to skincare and guitars.

So, in an effort to cover the whole range, I spoke to 20 tweens (from 10 to 12 years old) from across the country. But instead of asking what they want, I quizzed them on the things they already have, truly love and use regularly. Here are their tried and tested gift ideas for a range of prices.

I’ve read all nine of the Lottie Brooks books, and I can’t wait to read number 10, Twelve Disasters of Christmas. I really like them because they are easy to read and teach you about life. They make me laugh out loud. I also think kids my age would love to get a dance mat, they’re loads of fun. Millie, 10
My friend has a 3D printer, and I love it – I think kids my age would want one so we can make fidgets and other things. I’m definitely asking for one this Christmas. Sophia, 10
For my birthday this year, I got a size 3 football and Joga shin pads, which I think are good gifts for anyone who likes football. George, 10

Daise is my favourite brand. It does lip glosses, body mists and body creams. 10-year-old girls really love the lip glosses. My recommendations are Cake Pop, Cherry Bomb and Very Vanilla. The body mists I’d recommend are Sunny and Bloom. Emily, 10
The World of Skandar: The First Unicorn Rider by AF Steadman

items.title: A warrior poet shares her views on the Russia-Ukraine war
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
The war in Ukraine has been going on for well over four years, with U.S., Ukrainian, and Russian negotiators meeting this week to find a way to end the conflict.
There are currently more than two million Ukrainian veterans of the war, and the number continues to grow.
Yaryna Chornohuz knows the reality of what they are experiencing. She is a Ukrainian poet, UAV operator, and sergeant in Ukrainian Marine Corps.
VOA spoke to her during her current tour of the United States, where she is talking about the war and reading some of her poetry, much of it written about the struggles of Ukraine's military.

Chornohuz says Ukrainian soldiers are “tired and exhausted, especially those of us constantly on the front lines without any rotation." She and her husband served seven and nine years in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, respectively.
“Yet, at the same time, we all know that we have fought for and earned the right to have a voice," she says. "We live, after all, in freedom - even on the front line, even in a war of attrition.”
She also makes the case for a postwar Ukraine being led by veterans.
"They are the ones capable of building the nation-unburdened by the legacy of corruption or a focus on personal gain and instead driven by a commitment to the common good," Chornohuz tells VOA.

The poet also spoke about the current debate over female conscription. She says it's not currently being considered but, "in a war of this scale, regardless of whether or not there is a formal mobilization of women, it is essential to prepare everyone so that, if necessary, they can become soldiers."

She tells VOA she likes to joke that "if you gathered all of us - all 75,000 women serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine - we could defend an entire small European nation. The audience at that event joked back that they would love to have an army of women like that to defend their own country."
Chornohuz also has a 12-year-old daughter. She says fighting a war and raising a child is difficult but not impossible.

"One can serve as a UAV operator and, after returning from night missions, prepare breakfast for one’s child. I did this myself while stationed near the front line, and I don’t think I’m the only one; many women manage to balance all of this."
She also shared some of her poetry, which is a way to deal with the pain of losing her fellow soldiers.
"The brightness of those eyesthe eyes of those who decided one dayto die in battleare always brighter than others’."
She is also taking time to look ahead to a Ukraine not under threat. She says that "after every war, there comes a flourishing, an era of prosperity."

"If we win this war, we will no longer be a "victim" Ukraine, nor a post-colonial state; instead, we will become a "European tiger"- a nation with immense combat experience and a battle-hardened army, capable of defending other countries in the region."

items.title: Toby Jones stars in film about UK Mars mission
paragraphs: The film has been funded by BBC Film, BFI, Sky, Screen Yorkshire and CML Entertainment Finance
Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.

The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars

Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.
Mars Express is the first feature-length film to be directed by actor Mackenzie Crook

The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."
Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists, the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.
He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.
The film is expected to be released in 2027.

items.title: UN rapporteur tells VOA rights situation is worsening in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

A United Nations official told VOA the human rights situation in Afghanistan is getting worse, as a prestigious international affairs institute recognized Afghan women for their resistance to Taliban restrictions.

The Chatham House formally recognized the women of Afghanistan on Monday, awarding them its annual prize, in recognition of their "courage, resilience and determination in the face of systematic gender persecution."

At the same time, speaking to VOA on Tuesday, Richard Bennett, U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Afghanistan warned the human rights situation in the country “is gradually and step by step getting worse, not only for girls and women, ... but also for the whole community.”

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in August, in the last five years that the Taliban have been in power in Afghanistan, the group has imposed ‘draconian’ policies that have made Afghanistan one of the world’s “gravest human rights crises, particularly for women and girls.”

Under the Taliban in Afghanistan, women are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, attending secondary schools and universities, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
Bennett said the Taliban imposed more than 200 decrees and edicts primarily restricting human rights, including more than 100 targeting women and girls.

The U.N. special rapporteur on Afghanistan told VOA there are pressures “on freedom of expression, including for the media and public and civic space and special pressure on religious and ethnic and linguistic marginalized communities who are discriminated against, not allowed to practice their traditional religions and cultural practices.”

Bennett was appointed in 2022 to monitor the human rights situation in Afghanistan. However, he has been denied entry to Afghanistan since 2024, as a Taliban spokesperson accused him of a lack of professionalism, saying "his reports are based on prejudices and anecdotes detrimental to [the] interests of Afghanistan and the Afghan people.”
Bennett told VOA that the Taliban cannot deny their human rights violations.

“The way in which we analyze the very edicts and decrees that they have passed. They cannot deny that," he said. "Of course, we also collect evidence in other ways, visually and by talking to Afghans inside Afghanistan. There is no doubt. It is uncontestable."
He added that international pressure on the group to change its positions on human rights, particularly women’s rights, has so far failed to yield results.

“So far, the pressure is not making very much difference publicly on the surface. I think privately, underneath the surface, it is making a difference," Bennett told VOA. "And there are quite a number of Taliban who do want girls to get an education, who are even sending their own daughters to get an education. So, I think in time, this will change."
The U.N. Special Rapporteur, however, said that he remains willing to work with the Taliban to reverse restrictions on women’s rights.

“I stand ready to continue dialogue and technical assistance with the Taliban to reverse their policies, including on women's and girls' education and women's employment,” he added. “It's never too late. There is always time to change, and that change should take place."

items.title: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador
paragraphs: Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”
