items.title: Caá Porá Arquitectura and Jerome Haferd Studio design drum-like performance centre for Ecuador
paragraphs: Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.
The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.
The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.
Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.
Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.
“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.
“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”
“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”
The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.
These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.
Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.
A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.
An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.
As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.
These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” said the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.
The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

items.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
paragraphs: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

items.title: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
paragraphs: The Duchy, which covers around 51,800 hectares (128,000 acres) in 19 counties, plans to use the £500m raised from the property and land sale over the next decade to invest in local communities, affordable housing and environmental projects.

Former GP Mary Ryan, a local Lib Dem councillor who has lived near the Bradninch estate for around 35 years and is supporting the farmers, said some of those affected were "experiencing enormous mental and emotional distress" as a result of the planned sell-off.
She added that while the Duchy had reportedly apologised to tenants last month, the handling of the process had been "pretty dire".

The sales programme has now been extended from Bradninch, near Cullompton, to the Duloe Estate in Cornwall and to individual holdings elsewhere in Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands, according to the TFA.
The Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, told the BBC he was listening to feedback over how the sales were being handled and offering support and mental health advice to tenants.
Morris added that the Duchy was "still committed to agriculture" but that there "may well be other disposals in the future".
In terms of immediate evictions, he said, there were "no cliff edges here" and that the Duchy was working closely with every tenant to find a suitable outcome.
"In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained.

"For many of our farmers, it's a generational aspiration to own their farm. A few people have said it to me: 'My grandfather wanted to buy his farm. My father wanted to buy the farm. And now I've got the opportunity and it's an amazing outcome'.
"That's kind of what's driving me through what, at times, has been a little bit of turbulence."
The Duchy - which was established in 1337 - currently has around 700 agricultural lettings, with around 300 whole farm holdings made up of a farmhouse, land and buildings.
Farmers are on a mix of contracts ranging from time-limited to lifelong, with an option to pass the tenancy down through a family.

George Dunn, TFA chief executive, said the organisation was in "deep discussions" with the Duchy and that poor communication had led to tenants "facing prolonged uncertainty over valuations, timing and the options available to them".
"Once a family is told that its long-term relationship with the Duchy may change permanently, that uncertainty lives with them 24/7," he told the BBC.

He added that while he welcomed the Duchy's assurance that "nobody will be made homeless" not every tenant "will be able or want to buy the farms that they operate and fair alternatives must be explored for those for whom ownership is unaffordable".
A spokeswoman for the Duchy said: "We are engaging with people directly and supporting them through the process with care and respect.
"We recognise that each of our tenant's circumstances are different, and we are taking a careful, case-by-case approach."

items.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
paragraphs: Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.
Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked.

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.
Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.
"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.
Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.
Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.
The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.
Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.
Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.
To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.
They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.
Such tech has been under development for 20 years.
During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.
Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.
The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems.
The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them.
Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub, external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September.

The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board.

Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels.

What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran.
Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world.
Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch.
The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries.

It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine.
Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air.
Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014.
"There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk."
He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid.
"We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns."

The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture.

The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it."

items.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
paragraphs: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.
Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.
The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.

Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.

"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."
With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.
"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."
Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.
Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.
In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.
Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.

This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.
Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.
But the workers have a huge task on their hands.
Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.
The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.
Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.
Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades

"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.
He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely.
But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.

The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary.
However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers.

"Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."
Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.
Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.
But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.
A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".
So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.
In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.

Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall.

"For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean.
"We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."

The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.
Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.

In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.

The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.
The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.
Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.

It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

items.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
paragraphs: Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom given it is the sole manufacturer of a crucial computer chip required for successfully operating AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang was an executive at a Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained the US government did not inform the firm that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring of this year warning that the Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Beijing has rejected claims that Jensen Huang has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".
US President Donald Trump said Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the Nvidia boss told him "I had no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed the him.
However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.
The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.
The committee has the authority to subpoena Jensen Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before the committee, if deemed necessary.
When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

Joon Kim, who will lead Nvidia's investigation, is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focused on fraud and other criminal acts.
Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.
The investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with Nvidia.
He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.
It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any additional of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

items.title: Why Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed
paragraphs: David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.

He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.
His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.

In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.
Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.
This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.

Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.
There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.
The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.
But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.

The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.

The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.

Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest.
If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any wrong party seeks redress against journalists.
After Walliams lost last week, and the court's judgment underlines how seriously it considered the risks to him to be, Mr Justice Nicklin asked whether there were plans for an appeal.
But Walliams had not been able to give his lawyers instructions on how to proceed.

"There is a degree of urgency - the court has moved exceptionally quickly to accommodate this trial and produce this judgment," said Mr Justice Nicklin. "It is slightly concerning that there is not an ability to proceed today. I don't understand really. If I was satisfied that there were compelling reasons why permission to appeal should be granted I could say so now. "
Sara Mansoori KC, Walliams' counsel, said the case raised "novel issues of law based on unusual facts" but because of the vulnerable nature of her client - in hospital - she needed more time.
The judge gave Walliams until 16:30 GMT on Monday to come up with some proper grounds to challenge his decision. Those papers were never filed.
The failure to launch an appeal bid meant that ITN and the Guardian were free to publish.

While all this had been going on in court - there was a social media-sized elephant in the room. No end of people were posting 'It's David Walliams' and wondering why we bona fide journalists were not saying the same.

When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication. That is why bona fide journalists who understand the law did not wade in.
But there is a massive practical issue: how far does the writ of English law run in cyber space?
One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west". That comment underlines the concern among legal professionals.
But the question is how to enforce injunctions in an age of rapid fire digital gossip?

If a newsroom were to breach an order, the nature of a large media organisation's audience means that publication would be seen by judges to be rather grave and the editor would likely be up in court.

One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person by passing on gossip is obviously less impactful. If Chad from Utah reposts Dorothy from Liverpool's gossip, the chances of being hauled before a judge are even more remote.

But what happens when thousands of people are all saying the same - and then their claims, perhaps based on a kernel of unreportable truth, are magnified by AI summaries and algorithms dripping content into phones?
At that point, mathematically speaking the impact is greater than one single newsroom breaching an injunction.

The public's perception of the Walliams case was complicated because his name became known from the start - but the furious gossip over who "PPT" really was shows there is an existential threat to how courts try to control information to prevent harm. And it's not clear whether they have any answer to it.

items.title: UNESCO warns Afghanistan could lose a generation of professionals if ban on girls’ education continues
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

Afghanistan risks losing a generation of future teachers, healthcare professionals and other skilled workers if girls and women remain barred from secondary and higher education, a U.N. official told VOA.
“Our message is very clear: Afghanistan cannot afford to lose another generation of learners,” Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO Program Coordinator for Education in Emergencies, said in an interview.

Jaberian called for efforts to bring girls and women back to school, strengthen Afghanistan’s education system and ensure all children “can fully exercise their basic human right to quality education.”
A U.N. report, released in November, stated that the Taliban ban had excluded an estimated 2.4 million girls from secondary education, while no girls have enrolled in universities in 2026.
After seizing power in 2021, the Taliban banned girls from secondary education, barred women from attending universities in December 2022 and from studying at medical institutions in December 2024.

In addition to banning girls from secondary and university education, the Taliban also imposed repressive restrictions on women, barring them from working in government agencies and non-government organizations, going to public parks, beauty salons and gyms, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.
Jaberian said the first priority is to immediately reopen schools for girls.
“The return of all girls and women to the education system is fundamental for us, and no alternative learning opportunity can replace their formal schooling,” she added.
Jaberian, however, said efforts should also prioritize learning opportunities for children and young people currently excluded from education, particularly girls and women.
She also said that it is important to improve the quality of education in Afghanistan.

“Strengthening the quality of education through supporting teachers and teaching and learning materials, and of course, ensuring better education data and planning, as you can see within the recently published report.”

items.title: Shaw Contract Design Awards name top interiors of 2026
paragraphs: A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.
The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.
“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.
“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”
The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and new elements, as well as the important social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.
Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a new layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.
Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.
The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.
We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.
Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

It was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” interiors, which combine a wide range of workspaces with shared hospitality areas. M Moser Associates dedicated more than half of the building to community spaces.
Finally, DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects is a large workplace for a legal company. It was designed to cater to different work styles.
According to Shaw Contract, it won the prize for providing a broad range of workspaces suited to different needs, as well as wellbeing, dining and meeting areas.
The jury particularly enjoyed how materials had been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”.
The Best of Globe winners are selected from the programme’s Best of Region winners. Winners receive global media exposure and a donation to a charity of their choice.
Shaw Contract’s ambition for the award programme is to encourage discourse within the international creative community.
To learn more about Shaw Contract and the awards programme, visit its website here.

items.title: Imprisoned Iranian human rights lawyer suffers heart attack
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi, who was being held in solitary confinement in Isfahan prison, reportedly suffered a mild heart attack on November 8, according to Iranian human rights groups.

The Norway-based group Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), citing an unnamed source, said Davoudi was transferred to Al-Zahra Hospital in Isfahan for treatment but was discharged Monday and has since been returned to prison.

The source said Iranian authorities attributed Davoudi's deteriorating health to a change in his medication during his detention, even though Davoudi was not taking any medication at the time of his arrest.
The human rights lawyer was arrested on October 11, 2026, while attending court and defending one of his clients.

He was among the lawyers involved in the so-called “Alikhani Square” protests case. More than 50 people were arrested and put on trial for their alleged role in the January 2026 protests in Isfahan. At least 12 were sentenced to death.

Davoudi also officiated by phone the wedding ceremony of detained protesters Alireza Sepahi and Mahshad Keshani. The ceremony took place just hours before Sepahi was executed, and an audio recording of the event was later published by media outlets.
The report of Davoudi’s transfer to the hospital comes amid growing concerns about his health and personal safety while in detention.

items.title: Adobe's approach to AI has pleasantly surprised me
paragraphs: Adobe MAX is in full swing, and after this morning's keynote, I'm left feeling pleasantly surprised. I initially arrived with slight apprehension, expecting to leave fatigued and underwhelmed by the grand kickoff, especially regarding Adobe's ever-divisive AI developments. Instead, I must confess, I'm cautiously hopeful.

It's no secret Adobe is going full send on AI, after a full fleet of AI partnerships and Firefly taking centre stage, blossoming into a full-fledged creative studio. It could all start to feel a little existential, but beaming under the stage lights, future Adobe CEO Anil Chakravarthy assures me, "Adobe will meet you where you are”. And I start to believe him.

AI has persisted as a divisive topic among creatives, but Adobe has shown a refreshing self-awareness around the tension. Emerging on stage, vice president Deepa Subramaniam wastes no time addressing that "things feel uncertain” in the wake of AI.

Assurances of “reliability” and “safety” are thrown around, honing in on Adobe's legacy as a brand shaped and "built by creatives that care about the craft”. She assures the sceptics among the crowd (myself included) that for Adobe, "Creativity isn’t a side project; it’s a way of life,” and to my surprise, the typically eye-roll-worthy sentiment soothes me. At its core, it seems Adobe hasn't forgotten about the creatives that shaped its brand.

Deepa raises some valid points. In an increasingly content-driven world, more is asked of us. The humble graphic designer is now expected to be a web designer, motion designer, and social media maverick all in one – something that Adobe's “rich learning ecosystem” can solve, according to Deepa. Creatives are trapped in a battle with waning time and resources, with demand for content ever increasing. If handled correctly, time-saving AI could offer the respite we need, but it raises a moral dilemma. Where do we stop?
For more Adobe news, check out why Adobe's Google partnership hints at a radically different future for Photoshop or take a look at the new AI features coming to Photoshop.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
paragraphs: Fire crews in Aspen, Colorado are training to pilot new drones like this one from manufacturer Seneca. They can carry and drop fire-suppressing foam. Halle Zander hide caption
On a rare overcast day in late summer, red-and-white fire trucks pepper a grassy strip of land in the mountains of western Colorado.
A persistent buzzing rises and falls as several uniformed staff from the Aspen Fire Protection District huddle around an iPad, watching one of their volunteer firefighters control a massive drone.
This first-of-its-kind machine looks like a giant bug. Black and white with propellers attached to four large arms, it's about 10 by 12 feet wide — roughly the size of a small U-Haul trailer.
While firefighters have used drones to monitor wildfires for decades, this new product could use AI to help extinguish fires.

One of Seneca's firefighting drones hovers over private land outside of Aspen, Colo. on Aug. 24, 2026. Once its staff complete the training process, the Aspen Fire Protection District will be the first fire department in the country to operate the drones independently. Halle Zander hide caption

Developed by the California-based company Seneca, the drones are designed to work in a swarm. Similar to a small fire engine, five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters in Aspen reported they were easy to operate.
"We were just joking that my 12-year-old could fly these things," said Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire.

When Aspen Fire officially launches its new drone program, as early as next year, it'll be the first fire department in the world to operate the drones independently. So far, they've only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.
One of Seneca's drones releases a stream of water during a training session outside of Aspen, Colo. on Aug. 24, 2026. Halle Zander hide caption

Fisher wants to send these drones to hard-to-reach fires, like remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen, famously home to billions of dollars in real estate, is surrounded by dense forests — like an expensive tinderbox with few evacuation routes for residents and visitors.
"If we could get it quick, keep them small and attack them while they're smoldering instead of waiting for the wind to pick them up, I feel like that's the most ideal use case," Fisher said.
According to Seneca's founder Stuart Landesberg, the drones can bypass steep or otherwise treacherous terrain quickly and have a range of 5 to ten miles — double that if they're empty.
Hovering over a fire, they use an AI-supported "sensor suite," that can calculate distance and wind speed, then release water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity to tamp down flames.
"You can think about it almost like a flying Waymo," he said.

Landesberg said the drones won't replace air tankers on big fires, but they can carry tools, monitor ongoing fires and help extinguish lingering hot spots. Compared to helicopters, they could also make aerial firefighting more affordable.
"We can be the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost," he said.
Aspen Fire says it'll pay about $2.5 million over the next five years with private donors footing the bill.
Before other fire departments around the country invest in this experimental technology, many are keeping an eye on Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

Joe Stutler is a firefighter with nearly 60 years experience, including decades as an incident commander on wildfires. He's not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, and said he's a "big proponent of technology."
He's excited that the drones could help fight fires overnight when manned aircraft are often grounded, and he hopes they'll reduce risk for firefighters on the ground and in the air.

"You look at how many wildland firefighters that have died this year — some aviation accidents," Stutler said. "We say, 'Gosh, we really want a retardant or water drop here.' … We transfer risk to those people that are flying those helicopters and those air tankers."
But Stutler remains skeptical. Seneca has tested the drones on prescribed burns, not real wildfires yet.
"I haven't seen any results," he said. "It's one thing to make a claim. It's something else to back it up with data."
If he had access, Stutler said he'd definitely try the new drones, but no matter how effective they prove to be, he still has to put firefighters on the ground.
"I've seen very few times that a 3,000-gallon water drop or a 5,000-gallon retardant drop actually put anything out," he said.
The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, and once training is complete, Fisher said the department could start flying the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County.

They can't fly the drones over populated areas, and someone has to have eyes on them at all times. Firefighters can't blindly send a drone over a ridgeline without someone perched on top of a mountain or on the other side to watch them and communicate with the pilots.
But if the drones are useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires around the state.

items.title: Newly Elected US Senators Define Their Positions on China
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

From advanced semiconductor exports to Taiwan’s defense and agricultural trade, newly elected U.S. senators have outlined a range of priorities for relations with China. Their campaign platforms and legislative records offer a look at the issues they could pursue when the next Congress convenes in January.

Among the incoming Democrats, some favor tighter technology controls and stronger support for Taiwan while questioning the economic costs of tariffs. Newly elected Republicans have advocated measures addressing arms sales, supply chains and competition affecting industries in their home states.
However, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would determine U.S. policy as he sees fit, regardless of how Republicans fared in the midterm elections.

“Congress has a role to play in our foreign policy, particularly on what it funds and in its oversight function, but the No. 1 factor in determining foreign policy has always been and will remain the president,” Rubio said.

In a Nov. 5 newsletter, the New York based ChinaTalk examined the campaign platforms and records of 12 newly elected senators, highlighting their differing priorities on trade, technology and Taiwan. ChinaTalk describes itself as a hybrid think tank and media outlet focused on China and emerging technology.

Texas Democrat James Talarico advocates legislation enforcing and strengthening export controls to keep advanced super intelligence (commonly referred to artificial intelligence) chips from adversaries who could use them against the United States. He also wants data centers to pay for infrastructure they require rather than pass costs to households.

Illinois Democrat Juliana Stratton criticized Trump’s China trade tariffs in a Chicago Sun-Times candidate questionnaire, saying tariffs increase household and agricultural costs. She favors investment in infrastructure, technology and workers, while protecting intellectual property and data from Chinese cybersecurity threats and supporting Taiwan’s self-defense.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed argues that competition with China need not lead to military conflict. His platform supports competition through research and economic strength alongside cooperation on shared interests. His SI proposals nevertheless include computing controls, customer identification requirements for computing providers and an independent safety-testing agency.
New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas has pursued legislation addressing Taiwan’s defense, international participation and diplomatic representation.
In 2023, he joined Republican Jim Banks in introducing the Taiwan Peace Through Strength Act, seeking faster arms sales, expanded military training and exchanges, and access to critical munitions.

Pappas also backed proposals in 2022 and 2025 to rename Taiwan’s representative office in Washington the “Taiwan Representative Office.” According to ChinaTalk, he supported Taiwan’s participation as a World Health Assembly observer and in World Health Organization technical meetings.

Kentucky Republican Andy Barr joined Democrat Ami Bera in questioning Secretary of State Marco Rubio in June about proposed Taiwan arms sales, reported delays and the administration’s commitment to longstanding Taiwan policy.

Louisiana Republican Julia Letlow helped introduce the Safer Shrimp Imports Act in 2025, seeking stronger food-safety oversight. She also joined calls for a Section 301 investigation into unfair seafood trade practices. ChinaTalk identified competition from Chinese seafood imports among her concerns.

Oklahoma Republican Kevin Hern introduced the Countering Communist China Act in 2024, addressing investment, supply chains, research, education, Taiwan and defense. His proposals include disclosure of Chinese Communist Party funding for think tanks and nonprofits, restrictions on paid lobbying, and sanctions targeting senior party officials involved in threats to Taiwan’s sovereignty.

These positions are proposals and records, not decisions by the next Congress. Senators can introduce legislation, conduct oversight and consider presidential nominations, but individual preferences do not establish party consensus.

Their congressional influence will depend on committee assignments, negotiations and legislative support. The U.S. president ultimately retains a leading role in diplomacy and policy implementation, along with the power to veto legislation.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a Democratic-controlled Congress in January would not change the administration’s approach to foreign policy, emphasizing that the president has primary authority over its direction.

Rubio said Congress has a role in funding, appropriations and oversight, but added that “it won’t influence or change the President’s directives in terms of what he was elected to do. The president was elected to execute the foreign policy of the United States. That is a function of the executive branch.”

items.title: PPAA creates twin houses in Mexico as an "argument for building less"
paragraphs: Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

“Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,

“Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers’ houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.
“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture.”
The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.
From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.
To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.
The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical plans, though their place in the landscape differs.
Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.
A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.
Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.
The stepped arrangement of both floors, in plan and section, also operates as a device for privacy between the two houses, PPAA explained.

“The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.
The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.
“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.
“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first “all-wood” mass timber structure in Querétaro.
Architecture: PPAADesign Team: Pablo Pérez Palacios, Emilio Calvo, Miguel Vargas, Jonathan Reséndiz, Adriana Hernández Interiors: Mariana Morales

items.title: £568 off makes this a great budget PC for creatives as well as gamers
paragraphs: The RAM crisis has caused a spike in the price of PCs, and that's made 2026 a difficult year for creatives and gamers alike. The good news is that you might not have to wait to Black Friday at the end of the month to find a decent discount. Right now, AO has the Acer NITRO 20 N20-101 Gaming PC reduced by £568 to £1,031 – the price of a budget laptop.

The entry-level specs won't interest professional video editors (see our guide to the best desktop PCs for video editors if you're in that category), but dedicated Nvidia graphics mean this budget setup is ready to handle lighter content creation as well as gaming, and it would mark a step up from a laptop with integrated graphics.

Whether it's for gaming or content creation, there are two big advantages of a desktop PC over a laptop. Firstly, you tend to get more bang for your buck in the first place. As a rule, you tend to get more powerful internals, in the form of a superior CPU and GPU and more RAM, compared to what you would get in a laptop at the same price point (of course, some of this is outweighed by the fact that you also need to invest in a monitor and peripherals).

But the biggest advantage of a desktop PC is upgradability. If you find you outgrow the RTX 5060 too quickly, or processes are getting bottlenecked and you need more RAM, or more storage, you can buy the additional internals that you need as you need them and upgrade the configuration yourself, potentially multiple times.

items.title: Letter: Ian Berry obituary
paragraphs: By the time the photographer Ian Berry persuaded the Russian officer at the Czech border in 1968 that he was on the way to an architects’ conference, he had already been commissioned to contribute to Manplan, a groundbreaking series of photo essays in the Architectural Review in 1969-70.

Conceived by the journal’s visionary and somewhat eccentric editor/proprietor Hubert de Cronin Hastings, the eight editions, each with a specially commissioned photographer and editor, were not the publishing success that he had hoped for. Nonetheless, the series has since been described as “the bravest moment in architectural publishing”.
Berry’s contribution came in the second edition, called Society and Its Contacts, otherwise transport and communications, aiming to show what society needs, rather than what will pay best.

items.title: With £700 off, this LG soundbar is now the perfect upgrade for a home entertainment setup
paragraphs: There are a lot of all-in-one soundbars out there these days, but separates can still make the difference for a home entertainment setup, and they don't always have to cost so much more. Right now, AO has a massive £700 off the LG US80TR, reducing the price to just £399.

This is a full 5.1.3-channel package with real rear satellite speakers and a wireless subwoofer. This makes it stand out from all those one-piece soundbars, which use virtual processing to try to mimic the effect of surround sound. The result is a fuller, more rounded and more immersive experience (also see our best headphones if you want options for listening alone).

Modern flat-screen TVs are too thin to house quality speakers, often resulting in muddy sound and hard-to-hear dialogue. Soundbars provide a budget, space-friendly upgrade without having to run speaker wires across your room or buy an AV receiver.

Many of them come as a single piece and use processing to try to replicate the effect of surround sound. The LG US80TR 5.1.3 does things properly with physical rear speakers and subwoofer for more immersive sound while still keeping clutter to a minimum.

It comprises the main soundbar, wireless rear satellites and a dedicated subwoofer. With an output of 580W, it can handle quiet dialogue as well as loud sound effects and soundtracks with nuance and sensitivity. The drivers bounce sound off your ceiling to create overhead effects like rain, while the dedicated center channel puts dialogue at the fore where you want it and the subwoofer delivers a punch at the low end, also serving for music and gaming.

items.title: Is ArtStation's new AI art policy good enough?
paragraphs: When KitBash bought ArtStation, it pledged the address users concerns about the flood of AI content on the digital art platform. It took the first step back in September, when it turned on 'NoAI' for uploads by default, marking them as unavailable for AI training.

Now a new update introduces an attempt to police generative AI content along with more complete AI declarations and more control over filtering. The aim is to make it easier to users to control what they see, but it's got a mixed response from artists so far.

We're introducing the next phase of generative AI content controls. Creators will have clearer AI declaration requirements when publishing, and AI filtering is now on by default, with options that give you finer control. Learn what's changing → https://t.co/cuHmcoAuhw https://t.co/64PevA0XjmNovember 9, 2026

When publishing content on ArtStation, users will now be asked to declare whether generative AI was used in the creation of the piece. Creators can identify their work as primarily generative AI, mixed generative AI and non-generative methods or 100% non-generative.
This relies on users being upfront, and ArtStation says that most are. However, it's recognised that there is a problem with people uploading AI-generated content without flagging it as such.

That leads to the second aspect of the latest update, which is a dedicated channel for reporting AI content. If users come across artwork they think is AI-generated but which isn't labelled, they can report it. ArtStation says that every report will help improve its AI filtering for the whole community.

Users also get more control over what they're shown: they can choose whether to hide declared generative AI content, or to allow mixed generative and non-generative workflows, and they can adjust how aggressively ArtStation filters content based on user reports of suspected generative AI.

The 'Strict' setting hides artwork when just a few reports suggest it may be AI-generated. 'Balanced' filters it out when there’s a moderate level of reports and 'Loose' removes it only when user signals are strongest. By default, the filter will be set to not show any project declared as AI-generated, tagged with 'CreatedwithAI' or tagged with generative AI tools, and suspected as AI will be set to strict.

The platform risks becoming useless if it's impossible to find interesting work because of the sheer volume of low-quality AI-generated content. Many users have welcomed the latest update as a move in the right direction, while others have raised doubts about how effective the measures it will be.

There's a strong reliance on user moderation, which will depend on users accurately identifying AI art. Some may still go undetected completely, while the 'Strict' filtering could remove work falsely identified as AI.

It's not yet clear if artists will be notified if their work is flagged or whether they will have a way to contest that decision. That could be a concern when even long established digital artists like Loish have been falsely accused of using AI over on platforms like TikTok.

The update highlights the difficult balancing act of policing AI content. ArtStation has a big focus on concept art, and some in the industry now see generative AI as an inevitable part of the pipeline in this field. The new Disney deal with Adobe will focus on developing custom AI models specifically for concept work. In that context, KitBash probably sees banning AI art from the platform as counterproductive if not impossible.

items.title: Adobe's Google partnership hints at a radically different future for Photoshop
paragraphs: Adobe has announced an expanded partnership with Google at Adobe MAX 2026, and while the announcement is heavy on AI jargon, there implications for creatives could be interesting.

Perhaps most exciting is a collaboration with Google DeepMind to develop new AI editing capabilities for Photoshop. The companies are exploring a customised Google image model that could allow users to make near-real-time edits using text prompts, switching between variations without disrupting their workflow. In theory, that could make generative editing feel less like a frustrating cycle of prompting and waiting, and more like working with a traditional Photoshop tool. The catch? It's still exploratory, with no release date announced.

“Adobe’s mission is to empower everyone to create, and our AI innovations are helping more people express their ideas and create in ways that amplify their voice, while maintaining creative control,” said Anil Chakravarthy, president and incoming CEO of Adobe. “Our expanded partnership combines Google’s frontier AI with Adobe’s industry-leading creative and productivity tools at global scale, enabling us to deliver differentiated experiences and bring Adobe’s innovations to more people across Adobe and Google products.”

Meanwhile, Adobe is bringing its creative tools to Google's AI Mode in Search, potentially allowing users to go straight from searching for inspiration to creating something without opening a separate app.

Adobe is also expanding its integrations with Gemini and Gemini Enterprise, enabling users to enhance images, customise designs and work with PDFs through conversational prompts. For designers churning out multiple versions of campaign assets, for example, that could be a genuine time-saver.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the announcement, though, is what it suggests about Adobe's direction. Rather than expecting creatives to work exclusively within its own apps, it seems Adobe increasingly wants its tools accessible wherever people are already working, such as Google Workspace.
For more announcements from this week, take a look at our main Adobe Max 2026 page.

items.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
paragraphs: Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

items.title: Adobe unveils Photoshop 2027 with a host of new AI features
paragraphs: Adobe unveiled Photoshop 2027 at Adobe Max, and the headline additions are two new AI-driven adjustments: Relight and Generative Restyle. Both are layer-based, so you can return to them after making other edits. There are also other AI additions, designed to save you time.
This comes alongside a host of Firefly-based AI updates, which effectively turn it into a full creative studio. You can read more about that here.

Adobe is rolling out Creative Agent, an AI agent, across several Creative Cloud apps, Photoshop included. It’s pitched at handling busywork, and can also answer how-to questions, like where a tool lives or how to complete an edit. Photoshop’s AI Assistant also gets a new AI-first workspace built around natural language prompts, with a simpler interface. You can leave it at any time to get back to the full toolset.

items.title: Adobe Premiere Pro is getting an AI agent to do the boring editing jobs
paragraphs: Premiere Pro is getting Adobe's Creative Agent, and it looks set to take a lot of the grunt work out of editing. In a pre-Adobe Max 2026 demo, I saw it apply effects across every clip in a sequence, track masked subjects through frames, and adjust colour and exposure across an entire sequence at once. The use-case argument for more AI, now Agentic AI, in creative work, and particularly here in video editing, continues to be a replacement for repetitive jobs that most editors would happily hand off.

That, of course, raises questions about who used to be handed those repetitive but creative jobs and whether those roles are now no longer viable. But for many creatives, particularly freelancers, handing process work to an AI agent is likely very enticing.

So let's take a closer look at the new Generative Media Tool for those looking to speed up their workflows. Instead of jumping between apps and AI services, editors can generate video, sound effects, soundscapes, and music directly in Premiere's timeline. You can select a range, describe what you need, and add the generated media as an editable clip, so you don't have to break your editing flow to get the material you need. The demo was certainly impressive.

More controversially, Adobe is also bringing supported third-party AI models into the workflow, giving editors more choice in how they generate video but also opening up Adobe's app ecosystem to external AI models such as Kling and Seedance 2.5, which have greyer areas than Adobe Firefly. More practically, a new Generative Remove tool, currently in beta, can delete unwanted objects from a video frame and shot, filling the space with realistic detail, even figuring out where related shadows of a now-omitted object should be removed.

Color Mode is another big part of the Premiere Pro update. It's a dedicated colour-grading workspace that reshapes the interface around the job, with editable Style Presets that can apply a consistent look across an entire sequence. They're a bit like traditional Looks, only you can get inside them and adjust the individual elements.

You can also work across groups of clips, making it easier to fix inconsistencies between shots without grading each one individually. New on-screen HUDs provide feedback as you make adjustments, helping you stay focused on the footage rather than a wall of sliders.
Adobe is also expanding its AI-powered audio tools, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source, to clean up dialogue and separate elements in a mix.

Premiere Mobile is getting the Creative Agent in private beta, bringing agentic editing to phones. It can turn footage into editable first cuts, make changes using natural-language prompts and help refine videos while keeping the creator in control.

Adobe is also adding hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks from Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to Premiere Mobile on iPhone, with Android coming soon. There's a catch: the music is licensed for personal, non-commercial videos, while commercial projects can continue to use Adobe Stock Audio.

Finally, Premiere is included in Adobe's Local MCP integrations preview. This allows third-party agents to work with native Premiere project files locally, alongside Photoshop, Illustrator and After Effects. Importantly, sequences, bins and other project elements remain editable, meaning you can step in and make changes yourself.
As ever with these tools, the real test will be how much of the creative process editors are comfortable handing over.
