items.title: Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
paragraphs: Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.
Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.
The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.
Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.
Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.
Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.
Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.
These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.

In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter, external to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.
They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

items.title: Mori AI home robot "resembles a contemporary table lamp"
paragraphs: Robotics startup OKA has released a lamp-shaped artificial intelligence robot designed to offer companionship by greeting people, dancing to music and playing nature sounds.
Mori by OKA (One Kind Artificat) is 26.4 centimetres tall, with a cloth-covered base and an illuminated, dome-shaped head that lifts to reveal cartoonish eyes that blink and swivel.
According to OKA, Mori “resembles a contemporary table lamp” and was designed to “help people feel calmer, more at ease, and more connected to the world around them”.

“We wanted Mori to feel like a familiar object in the home rather than an unfamiliar machine,” OKA told Dezeen. “Many robots look technical, mechanical, or overly human, while a lamp is something people already live with comfortably.”
The robot exists in two modes: a lamp setting, when it’s compact and at rest, and a responsive setting, when the head is lifted and tilted.

Powered by the start-up’s proprietary AI system, the robot’s responses include playing audio informed by rain and other nature sounds, changing the colour of its lamp top and performing nonverbal communication through multi-axis neck and body movement.
Users tap the top of Mori’s head and it “retracts its face and becomes a quiet lamp”. As another part of its calming offerings, grabbing its base triggers a breathing exercise.
It also makes small sounds as part of these interactions.

“Mori’s soft silhouette and tactile materials let it blend into domestic interiors,” said OKA. “Its warmth, brightness, and subtle changes can suggest comfort, curiosity, or calm, which lets Mori express itself through illumination, sound, and movement instead of screens or conversation.”

According to the company, Mori will remember occupants, routines, and interaction history and adjust its behaviour accordingly, such as using “judgment to decide when to proactively engage or remain quiet”.

The AI model is based on the concept of Attentive Intelligence, built upon research by OKA co-founder Weizhe Chen. Attentive Intelligence is an emerging framework within AI, wherein a model is proactive versus reactive to prompts.
“It reads the room before responding and weighs whether to join in, so sometimes a small nod is enough and sometimes it stays quiet,” said OKA.

“Its responses are shaped by VIBE (Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, Emotion), an inner state that drifts with time and experience, so the same greeting can come out lively one day and gentle the next.”
Mori comes in a variety of soft colourways and is rechargeable with a 2.5-hour battery life. However, OKA suggests keeping it plugged in.

OKA was founded in 2024 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by entrepreneur and designer Hua Wang and robotics researcher Weizhe Che. The company is focused on creating robotic projects that “integrate seamlessly into human life rather than forcing human life to adapt to technology”.
OKA plans to release five major “artifacts” or products in its lifetime, according to the team. The Mori robot is the first.
Mori joins a growing number of home robots released recently with “embodied AI” – or the act of inserting an AI model into a robotic body.
Other home robots include the Droxel “droid butler” and Neo, a humanoid robot dressed in a cloth bodysuit.

items.title: Unreal Engine 5.9 divides game devs with an AI-heavy update
paragraphs: Unreal Engine 5.9 has received an early preview, and it's causing a bit of controversy among developers. The latest iteration of the platform that tops our pick of the best game development programs is all about AI, and that includes its own development.

The UE 5.9 Preview is Epic Games' first engine release built mainly via agentic workflows. A lot of the updates it introduces are also around AI-assisted workflows, including the use of Unreal MCP, Unreal Assistant and a new AI-driven content creation tool called Unreal Canvas.

The Unreal Engine 5.9 MegaJam Preview is here! It’s the first Unreal Engine release built primarily with agentic workflows and opens up a few new Experimental features: check out Unreal MCP’s expanded toolsets, work with AI coding agents directly in Editor, explore AI-assisted content creation, and run your projects in a browser. This isn’t your typical Unreal Engine Preview, but it’s ready just in time for the Epic MegaJam. Invite your agents and start experimenting: https://t.co/5WpPJnT4PWNovember 9, 2026

"Invite your agents," Epic tells developers in its announcement of the Unreal Engine 5.9 preview, highlighting the ability to work with AI coding agents directly in Editor and explore AI-assisted content creation.

Unreal Canvas is described as a shared workspace where people and agents create and refine content using Unreal Engine and the other connected tools. Its canvases include text, images, videos, and mesh generators that users can control with prompts and a chosen generation service.

The companion plugin Unreal Canvas Bridge exposes Movie Render Graph rendering to Canvas as MCP tools while Unreal Canvas Spatial Annotations places annotations in the 3D scene and captures the scene for use in Canvas.

Other updates in Unreal Engine 5.9 include improvements for animation, rendering and world-building with Lumen World Cache and improved Nanite culling. You can also run projects in browser again through WebAssembly and WebGPU.

Epic stresses that this isn't a conventional preview. It was put together in about a week for the 2026 Epic AI MegaJam, which runs from 12 to 15 November. It says the aim of the release is to learn how to build the engine with multiple people directing swarms of agents working in parallel. In addition, the timing seems intended to allow the jam to serve as a testing ground.

"A handful of people directed fleets of agents to port the AI tooling from our UE6 development branch and implement Web as a target platform. Agents wrote the web platform code, starting from UE4's retired HTML5 platform, with engineers directing, reviewing, and testing the work," Epic says of how it developed the preview.

It adds: "we're already seeing benefits from this approach, and it allows us to deliver more UE5 releases with faster bug fixes and development on targeted features, all without pulling focus from UE6."

Unsurprisingly the heavy focus on AI is causing debate among developers. Those not interested in using AI agents are making a note to steer clear over concerns for the stability of the release. Epic has already clarified that some of the agent-written code still and parts of the web renderer are prototypes that will need to be cleaned up before the full release.

"I think we’ll just be staying on 5.8. LLMs are a great help, but literally everything about this preview sounds like something that crosses a boundary. Focus on optimising your code, what possessed you to add 3D model generation?" one person comments on X.

Others feels that Epic's approach is reasonable. "I'm not a fan of the asset gen stuff. But I do love more integration for agents! Including not trying to force us to use an agent IN the editor," on person argues.
Let us know what you think below. You can learn more on the website (also see our roundup of Unreal Engine tutorials and Unreal Engine courses).

items.title: David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain
paragraphs: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.
He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.
Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.
His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.
In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.
Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.
He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.
Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.
Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.
Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.
Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.
Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.
Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

items.title: UK and Argentina clash over Falklands oil project as Hamburg tribunal starts
paragraphs: Argentina has told an international tribunal that Britain’s approval of oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has dramatically deepened a sovereignty dispute that led to war four decades ago.
At the start of an historic legal clash at the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos), an Argentinian legal team argued that the oil project must be suspended.

Javier Oyarzábal, chief legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said that the 3,400 inhabitants of the Falkland Islands, whose status as a British overseas territory is disputed by Buenos Aires, had no right to the resources around the south Atlantic archipelago.

Oyarzábal said: “[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution … What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong …
“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands whose interests will be duly taken into account.”

Oyarzábal said Argentina was ready to negotiate “all aspects of the question” of the Falkland Islands, which are known as the Malvinas in Argentina, “including the present aggravation of the dispute caused by the UK”.
He accused the UK of refusing to enter talks over the islands while pushing forward on the exploitation of its natural resources in a way that would entrench the status quo.
Oyarzábal claimed that the oil money from the drilling would “finance the very military base and presence that sustains the UK’s de facto control of the territory”.

Addressing the panel’s chair, Judge Maurice Kamga, from Cameroon, he added: “Mr President, the UK cannot have it both ways. It cannot invoke the sovereignty dispute to escape jurisdiction [of Itlos] while exploiting the natural resources of the disputed area as if a dispute had already been resolved in its favour.”
The Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin, led by the Israeli-firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper, has the potential to triple the islands’ GDP per capita.

It has been condemned as unlawful by Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and his government has applied for arbitration by Itlos over the future of the project, claiming Britain’s approval of is in breach of a 1976 UN resolution calling on both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands until the sovereignty dispute is settled.

Argentina is requesting urgent provisional measures, including a commitment from the UK to “stop the drilling” which, Oyarzábal said would do no more than “preserve the present situation” and allow for constructive talks over sovereignty to begin.

At the start of the two-day hearing, the tribunal’s panel was told that a decision by the UK government to allow drilling to start in March next year was the “unilateral conduct” of a “colonial power”.

It was further claimed by Argentina that the Sea Lion oil project risked an environmental disaster on Argentina’s doorstep and that it would make the sovereignty dispute over the islands “more difficult or impossible” to resolve peacefully.

He added: “In the event of a blowout or spill, it is Argentina that would bear its consequences and be called upon to respond, not a state that is 12,700km away. More over the project lies within the search and rescue region for which Argentina is responsible”.

The long-standing dispute between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the Falklands led to war in 1982 at the cost of the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
The hearing is the first time that substantive matters relating to the Falklands have been litigated at an international tribunal.

The oil project is seen on the islands as offering the opportunity to secure their economic future, and build a sovereign wealth fund, at a time when fisheries catches on which they depend are declining.
In a show of solidarity, Princess Anne arrived in Port Stanley on Monday. Ellie Reeves, the UK’s attorney general, attended the Itlos hearing on Tuesday.

She claimed that Argentina was seeking to litigate the issue of sovereignty through Itlos, an independent judicial body established by the 1982 United Nations convention on the law of the sea to oversee maritime disputes.
She said: “We don’t think this is the forum to effectively determine sovereignty issues.”

Asked whether the UK would abide by any ruling, Reeves said: “We don’t know what’s going to happen in terms of the outcome but we don’t consider they have jurisdiction on sovereignty issues. We respect the court and the institutions … but I don’t want to get ahead of what the tribunal may or may not say.” The hearing continues.

items.title: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut
paragraphs: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.

It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.
Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

items.title: Yabba dabba doo! Could these bulging, Flintstones-style towers be the future of eco-building?
paragraphs: There’s been a geological eruption on London’s Finchley Road. Great chunks of pink basalt and igneous larvikite appear to have exploded from the railway cutting, shooting skywards to form teetering towers. Anyone trying to find Finchley Road & Frognal station need wonder no more: just look for the multistorey Stonehenge.
Countless apartment towers have sprouted above London’s stations in recent years, a result of public transport-oriented policies, but none have looked like the Flintstones were in charge.

“This is one of those stations where people are always scratching their heads trying to find it,” says architect Amin Taha, standing at the foot of his rocky megalith, an unmissable landmark next to the Overground entrance. “We’re unlikely to start building church spires or grand civic buildings with clocktowers again, so we wanted to make something people could point to and say, ‘It’s next to that building.’”

They might add that the towers, called Petra Heights, look like they’ve been assembled by a giant child, with building blocks chiselled straight from the quarry. The igneous rock that holds up these flats has been stacked with deceptive simplicity. Each slab weighs about three tonnes but they look like rustic Jenga blocks, their faces left with marks from drills and saws where they were prised from the bedrock. “Quarries normally expect architects to want everything absolutely clean cut,” says Taha. “But we just use it as it comes, saving the cost and waste of cutting. And the beauty is, you never quite know what the finished result will look like.” If only more clients were so brave.

Building a trio of six- to 10-storey towers out of solid stone may sound like an expensive proposition, but Taha says it is not only cheaper but saves a huge amount of carbon emissions compared with a concrete or steel-framed building – around 30% less in this case. If the internal frame had been made of cross-laminated timber as originally intended, instead of concrete, as built, it could have saved around 75%.

The project marks the latest step of Taha’s and engineer Steve Webb’s radical campaign to bring structural stone back into use, after more than a century of it being relegated to cladding. It follows their striking Clerkenwell Close office and residential project across town, built from similarly rugged chunks of limestone, stacked with primal relish, which was shortlisted for the Stirling prize in 2021. The duo have become evangelical about the wonders of stone, creating experimental stone beams, laminated vaults and floor slabs, using pieces of rock that quarries often treat as waste.

Webb’s firm, Webb Yates, has even developed a slender pylon prototype, exhibited at the Royal Academy, using stone’s stiffness and buckling stability to reduce the amount of steel required. It’s only a matter of time, they hope, before the industry embraces the dawn of the new stone age.

Petra Heights is their biggest proof of concept yet. It rises above the station platform like an elemental cliff, with chunks of stone bulging out at points in bouldery lumps. The three towers, which taper as they climb, are connected to a central lift and stairs, and joined by a precipitous bridge at the upper levels. Wrapped with steel mesh, the stairway is open to the elements and spills on to a lush communal roof garden, all adding to the feeling of hiking up a rocky mountain path.

The foliage will soon grow its way up the facade, as at Clerkenwell, lending it the air of an ancient ruin. In a world first, even the lift shaft is made of stone. The slabs, three metres high and 10cm thick, were shipped from Norway and assembled on site, reaching the shaft’s full height in a single day. You half expect the lift itself to be a hollowed-out boulder winched up on a rope, but even Taha’s clients have their limits.

Originally designed in 2015, the project had a bumpy ride. As is not uncommon for developments in London, the site went through three different owners before the towers were built, each time seeing the original ambition somewhat diluted as successive developers cashed in on the increased land values. The proposed mass timber frame was deemed too expensive, although Taha says the switch to concrete ended up costing much more. That change also had knock-on effects, with stone elements getting chunkier to hold up the additional weight, and braced in places by steel diagonals.

The pandemic added further setbacks. The lower floors of Sicilian basalt were already up when Covid interrupted supply, leading the remaining floors to be built with igneous grey larvikite from Norway. Both were stained with a reddish wash to match. The colour variation gives an appropriately antique feel, heightened at the base by fragments of Celtic patterns carved into the pillars, as if these venerable columns might date back much further. This archaic quality is emphasised by the names of the architects, engineers, masons and contractors being carved in a runic typeface and picked out in gold. Perhaps more architects should sign their buildings, so passersby know where to direct their praise – or ire.

“The common reaction from developers is that structural stone is too shocking,” says Taha. “They think the British population aren’t ready for it, and that people prefer brick. But if you look at the lists of the most popular towns and villages in the UK, it’s often Bath, Edinburgh, the Cotswolds. Guess what? They’re all made of stone.”

Webb is fiercely critical of the scourge of carbon-hungry bricks as the default. “Bricks are the heaviest form of decoration you can imagine,” he says. “They require a huge amount of energy to fire – often using coal – and they’re weak as shit. They put a lot of weight on the building’s frame, so the frame and the foundations have to get bigger, and they’re really inconvenient because they expand and contract, so you have to put movement joints everywhere. And they’re not holding anything up – it’s just really heavy and expensive wallpaper.”

In the last 10,000 years of building history, he argues, walls have held the floors up. But now we’ve got it back to front. “In the last 50 years or so, we’ve moved to floors holding the walls up,” he says, “which is utterly stupid.” He gestures out of the window of his office to a host of new high-rise blocks, where precast brick cladding panels are being craned on to concrete frames, each hefty piece of wall connected with steel brackets to the floor below. A stone-framed facade, however, can play the role of superstructure and cladding in one. It has a fraction of the embodied carbon, doesn’t move as much, and it’s cheaper. The slabs of Norwegian larvikite, for example, were rejects, of the kind usually used for motorway embankments.

British quarries are slowly catching up. Taha and Webb see the most potential in smaller-sized offcuts, which could be used in the same way as bricks and laid by regular bricklayers, without the need for stonemasonry expertise. They have put their ideas to the test in a remarkable “stone demonstrator house”, a temporary structure in Earl’s Court that showcases pre-tensioned stone beams and columns, stone floor slabs and a self-supporting stone brick facade.

Commissioned by the Design Museum’s Future Observatory research hub, it represents up to a 90% carbon saving compared to conventional construction. And for anyone wondering if there is enough stone to go around, Webb has a sobering fact. If all eight billion people on the planet decided to rebuild their homes in stone, the total volume required would be about the same as Ben Nevis.

Taha is busy on his next lithophilic project, a mixed-use development on the canal in Hackney using stone bricks and blocks, with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, making it “carbon negative”. Incorporating photovoltaic brise-soleil shading panels and a canal water source heat pump, he says the building will generate 135% of its energy needs. It will sell power back to the grid in the warmer months, offering a bill-free life across the year.

Webb, meanwhile, is working on a load-bearing stone option for a 200-metre tower near Liverpool Street, which he says would do away with the usual colossal concrete core and columns. Heavy, dark granite elements at the base could transition to lighter, thinner limestone pieces towards the top, expressing the structural loads on the facade, and using each kind of stone for what it does best.

“It’s a massive opportunity for architects to change it up – a reason to make a new style,” says Webb. “The first iron bridge in Telford was designed with timber-like connections, because that’s all we knew. Similarly, the first concrete buildings copied stone techniques. At the moment, we’re basically just reinterpreting concrete buildings, but using stone. We’ve shown that you can make stone trusses, stone grid-shells, really high-tech stone structures.” His eyes widen. “Imagine a future of stone electricity pylons everywhere!”

items.title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
paragraphs: A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids. That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm, citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”.

The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew, and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie.

Usually, storyboards are made together by a director, an artist and other crew members responsible for the film’s visual storytelling, such as cinematographers, editors, production designers, stunt co-ordinators and more. “I find it very fulfilling to make art in such a collaborative way,” says Alex Clark, a British storyboard artist whose recent films include Bong Joon Ho’s sci-fi comedy Mickey 17, adventure romance The Gorge and Louis Leterrier’s recent thriller The Last House. “It’s about people sitting down to discuss each other’s ideas. You might act things out, make sound effects, read dialogue. You develop a creative relationship with one another.”

For Clark, the process of creating a storyboard is just as important as the finished product. “A common misconception is that storyboarding is about making nice drawings. But it’s more than that – it’s about relating to how the director is thinking, and conceiving the most appropriate ways to tell the story of a scene,” he says. Dune director Denis Villeneuve articulated this relationship when describing his frequent collaborator, artist Sam Hudecki, as “an extension of my brain”. For Villeneuve, storyboarding is “a new way of writing”: writing a screenplay might provide the words, but storyboarding is the first step in creating the “cinematic language of the movie”. He views it as “a way to dream” as the film begins to come to life on the page.

Clark says that there is a balance that must be struck between “capturing the essence” of a scene and figuring out how the shots are going to work once the cameras are rolling. “The act of how you mark the page – to convey forms, tones, compositions, blocking and so on – forces you to thoroughly think about how all these different details will affect the scene. It gives you a rigorous understanding of how the scene is going to work.” Clark’s work reflects the fact that storyboarding is one step in an ongoing collaboration that continues through pre-production, shooting on set and beyond. “Sometimes I try to scale the drawings back, when it feels appropriate to leave space for others to build on it – whether it’s an actor’s performance, the way the set is decorated, lighting setup or subtle movement of the camera. I like finding space for happy accidents.”

For researchers and film enthusiasts, storyboard art offers a glimpse into the journey that lies behind a film, including fascinating changes in direction like this. “Storyboard art shows us the evolution of the creative vision,” says Ferdinando Cocco, a lecturer in film at Abertay university in Dundee. He points to Disney’s 1991 film Beauty and the Beast as an example: when it was first being worked on in the late 1980s, the storyboards had a rococo-inspired aesthetic, contemporary to the fairytale’s origins, styling Gaston as a bewigged 18th-century French aristocrat rather than the swollen, strong-jawed hunter who exemplified more modern ideals of masculinity.

As a film-making technique, the storyboard was first used regularly by Disney animators in the 1930s and and it plays a key role in their production process (as evidenced by displays of concept and storyboard art, and the side-by-side videos Disney posts online. (Disney also announced a $1bn investment into OpenAI’s video tool Sora last year.)

Storyboards were swiftly adopted by live-action productions, dating at least back to Gone With the Wind (1939). Since then, many film-makers have left behind storyboards that are beautiful and evocative images in themselves. Alfred Hitchcock created meticulously detailed storyboards, which spawned some of the genre’s most recognisable images: such as the shower scene in Psycho sketched beforehand by his frequent collaborator Saul Bass, the graphic designer behind many classic posters of the era. And before that, Hitchcock had worked with Salvador Dalí on surreal designs for the dream sequence in his 1945 film Spellbound.

Other directors, including Akira Kurosawa and Ridley Scott – whose storyboards are known as “Ridleygrams” – draw their own. Some of Bong’s self-drawn sketches are currently on display at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles, and his panels for Parasite have been published as a graphic novel. “Whenever I go to set without storyboards, I feel like I’m standing in the middle of Grand Central Terminal wearing only my underwear,” Bong writes in the book’s preface – however he does encourage the reader to see the differences between the storyboards and the film as “exciting moments of fear and spontaneity”.

Fan interest in behind-the-scenes material has created a market for storyboard books, while last year an exhibition devoted to storyboard art held in Milan displayed panels from films made by arthouse auteurs such as Ingmar Bergman and Federico Fellini, to artists Isaac Julien and Carrie Mae Weems, to Hollywood royalty – including Scorsese.

Creating engaging images is not without a practical function either, as storyboards are often pinned up on set to give the crew a sense of what will be shot that day. “I feel a responsibility to produce work that inspires and captivates everyone about what they’re making,” Clark says. “If the level of artistry and attention is evident at this stage, I believe it can set the tone on set, of valuing the craft involved.”

All hope is not yet lost. Cocco has observed a return to analogue practices and suggests that AI can be used in a way that fosters rather than dilutes the creative process. “Perhaps the difficulty that AI purportedly overcomes was the whole point from the start,” Cocco says. “Having to communicate with others forces an expansion of the artistic vision in ways that cannot be pre-empted.”

Clark meanwhile predicts that, as AI usage in the industry increases, people will come to have a greater appreciation for films with a human touch. “Ultimately, I think most successful films make you feel something as a human being. One advantage of hand-drawn storyboards is that you have a direct sense of that human authenticity right there on the page.”

items.title: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
paragraphs: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. “They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue. “Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … So no major drama.”

items.title: Viking legend informs ring-like viewpoint on Icelandic mountain ridge
paragraphs: Ring of Bjólfur is a mountain viewpoint in Iceland, designed by local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking.
Located in Seyðisfjörður, a fjord in eastern Iceland, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.
Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture‘s design draws on the legend of Bjólfur, an Icelandic Viking settler believed to have claimed this landscape and been laid to rest on the mountain.
Local lore says Bjólfur was buried on the mountain with his most precious belongings, though they have never been found. The viewpoint, therefore, evokes a ring that has been left for him.
“The medieval Book of Settlements, or Landnámabók, tells of Bjólfur, the settler who first claimed land in Seyðisfjörður and gave the mountain its name,” Arkibygg Architects told Dezeen.
“The book says little about him, but local tales tell that he was laid to rest in a burial mound high up on the mountain,” it continued.

“By ancient custom, chieftains were often buried with their treasures, silver and jewellery. Bjólfur’s grave goods have never been found, but we let our imagination run free and left him a great silver ring.”

Arkibygg Arkitektar and Esja Architecture won a competition to design Ring of Bjólfur in 2021. The project was shortlisted in the small projects category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and also won the public vote for the same category.
Ring of Bjólfur takes the form of a perfect circle, measuring 32 metres in diameter. While emulating a ring, this was also designed to “work with views in every direction”.

Positioned on a mountain ridge 650 metres above sea level, the structure was built from post-tensioned concrete with stainless steel railings, chosen for durability and for colours that emulate silver. It partially cantilevers on one side.
“The ring can be used in many ways, and the view changes depending on where you are in the circle – and whether you are standing or sitting,” said Arkibygg Arkitektar.

“The choice of materials grew from the idea of creating a silver ring, while also having to withstand wind and weather at 650 metres, with the structure being submerged in snow for parts of the year,” said the studio.
A major focus for the studios was ensuring accessibility, creating “an experience that everyone can enjoy, including wheelchair users”.

To achieve this, they designed accessible parking next to the ring as part of the project. Further general parking is located further downhill to encourage people who are physically able to walk to the platform.
“The project has been very well received, not only by visitors but just as much by local residents,” it continued.

“The ring is already strengthening tourism in the town, and it has also become part of residents’ daily lives, widely used for outdoor recreation. People walk, cycle or even ski up there to take in the view.”
The landscape surrounding the viewpoint was preserved as much as possible, with any boulders that needed to be temporarily removed lifted back into place upon completion.
“The immediate surroundings – the soil and the rocks – matter a great deal. The aim was to disturb the ground as little as possible and to repair what was disturbed.
“Other areas affected by the works were restored with native vegetation. Having one clear destination also keeps visitors from wandering across the fragile ridge.”
Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include an arrow-shaped structure in Denmark by Arup and the Lech Mountain Mirror by Snøhetta in Austria.

Architects: Arkibygg Architects and Esja ArchitectureStructural engineer: Exa NordicLandscape designer: Anna Kristín Guðmundsdóttir and Kjartan MogensenClient: Múlaþing MunicipalityConstruction: MVA Byggingarverktakar, EgilsstaðirFunding: Tourist Site Protection Fund

items.title: ZAV Architects extends house in Iran with ombre "architectural limbs"
paragraphs: A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.
Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.
ZAV Architects‘ intervention extends both ends of the home into three adjacent orchard plots acquired by the client.
Constructed from masonry, the extension is coated in plaster to blend in with the earthen exterior of the original home, while its curved geometries set it apart from its predecessor.
Aiming to appear as if organically growing from the home, Golmorad emerges as a series of overlapping arched roofs.

At one end, the vaulted extension branches into two curved forms that gradually decrease in height – one wing containing a bedroom and ensuite, and the other an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room that opens onto an outdoor pool.
Openings between the overlapping roof planes let light into the home’s interior.

“Rather than approaching the extension as either a replication of the original structure or a distinctly separate addition, the project explores a third possibility: an architecture that emerges from within the existing building itself,” ZAV Architects told Dezeen.

“This intervention can be understood as a process of grafting, in which new needs and aspirations are grafted onto the existing body of the villa, giving rise to new architectural limbs that branch out and grow from it,” it continued.
“It is as though the original building, while retaining its underlying architectural logic rooted in thick-earth construction, has developed new and distinct organs of its own.”
ZAV Architects created a gradient effect across the building with terracotta tones fading into blue, intending to strengthen the appearance of the extension growing from the home.
“The uniform colour of the original villa develops into a chromatic spectrum that radiates outward from the existing core towards the newly formed branches,” the studio said.
“This transition makes the process of transformation visible, with each segmented shell expressing a distinct stage in the building’s evolution.”
Golmorad is shortlisted in the house extension category of this year’s Dezeen Awards. It recently won the awards’ public vote alongside a playground also designed by ZAV Architects.

Last year, ZAV Architects was among the winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, a colourful domed cultural retreat on the Iranian island of Hormuz.
Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated

items.title: Primary Architects crowns carpenter's studio in rural China with undulating timber roof
paragraphs: Chinese studio Primary Architects has topped a carpenter’s studio in China with a sinuous timber roof that responds to the local mountain terrain.
Located at the entrance of Haotang Village, Xinyang, in China’s central Henan Province, the building belongs to Zhang, a local carpenter.
It was designed by Primary Architects to incorporate his studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

Primary Architects conceived of the project, called the Carpenter’s Home, as a lightweight timber structure nestled between the mountain and the village and aligned with the natural elevation of the terrain.
The 405-square-metre building sits at the foot of the mountain and is topped by a roof made up of hyperbolic curved beams that span up to 26 metres.
This sloping roof appears to gently descend from the mountainside and reconciles the elevation difference between the mountain and the village.
“The building responds to the rolling mountain terrain naturally by treating its roof as a gentle extension of the mountain ridge stretching into the village,” Primary Architects explained.
According to the studio, its undulating outline not only echoes the surrounding mountain terrain, but also forms a structural system that enables a flexible arrangement of internal spaces.
The roof’s structural system, which is comprised of glued timber and steel joints, was created through parametric control and digital modelling.
Prefabricated in a factory, the modular roof was assembled on site to improve construction efficiency.
Inside Carpenter’s Home, the ground floor houses the carpenter’s own woodworking shop as well as an area that is open to tourists and visitors, where exhibitions and tours are held.

A mezzanine floor has a tea room for visitors. Like the rest of the space, it is lit by a series of curved skylights that were incorporated into the timber-structured roof to introduce natural light into the interiors.
The angle of each skylight was carefully positioned in accordance with the movement of the sun to allow the interiors of the studio to be well-lit during working hours.
The open interiors were designed both to accommodate the traditional wood-working practice and to function as an education centre for the craft.
An expansive staircase that doubles as seating connects the studio space on the ground floor to the mezzanine tea room.
From here, visitors can observe Zhang’s working process, as well as his tools and material samples displayed on the side walls.
Primary Architects also created a series of working benches that can be combined and divided to support various aspects of the carpenter’s work.

“The Carpenter’s Home seeks to break through the existing formal paradigms of rural construction, responding to the land, craftsmanship and daily life in a more imaginative way,” said Primary Architects.

“With contemporary timber structure as its medium, it brings traditional woodworking back to rural daily life, making the building not only a space for accommodating activities, but also a continuously unfolding lifestyle,” it continued.
“For Haotang Village, it is not only a craft workshop, but also a timber vessel embodying local memory, artisan spirit and the vision of the future countryside.”
Primary Architects is a Beijing-based architecture studio founded by Xiang Huang in 2020. This project was shortlisted for workplace project (small) category at this year’s Dezeen Awards.
Elsewhere in China, Büro Ziyu Zhuang designed a museum cluster to “blend seamlessly” into a meadow, while RSHP completed a skyscraper in Shenzhen with a “striking butterfly layout”.

Chief architects: Xiang Huang, Songyan Mao Architectural design team: Cong Liu, Zhiyan Lin, Xiaoxia Wang, Junjie Liu, Xiaofeng Zhang, Yao Lu Grade A design institute: Zhongke Architectural Planning and Design Research Institute Wood structure detailed design: Bowen Li Construction company: Shanxi Junchen Construction Co., Ltd. Client: Xinyang Pingqiao District Juxing Agricultural Investment and Development Co., Ltd. Building area: 405 square meters

items.title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test
paragraphs: You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15%.

However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills.

When coupled with a standing desk, walking pads can be used while working – or when watching TV in the evening. Just a couple of 30-minute sessions add thousands of steps to your daily tally. In fact, a 60-minute walk at an easy 3km an hour can burn between 200 and 300 additional calories.
Walking pads are often cheaper than full-size treadmills, simple to use and relatively easy to store, and they’re perfect for adding more movement to your life without having to give up the day job.
Best walking pad overallUrevo SpaceWalk 5L smart walking pad
Best budget walking pad and best for beginnersBigzzia Walking pad with incline
Best lightweight walking padJTX MoveLight

I’m a keen fitness fan who does everything from gym-based strength training and kickboxing classes to outdoor trail runs and cold-water surfing. As a result, I’ve often been tasked with testing fitness technology for industry magazines, and I’m always keen to get stuck in.

I strongly believe that you need to live with new tech for a bit to grasp how it fits into daily life, so I aim to test products for as long as possible and in the right environment. With walking pads, that meant strolling along, racking up the steps and burning calories – even while I wrote up this feature.

There was only one way to properly trial the eight walking treadmills selected for this test, and that was to mimic the customer journey by ordering, taking delivery, unboxing, setting them up and then using them day to day.

The best walking treadmills – or walking pads – aren’t quite as bulky as regular running treadmills, so I could have multiple models on the go at home at once: one under my desk, one in front of the television and one in my wife’s office upstairs, testing each for at least three days.

The testing process involved a lot of additional steps and – in some cases at least – a whining soundtrack that drowned out whatever Netflix series the family was watching. Besides general observations on the heft, ease of storage and operation, quietness and build quality, I tested any additional features such as incline and speed adjustments, as well as any remote controls or apps.
To get a good idea of energy consumption and the overall cost of running a walking treadmill, I plugged each unit into a power meter to calculate the cost based on the October energy price cap.
Here are the four best walking pads you can buy now.
What we loveQuiet, sturdy and packed with genuinely useful app features

The Urevo SpaceWalk 5L is one of the most fully featured walking pads I’ve tested. It combines excellent build quality with a quiet motor, automatic incline and a great free companion app – which makes it feel more like a proper piece of fitness equipment than a basic under-desk treadmill. It’s slim enough to slide under a sofa when not in use, yet robust enough to cope with daily walking or even light jogging.

Why we love it Unlike most rivals, the SpaceWalk 5L’s accompanying app is genuinely useful. It allows you to record workouts and track steps, distance and walking time, while also offering structured walks with automatic incline adjustment.

The software also syncs with Apple Health, while the proprietary app lets you take part in a number of on-demand workouts, where incline and speed are controlled automatically. It also offers virtual walks, where you can take a sort of video tour of exotic locations. Unfortunately, it doesn’t feature the FTMS protocol that allows it to beam speed, cadence and incline data to a third-party app like Zwift. So your virtual avatar won’t move on the screen without a workaround such as a third-party, cadence-sensing footpod or compatible smartwatch.

It is one of the quietest walking pads I’ve tested, though. At my preferred 2.5km/h working/walking pace, the motor averaged just 48dB – barely louder than my keyboard as I was furiously typing up this review.

Build quality is also noteworthy. The weighty, front-mounted motor gives it a reassuringly solid feel, while adjustable feet make levelling on uneven floors easy. Its claimed 12-point shock absorption system also provides enough cushioning for walking in just socks, although I’d still recommend trainers for longer sessions.
The incline, which can be automatically controlled when using Urevo’s app, adds another dimension for anyone aiming to increase the intensity of their walks.
Energy use is impressively low, too. At a comfortable 2.5km/h, the SpaceWalk 5L drew around 40W during testing, costing roughly 1p an hour based on the 1 October electricity price cap.
At its 6km/h maximum speed, this rose to about 3p an hour, with the incline motor briefly drawing more power when adjusting the deck.

While 6km/h is no more than a brisk walk or gentle jog, the SpaceWalk 5L feels stable throughout. It doesn’t fold, but its slim design and the integrated wheels make it easy to roll under a bed or sofa for storage.
It’s a shame that … the incline functionality makes it slightly bulkier than the simplest ultra-slim walking pads.
Size: 124 x 51.5 x 15.5cm (LWH) Weight: 23kg Walking deck size: 40 x 100cm Maximum user weight: 181kg Incline: 0-9% automatic Maximum speed: 6km/h Folding: no
What we loveQuiet, sturdy and packed with genuinely useful app features
What we loveA very cheap pad with a surprisingly high top speed
What we don’t loveShort deck, noisy motor and basic controls

The Bigzzia is very much a budget walking pad, and it shows. The construction is basic, the running deck is narrow and short, and the display is hardly sophisticated. But it’s remarkably cheap and has a surprisingly high 10km/h top speed and a manual incline setting.

Why we love it The Bigzzia’s biggest selling point is that 10km/h maximum speed. That’s considerably faster than most under-desk walking pads, and means it can double as a basic treadmill for walking and light jogging.
However, the deck is so short that running at anything approaching its maximum speed feels unnerving. I’d be much happier using it for walking or, at most, very short bursts of jogging.

The running surface has a surprisingly good grip, but there’s little flex or meaningful cushioning underneath, making longer sessions uncomfortable. It’s better suited to shorter walks than all-day use.

It does come with an 8% incline, although this isn’t a motorised function. You simply flip out two feet at the sides and put the supplied rubber supports underneath them to raise the deck. No range of settings here.

The simple display shows the basics: speed, calories, time and distance, automatically cycling between the figures as you walk. There isn’t really a way to lock it to any particular metric – another reminder that this is a very simple machine.
Interaction is equally basic – via a small wireless remote control. Lose or break it, though, and you’ll be stuck. You also need to supply the AAA batteries for it.

For portability, however, the Bigzzia shines. At just 12.86kg, it is light enough to pick up and carry, something I can’t say about many of the walking pads here. It also has a couple of small wheels at the front, so you can tip it and wheel it around if you prefer. And while the short deck might prove a drawback for running, it’s great for storage: it slides easily under a sofa or can be stored upright against a wall.

Noise is another compromise, however. Walking at 2.5km/h, I measured about 52dB, with a noticeable whine and plenty of foot thump from the deck. It’s not disastrous for a walking pad at this price, but it’s certainly more obvious than the best machines I’ve tested.

Power consumption is also higher than that of some rivals. I measured 54W at 2.5km/h (about 1p an hour at the UK electricity rates at the time of writing) and 166W at its 10km/h top speed (about 4p an hour). Running costs remain low overall, but it’s less energy efficient than some more sophisticated walking pads.

Another omission worth knowing about is the lack of an automatic stop function. That means the motor will continue running if you fall or simply walk away, so you need to be a little more careful about how you use it.
It’s a shame that … it’s let down by the short deck, noisy motor and basic controls, but it’s one of the cheapest walking pads out there.
Size: 104 x 49 x 11cm (LWH) Weight: 12.86kg Walking deck size: 37 x 90cm Maximum user weight: 130kg Incline: 0 or 8% manual Maximum speed: 10km/h Folding: no
What we loveA very cheap pad with a surprisingly high top speed
What we don’t loveShort deck, noisy motor and basic controls
What we loveGreat build quality and crisp display
What we don’t loveIt’s heavy and awkward to move around

JTX often appears in the “best value” section of home fitness equipment reviews, known for offering reliable build quality at affordable prices, but its machines tend to prioritise function over flashy design and cutting-edge technology.

The MoveLight walking pad is different, however. It’s the most expensive walking pad in this roundup, and there’s a tangible difference in the build quality compared with cheaper walking pads. The JTX also offers a sizeable display, cushioned walking deck and quiet 1hp electric motor. It’s a solid treadmill offering speeds of up to 6km/h, meaning it’s possible to use it for slow jogging without the worry of it falling apart.

Why we love it The MoveLight is similar in design to the BodyMax reviewed below and has a solid plastic chassis that gives it a more premium feel than its cheaper rivals. The running deck is generously sized and well cushioned, making longer walking sessions more comfortable.

The extra-large LED console is easy to use and neatly scrolls through speed, time and step count as you walk. The shrill beeps upon startup and when you adjust the speed may cause office mates to want to throw a pencil at you, however.
With the small plastic remote, you can adjust the speed, stop or start the unit and scroll the display between distance, calories and time on one half, and speed and step count on the other.
The 1hp motor is powerful enough to propel the deck up to 6km/h, where it remains much quieter than some of the others tested.

Overall, it feels like a walking pad that will go the distance – and so it should, given the price – but that solid build does make it a pain to move around the house; it will require some serious muscle to tip it up on to its wheels. It also doesn’t fold like the BodyMax machine.
Oh, and one final public service announcement: those with wooden floors will want to take care that the wheels and plastic feet don’t scratch the surface during transport.
During testing, I found it to be slightly more power-hungry than rivals, supping about 100W at 3.5km/h, meaning it costs about 3p an hour to power.
It’s a shame that … it’s so big and heavy to move around, which makes storing it after each session a chore.
Size: 147 x 60 x 12.5cm (LWH) Weight: 29.5kg Walking deck size: 45 x 122cm Maximum user weight: 100kg Incline: none Maximum speed: 6km/h Folding: no
What we loveGreat build quality and crisp display
What we don’t loveIt’s heavy and awkward to move around
Prefer to sit while you work? We’ve also reviewed the best office chairs
What we loveGenuinely foldable with an excellent walking experience

One of the most expensive models on test, the BodyMax walking pad is also one of the best built and easiest on the eye. It’s the only model that genuinely folds in half, making it easier to squeeze into a cupboard or wardrobe.
However, at around 30kg, it’s not the easiest to move, despite wheels at the front that allow it to be tipped on its end and rolled around.

Potential portability issues aside, this machine offers a fantastic walking experience, with a neat, bright and easy-to-read LED panel that gives clear and scrolling readouts of workout time, distance, speed and average calorie burn.
Very much the Porsche of the walking pad world, the BodyMax unit combines stylish looks and powerful performance.
Why we love it Like most walking pads here, the BodyMax comes with a remote for adjusting speed, but its clever A Mode goes a step further, using foot placement to automatically adjust the pace.

Stay in the middle, and it maintains pace; walk towards the front to speed up or hang back to slow down. It’s a useful touch that saves you constantly fiddling with the remote. The deck itself is nicely cushioned, and the motor is among the quietest on test.

Those wanting their walking pad to double up as a running treadmill may be disappointed, however: the WP60 tops out at 6km/h, which is a very fast walking pace but a slow jog for most. Not a single walking pad I’ve tested has done a convincing job as a running treadmill, though, being either too flimsy underfoot, too noisy, or simply not built to withstand the endless thumping of a sprint session.
If you’re seeking robust build quality, the BodyMax WP60 walking pad is well worth the additional outlay. As it folds in half, it can be tucked under a desk or rested against a wall when not in use.
It’s a shame that … it’s heavy and awkward to move around when folded.
Size: 143 x 55 x 13cm (LWH) Weight: 28kg Walking deck size: 42 x 120cm Maximum user weight: 100kg Incline: none Maximum speed: 6km/h Folding: yes, folds in half for storage
What we loveGenuinely foldable with an excellent walking experience

The biggest difference between walking pads, aside from overall build quality, is their top speed. Most max out at about 6km/h, which is ideal for walking while working at a standing desk or a brisk stroll in front of the TV. If you’re hoping to jog as well, look for models that reach 8-10km/h – although be aware that you’ll generally sacrifice some stability and comfort compared with a full-size treadmill.

Next comes incline. Premium models tend to offer a motorised incline function that can be adjusted at the touch of a button, while cheaper alternatives rely on manually extending support feet for a fixed gradient. Even a small incline can noticeably increase calorie burn and make walks feel more challenging.

Also pay attention to the size of the walking deck. A longer, wider belt will feel far more comfortable and safer, particularly if you’re tall or have a long stride. Finally, think about practicalities such as noise, storage, transport wheels, companion apps and maximum user weight. If you plan to use your walking pad for several hours a day while working from home, spending a little more on a quieter, sturdier model is usually money well spent.

Prices vary when it comes to walking pads, with the most affordable costing about £90. Anything less than that is unlikely to be long-lasting. From my testing, the sweet spot seems to be about £250, where you can get a good blend of value and decent build quality. Some of the best I tested were, predictably, among the most expensive. These high-end models typically cost about £500.

If you’ve got good clearance underneath a bed or sofa, most walking pads will happily slide underneath without the need to fold them up. Imagine a slimmed-down treadmill without the safety handle, and you’re basically there.

Models such as the BodyMax WP60 fold in half, which drastically reduces the length (or height, depending on how you store it), making them much easier to slide into more compact spaces such as a cupboard or wardrobe. But bear in mind they can weigh up to 30kg, so they can be tricky to move without help.

Most walking pads come with a small bottle of silicone oil. This is used to lubricate the underside of the walking belt every couple of months to ensure smooth movement, depending on use. Most manufacturers also supply the required hex key so you can adjust the belt if it’s slipping or has moved slightly off-centre.
Quickly check the belt alignment and any moving parts every couple of months, and it should be enough to keep a walking pad running smoothly for years.

Some walking pad speeds are capped at about 6km/h, which makes running on them tricky. A plodding jog is a better description. A few of the walking pads I tested did reach much higher speeds, and most of these came with a folding safety handle that extends to allow them to safely reach those speeds, giving the runner something to hang on to should the worst happen. These also came with a separate safety system: a small magnetic tag that attaches to clothing. If this becomes detached, the machine shuts off.

The general build and robustness of walking pads aren’t up there with their running-focused counterparts, though. That means they can be noisy, shift around underfoot and generally feel a bit flimsy during faster and longer runs. On top of this, those without handles don’t always have the automatic shut-off functionality, which can make them more dangerous, particularly when using them at higher speeds.

In summary, running treadmills are better suited to those wanting to move at higher speeds. They feature more underfoot cushioning or built-in suspension systems, which make longer, faster sessions more comfortable and easier on the joints.

In most cases, yes, but it depends on both the walking pad and the type of carpet. Most manufacturers recommend using a walking pad on a hard, level surface as this provides the best stability and allows air to circulate around the motor. Thick, plush carpets can restrict airflow, increasing the risk of overheating, while also making the machine less stable underfoot.

If carpet is your only option, a low-pile carpet is usually fine, especially with a treadmill mat underneath. This helps spread the load more evenly, protects the carpet from compression and reduces vibration travelling through the floor.

Regardless of the surface, ensure enough clearance around the machine for safe use and so that the belt runs freely without rubbing. It’s also worth checking underneath every so often to remove dust and fluff, especially if you have pets, as debris can build up around the motor and rollers over time.

Maximum user weight isn’t just about whether a walking pad can physically support you – it’s also an indication of how robust the frame, motor and deck are. Choosing a model with a higher weight capacity can often mean a more stable, longer-lasting machine.

Beyond that, look for an emergency stop function or safety key if you intend to jog. Some walking pads automatically stop the belt if they detect you’ve stepped off, while others continue running until you turn them off manually. As I found during testing, not every budget model includes this feature, so check before you buy.

A wide, grippy walking surface also improves confidence, particularly if you’re working at a standing desk, while decent shock absorption can reduce fatigue during longer sessions. Finally, ensure the walking pad has non-slip feet and is sitting securely before every use, as even slight movement can become distracting or unsafe – not to mention damaging to expensive wooden floors.

Although they look similar, walking pads and treadmills are designed for different purposes. Walking pads prioritise compact size, low noise and easy storage, with many slim enough to slide under a sofa or bed. They’re primarily designed for walking rather than running, making them ideal for staying active while you work or watch TV.

Traditional treadmills are larger, heavier and more versatile. They typically offer higher top speeds, wider and longer running decks, better cushioning and features such as adjustable incline, heart rate monitoring and structured workout programmes. Their larger belts also make them far better suited to regular running.

The trade-off is space. If your goal is simply to increase your daily step count or stay active while working from home, a walking pad is usually the more practical choice. But for race training or more serious fitness goals, a conventional treadmill remains the better investment.

Leon Poultney has been traversing the worlds of consumer technology and automotive for some of the biggest lifestyle websites and magazines for longer than he cares to divulge. A lifelong fitness enthusiast, he can often be found trying not to injure himself on a mountain bike/surfboard/other extreme thing, often at the request of an editor. Whether it is getting to know the latest connected kettlebells or partaking in CrossFit sessions, Leon is always willing to put his body on the line for great editorial
