items.title: UN: 700 healthcare facilities expected to close in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The U.N. says that more than 40 percent of primary healthcare facilities, about 700 of Afghanistan’s 1,900 health posts, are expected to close between 2025 and 2026.

The consequences are “very, very, very significant,” said Bruno Lemarquis, the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Afghanistan and the U.N.’s Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in the country, on Friday in a press conference in New York City. “The consequences could go beyond the Afghanistan border, potentially affecting regional security, regional stability and migration pathways.”
According to the U.N., humanitarian funding to Afghanistan has dropped from $2 billion in 2023 to $570 million so far in 2026.
Afghanistan under the Taliban has been facing one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises.
The U.N. said last week that about 15.9 million people in Afghanistan, about one-third of the population, face serious food insecurity and acute malnutrition.

UNICEF said the humanitarian situation in Afghanistan remains critical, driven by worsening food insecurity and malnutrition, outbreaks of diseases, the return of millions of Afghans from neighboring countries and recurring climate disasters.
“Funding shortfalls and pressure on essential services further compounded humanitarian needs, particularly among children, women, returnees and disaster-affected communities,” the UNICEF report said.
Lemarquis called the restrictions on women and girls in Afghanistan, “severe and sweeping,” depriving women and girls of learning, work and participating in public life.
Claudio Miglietta, country representative of Doctors Without Borders or MSF, told VOA that the restrictions on women and girls have an impact on healthcare access in the country.

“Access to care is becoming more difficult in many places. What matters is not only whether a health facility exists, but whether a woman can actually get there; whether she can afford the trip; ... whether there is a female health worker available when she arrives,” Miglietta said.
He added that although healthcare in Afghanistan is still functioning, it is under considerable pressure.
“Growing pressure from funding reductions weakened public services, high humanitarian needs, and continued dependence on humanitarian actors to sustain essential services,” he said.

Miglietta said that hospitals and medical facilities remain among the few places where women can access essential healthcare, “so simply keeping these services available, functional and accessible matters enormously.”

items.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
paragraphs: For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.

But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair.

Initially, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader.
Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton.

Spencer, for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan.

In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation.

“This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”
Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board.

“The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.”

Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said.

“Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.”

Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate.

Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly.
Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value.

“When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. “It’s not just a question of romance or morality any more. It’s a question of judgment, national security exposure, shareholder trust, and whether the person at the top can be relied on to protect the enterprise.”
In a statement, Nvidia’s board said they do not believe either national security or company secrets were compromised but they will “examine all available information.”
“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” the board said in a statement.

items.title: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
paragraphs: In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.

There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.
France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.

It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.

Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.
Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.

Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.
“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.

The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.

However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

items.title: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined.

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

OK, but legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

items.title: Birds return to waterfowl park after oil vandalism
paragraphs: The birds (pictured previously) have returned to the park after being cared for by the USPCA
Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.
The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised, causing the oil spill into the pond.
In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.
The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nenes.
Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.
The birds returned to the park on Monday morning
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil or kerosene.
Police said about 44 gallons (200 litres) of oil had leaked from the tank which had been damaged at a business premise in the Main Street area of Broughshane.
Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.
"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.
He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.
Gary Hayward said the USPCA were a "great help" at looking after the birds
The USPCA has also been a key part of the rescue operation.
They said that all of the birds, including geese, ducks and swans, needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.
Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.
Several birds were injured after the incident
The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.
"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."
It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.
"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."
Police have said that enquiries into the incident are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to come forward.

items.title: 'I've got a band now' - Club anthem star Shygirl on why she's switching up her sound
paragraphs: Shygirl is known for big dance bangers, but her latest album has a more stripped-back sound
Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.
But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.
Shygirl hasn't totally left her electronic roots behind though.
You can still hear the sweat-soaked energy of Charli XCX's 365 remix and relentless pulse of 2024 hit mr useless on her latest record.
But there's also guitar strums, heartfelt songwriting and a dreamy haze, giving it an indie edge.
"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.
"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."
Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.
Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".
"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.
Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.
Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.
The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.
"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."
The album's artwork shows a chick hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth
There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.
She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.
But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.
"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.
"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."
That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.
It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".
Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.
"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.
"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."
Shygirl's the latest artist known for electronic music who's embraced a more organic sound.
Her close friend Charli XCX featured a rockier, guitar-driven style on her latest album Music, Fashion, Film.
One of the standout tracks on that album for Shygirl is SS26, because "her voice is so natural and exposed".
"You forget other people don't know that voice and they need to get to know that starting point to be able to appreciate everything else."
Shygirl believes that same stripped-back approach is shaping much of the current wave of British dance music, including her latest album.
"There's so many of us now, especially coming from the Brit pack, that are doing the same thing," she says.
Shygirl's friend Charli XCX introduced drums and guitars for her latest album
Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".
"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.
"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."
So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?
For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.
"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."
Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

items.title: Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?
paragraphs: Student Ma Yeonwoo, center, raises his hand during a Great Books summer camp seminar about Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein at the Toegye elementary school in the city of Chuncheon. Teacher Han Kyoung-min, to Ma's right, leads the discussion. Anthony Kuhn/NPR hide caption

CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein.
"I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.
The Toegye school has adopted the "Great Books" educational model used by St. John's College, whose main campus is in Annapolis, Md.
The class's discussion then shifts to whether artificial intelligence is human.
"No," Ma Yeonwoo responds, because humans created AI, and although it is intelligent, it "has no creativity."

In the "Great Books" model, teachers do not lecture, they only guide discussions. There are no majors or elective courses. Students do not seek answers from outside sources such as the internet and rely only on their readings, their own reasoning and class discussions with their peers.
That suits Ma Yeonwoo, who says he enjoys debating with his classmates.
"If only the teacher talks we can have one idea, but if we all debate together, like, we can get many ideas together," he says.

This nascent educational movement addresses several concerning trends. One is that international tests such as PISA have shown a post-COVID drop in South Korean reading skills, after decades in which South Korean and other East Asian students outperformed their American counterparts.

Another is South Korea's rapid adoption of AI in education. 51% of South Korean students say they use AI chatbots to study at least once a week, according to Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) figures. Students also face intense competition to pass college entrance exams, which piles pressure on them down to the pre-K school level and prompts many South Korean families to send their children to cram schools to gain a competitive edge, or to foreign schools to escape the system.

Incheon National University Professor Lee Yonghwa (center) guides a Great Books summer camp seminar at Chuncheon High School. Lee, a St. John's College graduate, established South Korea's first Great Books program at his university in 2019. Anthony Kuhn/NPR hide caption

"We all feel that this system leaves students with no time to read and think," because they're too busy memorizing facts to pass tests," says Lee Yonghwa, a professor of English language and literature at Incheon National University, where he co-founded South Korea's first "Great Books" program in 2019.
But now, Lee laments, "Korean students are even losing their old capacity to memorize facts because they collect facts and ideas mainly from A.I."
And if they can't reason and think independently, he adds, they can't judge the quality of the results that AI generates for them.
The limitations of their educational system motivates many South Koreans to look for alternatives, from education overseas, to educational experiments at home.

"As someone who went through this system, I felt those limitations keenly," Chuncheon Mayor Yook Dong-han said in an interview at city hall. "When I became mayor, I wanted to introduce a different kind of education and a distinct educational philosophy to the city of Chuncheon."
Chuncheon draws visitors from neighboring Seoul to enjoy its mountains, lakes and rivers, and dakgalbi, a local dish of grilled or stir-fried marinated chicken.
Chuncheon's government established an academic partnership with St. John's College last year to promote the "Great Books" educational model.
There are now 120 college students and some 770 younger students taking the "Great Books" program in South Korea, and 40 teachers in training, according to Lee Yonghwa.

Although the program is still in its infancy, Yook says it represents a "small but revolutionary achievement — a breakthrough that challenges established practices," and generated interest among participating students that has exceeded his expectations.
South Korean students following the "Great Books" model read Aristotle, Shakespeare, Euclid, and Korean authors including Nobel laureate Han Kang.
Student Shin Donghyun reads from Martin Luther King, Jr's. Letter from a Birmingham Jail at a Great Books summer camp seminar at Chuncheon High School. Anthony Kuhn/NPR hide caption
In one Chuncheon high school, students read Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 Letter from Birmingham Jail.
They discuss King's ideas about what kind of laws are just and unjust, and which laws citizens should obey or disobey.

Lee Yonghwa says he's impressed that students connected King's letter to their own country, such as in 2024, when citizens and lawmakers defeated former President Yoon Suk Yeol's attempt to put South Korea under martial law.

That fits the purpose of the "Great Books" model, in which "each seminar table really becomes a miniature republic, where ideas clash but people cooperate," St. John's College President J. Walter Sterling wrote last year in an opinion essay.
Through civic participation and liberal education, he adds, "we quietly stitch the fabric of our democracy…before it unravels beyond repair."
NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Chuncheon and Seoul.

items.title: Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
paragraphs: Sen. Jon Tester, D-Mont., speaks during a hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, on May 2, 2023. Andrew Harnik/Associated Press hide caption

Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for the industry's ties with the Trump administration when they take over Congress in January. In anticipation, many are hiring former Democratic lawmakers and aides to make their case to the incoming House and Senate majorities.
Among the latest to make that move is Palantir, which has hired former Sen. Jon Tester, a colorful Montana Democrat who's also an organic farmer.
"My agreement with Palantir is advisory in nature, it is not lobbying," Tester, who lost reelection to the Senate in 2024, told NPR in an interview.

The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term. Palantir — named by billionaire founder Peter Theil after the mythical "seeing stone" from J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings — has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants.

"Perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general," said Tester. "But the fact is, I think Palantir has got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it."

Palantir has long denied claims it aids mass surveillance on the American public — saying it doesn't gather or manipulate data at all, but instead creates tools for government agencies and private companies to organize and optimize their own information. The company has said it is committed to "protecting privacy and upholding liberal democratic values."

Earlier this year, while in the minority, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., along with 30 other Democratic lawmakers demanded answers about Palantir's contracts with the Department of Homeland Security and whether its tools are part of efforts by the federal government to surveil Americans. Palantir denied the accusation and said it is "neither conducting nor enabling mass surveillance of American citizens," but Wyden wasn't fully satisfied with its response, according to his Senate office.

"Senator Wyden has a number of questions about Palantir's work to facilitate the Trump-Vance abuse of government data that he intends to ask again as chairman of the Finance Committee," Wyden's staff wrote in a statement to NPR. "If Palantir is not responsive next year, compulsory processes will be on the table."
It's not a coincidence that tech companies are turning to Democrats to help burnish their reputation, said Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former State Department official.
"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Ibrahim said.
During Trump's second term, Palantir's CEO and co-founder Alex Karp — a self-described liberal — has been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration and AI.

"I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope many," Karp said in an interview with Axios in 2025 specifically referencing his support for much more restrictive immigration policies. "You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private."

During his 18 years in the Senate, Tester was an outspoken critic of the PATRIOT Act that passed shortly after the 9/11 attacks that expanded the Justice Department's surveillance powers. When asked whether his concerns over government surveillance remain and whether he has the same concerns with his new employer, Tester said Palantir is different and that the company doesn't build "big databases" or trade in private data.

"I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy."

Last year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products.

Valued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.
Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.
The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment."

"It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward."

items.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's alleged relationship with Chinese spy
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6034057/nx-s1-9996878" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Chipmaker Nvidia is launching an investigation of its CEO Jensen Huang after news reports he had an affair with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for Beijing.
The most valuable company in the world is investigating its own CEO.

Nvidia is a designer of computer chips for AI. And it's looking into its leader Jensen Huang. The question is whether he left himself open to spying by China. Nvidia produces some of the world's most sophisticated chips, leading to constant debate about whether they should be sold to China.
FADEL: NPR tech correspondent John Ruwitch is here to tell us more. Good morning, John.
FADEL: So why did Nvidia launch this investigation?

RUWITCH: Yeah. The board was following up on reports not yet confirmed by NPR that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was recruited by China's main spy agency to gather information on him and potentially to try to influence U.S. policy. Nvidia did not mention China in its announcement online of the investigation. But it did say the spark for this was reporting that Huang was, quote, "the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

The company also posted a memo that Huang sent to staff at Nvidia admitting to having an affair and apologizing for it. In the memo, he said he supports the board's investigation and will fully cooperate. Now, for China's part, they've said that the allegations are unsubstantiated.
FADEL: Now, we don't cover many stories about allegations of corporate espionage. Explain why Nvidia and Huang are different.

RUWITCH: Yeah. There's two huge reasons. No. 1 is that Nvidia is a linchpin of the U.S. economy. It's one of the biggest companies in the world. And right now, it's at the heart of the AI revolution. It makes the most widely used microchips to train and run AI. The second reason that this is a big deal is that Jensen Huang has enjoyed extraordinary access to the president of the United States. They talk on the phone. He even traveled to China with President Trump in May aboard Air Force One.
Now, according to news reports, Trump was briefed on intelligence about Huang's relationship over a year ago. And yesterday he was asked by a reporter if in hindsight, he should have acted on it.
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER #1: ...Briefed about...
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: No, I don't think so.
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER #1: ...The spying last year?
TRUMP: I think - you know, I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it, you know. And you have to hear it.
FADEL: What has Huang's stance been on the AI race with China?

RUWITCH: Yeah. The U.S. restricts exports of certain kinds of cutting-edge chips to China, including Nvidia's best microchips. And Jensen Huang has made the argument that if we let China buy these chips, they would get hooked. Their own chip-making industry will develop more slowly, and that that would be good for America. Samuel Bresnick of Georgetown University, though, says the spy allegations just raise a raft of questions about what Huang has said.

SAMUEL BRESNICK: It calls into question the - that entire approach. It calls into question, you know, was he acting in the best interests of the United States to a certain degree, right? Has he compromised U.S. national security because of this relationship?
RUWITCH: And I will note that the Trump administration has loosened some of the chip export controls, and some previously restricted Nvidia chips can now be sold to China.
FADEL: What does this mean for Nvidia as the investigation moves along?

RUWITCH: A spokesperson said the investigation will not slow Nvidia down and that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company. So he's still in charge. In its statement online, the company said the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised. But this issue does seem to be snowballing. Last week, members of the House of Representatives made a request for Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman who's at the center of this whole thing.
FADEL: NPR's John Ruwitch. Thank you, John.

items.title: Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin
paragraphs: The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.
The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.
Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.

The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.
"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."
On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service, external confirmed that October was the hottest on record.
But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday, external, and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.
It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".

items.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
paragraphs: The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."
He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."
Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.
Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.
He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.
"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."
With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.
It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version, external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said, external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.
Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.

items.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
paragraphs: A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.

John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.
"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.
"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

items.title: The Silicon Valley superstar engulfed by personal scandal
paragraphs: ByLily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondent and Peter HoskinsBusiness reporter
Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.
He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.
As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.
The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.
Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.
"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".
Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.
Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.
Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.
Huang is commonly referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan where he was born
Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.
The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.

"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recongnised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."
Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.

"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."
Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".
Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.
Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.
They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.
He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.
Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.
"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," says Witt.

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia. Spencer and Maddison. The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
Huang for his part released a statement which said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
US officials had concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reports.

She was a top executive at Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.
"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.
Additional reporting by Ayeshea Perera in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

items.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least four
paragraphs: At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

items.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
paragraphs: African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

items.title: Google, Meta and TikTok sue to block California youth social media law
paragraphs: Google, Meta, and TikTok have sued California to block the enforcement of a state law meant to protect children from getting addicted to social media.

items.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
paragraphs: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegations
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."
That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after the BBC's Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.
The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.
None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.
Shona Manderson appeared on the 2023 series of Married at First Sight UK
Shona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard.
"Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.
Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.
Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.
One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part.
April Banbury took part in the 2023 series of MAFS UK
Others we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.

They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false".
"I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us.

"Cancelling the show does not make what happened go away," added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place."
Others writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.

Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".
A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.

Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show.

"I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said. "Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."
As the dust settles, there are still many questions.
Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4’s review has been released, rather than the full report.
We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company.
Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm?
We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out.

In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review “did not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authorities”.
Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.
It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.
Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.
Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.
The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.
If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course” - then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.
Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.
And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

items.title: North Korea’s Binance hack raises global financial security concerns
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

Cybersecurity experts tell VOA that the recent North Korean hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange is particularly concerning because of the speed of both the attack, and how quickly the hackers moved the assets through financial networks.

Michael Barnhart, lead nation-state threat researcher at California-based cybersecurity company DTEX, told VOA that “one of the most significant aspects of the Binance incident was the speed at which the stolen funds were transferred."
"Rather than holding onto the cryptocurrency, the attackers moved it to Chinese money launderers within minutes," he said.

More than $6.3 billion worth of virtual assets were stolen from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and “about $2.8 billion was frozen before it could be fully laundered or integrated into North Korean control,” Barnhart said. Some $3.5 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency remains in circulation, and efforts to trace and freeze the funds are continuing.

Nick Carlsen is a senior Investigator at TRM Labs who spent 12 years as an intelligence analyst at the FBI initiating major U.S. investigations into North Korea's illicit financial networks. He told VOA in a recent interview the speed and scale of the response to the hack “were unprecedented." He said stablecoin issuers and industry partners moved quickly to freeze substantial assets, but recovering the remaining funds will be difficult because laundering methods have become increasingly complex.

"The stolen funds appeared to have been divided into tens of thousands of transactions, many of them seemingly automated, making them harder to trace," Carlsen said, noting that he expects a substantial portion of the proceeds will ultimately reach the North Korean government, “although the final amount that can be recovered remains uncertain."

Large cryptocurrency exchanges face security challenges because of their size and global reach. Carlsen said exchanges “with thousands of employees have numerous potential entry points for hackers." He said companies handling large amounts of financial assets therefore need multiple layers of security, so that a single compromised account or system cannot expose their holdings.

Analysts also point to the financial objectives behind North Korea’s cyber operations. While Russia and China have often focused on espionage, including the theft of sensitive information and industrial technology, North Korea has increasingly used cyber operations to generate revenue.

“Cybercrime and cryptocurrency theft have become the North Korean government’s largest single source of foreign currency," he said. "The proceeds can be used for a range of government activities, including potentially supporting the country’s nuclear and missile programs."
Barnhart said North Korea has little reason to stop targeting cryptocurrency exchanges.

Previous attacks on platforms including Axie Infinity and Bybit, followed by the Binance breach, show that the sector remains an attractive target. The financial returns remain substantial, while the risks to the North Korean government are comparatively limited.
Both experts said stronger corporate cybersecurity measures are necessary but insufficient to address the threat.
Barnhart argued that “companies can do only so much to defend themselves against repeated attacks without a policy response."
"Governments, particularly the United States and South Korea, must take a more active role in responding to North Korea’s cyber theft operations," added Carlsen.

The Binance breach is part of a series of major cryptocurrency thefts attributed to North Korea. While exchanges continue to strengthen their defenses, the experts say a broader response from governments will be needed to disrupt the networks that move and launder stolen funds.
